Ms. Nakamura lived three doors down from the pharmacy, and as the three of them left she was coming out with her recycling, so Alexis, feeling bold, told her the whole thing, the drawer, the run, the five minutes, the lower number. She listened without interrupting, which he appreciated, and then asked him what diet and exercise had to do with it, and he said, slowly, assembling it as he spoke, that if the numbers shifted within an hour then they could shift over months too, that the reading was less a sentence and more a running commentary, and that his father's salt habit and coat-rack bike were both talking to that machine whether he listened or not. Ms. Nakamura said she'd save him the first week of the term, then, and Ruth said "he beguiled the machine into mercy, that's his whole method," and Alexis admitted the five quiet minutes did feel a bit like charming a small stubborn god.

He still didn't know what his father's actual baseline was, or whether one lower reading after sitting still meant anything at all about anyone's long-term health, and he was honest with himself about that hole in the middle of his knowledge. But that evening he cleared the bike of coats, set it facing the window, and put the cuff machine on the kitchen table where his father would see it at breakfast. Then he sat down across from the empty chair, feet flat on the floor, and waited, watching the second hand on the stove clock make its slow judicious circle.

Nicola had claimed the corner table by the window of the Bean Counter before Madison even got through the door, which was unfair, since Madison had texted first. The place smelled like burnt espresso and pumpkin, that desperate autumnal pumpkin that arrived earlier every year, and Nicola was guarding two cups with the posture of a woman defending a fort.

"You're late," Nicola said. "Your cocoa is getting a skin."

"I've been thinking about my ballot." Madison sat down hard enough to slosh her own cup. "It came in the mail yesterday. My actual ballot. My name, misspelled, on an official envelope."

"Thrilling."

"It is thrilling. It's the first one. You get one first one."

Nicola rolled her eyes, a mannerism she'd been polishing since seventh grade until it had achieved a kind of fluent, dismissive elegance, like a fencer's parry. "It's a municipal election, Madi. It's a school board and a drainage levy and a woman who wants to be county clerk."

"Democracy is not a spectator sport," Madison said, in her best imitation of Ms. Qureshi, their civics teacher, who said it so often that the whole class could perform it.

"Democracy is a drainage levy," Nicola said.

"You know what my grandfather said at dinner?" Madison leaned in. "He said when he was eighteen, he couldn't vote. Eighteen. Drafted into a whole war, no say in anything. I thought he was being grumpy, but I looked it up and it's true. They fixed it with the Twenty-Sixth Amendment. That's the one that set the voting age at eighteen."

"Congratulations on your amendment."

"In 1971. And here's the part that killed me. It was ratified in about three months. Faster than any other amendment. The whole country pulled that off before summer."

Nicola frowned into her cocoa. "That's it? That's the slowest thing America ever did quickly?"

"It took forever to get started and then went like lightning," Madison said. "Which is honestly my entire personality."

Martin arrived then, shaking rain off his jacket in a way that deliberately splashed both of them. He dropped into the third chair and stole a sip from Nicola's cup before she could slap his hand away, a ritual they performed like a courtly dance.

"Tell him," Nicola said.

Madison told him, the amendment, the war, the grandfather, the three months. Martin, who planned to study marine biology and could not go ten minutes without mentioning it, was currently obsessed with a poster over the register advertising some documentary, and he interrupted her twice to say the fish on it were pelagic, open-ocean fish, not reef fish, and that whoever designed the poster should be ashamed.

"Focus," Madison said. "The point is, young people had to fight to get enfranchised, and now the drainage levy, which affects literally the street I live on, is going to be decided by people whose average age is deceased. So you two are coming with me on Tuesday. Early voting is at the rec center."

"I'm registered in my mom's district," Martin lied, badly, because he had moved in August and everyone knew it.

"You can update your address at the counter."

"I don't have time between classes."

"You have one class. It's Tuesdays."

"Fine," Martin said finally, raising both hands. "Fine. I'll update my registration and I'll vote on the drainage. If it floods, that's on you."

Nicola sipped her cocoa with the composure of someone who had won. "See how easy that was? All that lightning, 1971 speed, and it still took you three months of friendship to move him."

Ms. Qureshi came in then, in her raincoat, and got in line behind them at the register while Madison ordered a refill. She greeted them, asked what they were plotting, and Madison announced, grandly, that she had organized her first electorate, that two formerly unregistered citizens would be voting Tuesday.

"Wonderful," Ms. Qureshi said. "I'll look for you there."

She paid for her coffee, and as she turned to go she mentioned, almost apologetically, that the deadline to update a registration had actually been the previous Friday, and that Martin would have to sort out a provisional ballot, which would take longer and require a form, and possibly a second trip.

Martin smiled at Madison with enormous, serene sweetness.

"About three months," he said, "should do it."

Jonathan had the kitchen table to himself, which meant the laptop, the textbook, two mugs of cold tea, and a printout of population pyramids were arranged in a kingdom of one. The assignment was due at eight the next morning, and Mr. Pham had been specific: choose two countries, analyse the shape of their pyramids, and argue whether each would need to build more schools or more nursing homes over the next thirty years. Jonathan had chosen Japan, which was easy, a tapering top like a squeezed balloon. The second country he had picked almost at random from the folder of charts, and now he sat staring at it, certain there had been a printing error.

The pyramid for Qatar was wrong. It had to be. Every pyramid he had seen so far curved smoothly, wide at the bottom or wide in the middle, but this one had a strange protrusion on one side, a bulge in the male bars between roughly twenty and fifty, so lopsided the chart looked bruised. He measured the bars with his pencil, wondering whether the female side had failed to print. He checked the page number, then the source line at the bottom, then the page number again.

He called Kellan, who answered with his mouth full. "You're doing Pham's thing too?"

"I think my chart's broken," Jonathan said, and held the printout up to the camera. "Look. The men's side sticks out. It's like half a pyramid."

Kellan leaned closer, chewing slower. "That's not broken. My cousin works at the airport in Doha, and she showed me a chart like that. Some Gulf states, Qatar and places like it, show a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there."

Jonathan lowered the page. "Foreign workers. So those aren't residents having babies."

"That's all I know. I don't know the numbers. Don't put numbers in unless you check them."

They hung up, and Jonathan sat with his hands flat on the table, annoyed with himself. He had been about to write a whole paragraph about a data error, and Mr. Pham would have marked it, and the mistake would have been his, not the chart's. The clock above the stove said ten forty. He opened the atlas his mother kept on the shelf under the phone books, found the Gulf, and looked at Qatar for a long moment, a small country with an outsized shape on the page, which was apparently also true of its population.

Here was the problem he now could not stop thinking about. Mr. Pham wanted a prediction: schools or nursing homes. For Japan the logic felt solid, a wide elderly cohort moving upward, a narrow base of children, so the country would need care for the old and fewer primary classrooms. But Qatar's pyramid was not telling one story. The bulge of working-age men was not the same thing as a generation being born; it was people arriving, and people who arrived could leave, and Jonathan did not know whether the chart was showing him the future or only the present wearing a costume. If he treated the bulge like an age cohort, he would predict nursing homes for men who might be gone by then. If he treated it as temporary, he had almost nothing to predict from at all.

He tried to verbalize the difficulty out loud, partly to hear whether it made sense, partly because the house was too quiet. "The shape shows people, but it doesn't show whether they stay," he said to the kitchen. It sounded thinner spoken than it did in his head. He texted Amin, who was the pragmatist of the three of them and would tell him to just pick an answer and sleep.

Amin's reply came in three bubbles. "Does Pham grade for being right or for the argument?" Jonathan typed back that he didn't know. "Then write the argument. Say what you'd predict if the bulge is permanent and what you'd predict if it isn't. Say you can't tell from the chart alone." Jonathan stared at the screen. It felt like a dodge, but it also felt true, and he could not find the line between those two things.

He wrote both paragraphs anyway. For the first, he reasoned as though the working-age men were a lasting feature: the country would eventually need services for them as they aged, though not schools, since the chart showed no wide base of children. For the second, he reasoned as though they were not: then the pyramid said little about the future at all, and planning would depend on choices the chart could not show him. Between the paragraphs he wrote a single sentence acknowledging that he could not decide which reading was correct from the data he had. He read it four times, worried it looked lazy, then left it, because he could not honestly write anything else.

By one in the morning the essay was saved and the pyramids were stacked in a folder, Qatar's crooked shape on top. He was too tired to be blase about it, which surprised him; he had expected the whole thing to be busywork, and instead he was lying in bed still turning the chart over in his mind. Through his wall he could hear his father's radio, tuned to the news, some announcer reading figures about a part of the world Jonathan had never thought about before tonight. He listened until the signal faded between stations, and then he got up and turned the folder over, so that Japan, with its smooth and ordinary curve, faced the ceiling instead.

The kitchen smelled of cardamom because Dadi was boiling tea for the third time that afternoon, having forgotten the first two. Layla spread her books across the table anyway, claiming territory the way she had every June since she was small, and pulled out her phone to look at the photographs Aleena had sent at midnight: six derivative problems, solved in Aleena's round, hurried handwriting, due to be submitted online before the exam on Monday.

She had told Aleena she would "glance" at them. What she had not told Aleena, or anyone, was that she had spent the whole train ride here rehearsing a small, satisfying speech about how some people thought calculus was beneath checking over.

The house helped her think, that was the truth of it. At home her desk faced a wall and a poster of a tropical beach she no longer saw. Here the window gave onto the neem tree and the lane where the vegetable seller called out prices all morning, and the noise arrived as rhythm rather than demand. Dadi moved through the kitchen without comment, adjusting the flame, and Layla bent over the first photograph with the particular acumen of someone who wants to find a mistake more than she wants the work to be right.

She found it in problem one, and then again in problem two, and by problem four her pencil was ticking the margins so hard it tore the paper she was working on. The derivative of x cubed, Aleena had written, was 3x cubed. She had done the same thing everywhere: multiplied by the power and then left the power alone, never lowering it by one. Layla sat back. Last summer, before the exam that had decided their class rankings, Aleena had sat across from her at this very table and copied Layla's method off the page, saying it was faster, saying why did the exponent matter if you'd already used it. Layla had laughed and not corrected her, because the method had still produced answers close enough to pass, and because it had felt good to be the one laughing.

Now the exam was a real one, the one that counted, and the method had calcified into six wrong answers. Layla wrote out the correction on a napkin, then a proper page. The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, she wrote, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared, not 3x cubed. She checked it against her textbook, twice, the way she checked anything she was about to be smug about. Then she photographed her page and typed a message that began, Aleena, before you submit, look at your powers.

Dadi set a cup of tea down beside her elbow and stayed, drying her hands on her dupatta, watching the way she watched everything, as if she understood more than she said. Layla covered the phone with her palm out of old habit, secrecy being the one skill she had truly mastered in this house.

The reply took eleven minutes. Layla read it standing at the window, where the light was going amber over the lane and the vegetable seller was packing up his unsold tomatoes. She read it a second time to be sure.

I already fixed them, Aleena wrote. I was up till two. I checked everything against the notes you lent me last week, your blue notebook, the one you said was your best work. It's all over my kitchen table. I was going to text you this morning.

Layla looked down at the napkin, at her careful page, at the turgid little paragraph she had drafted in her head on the train, all that eloquence prepared for an audience that had already left the theatre. She scrolled up to the photographs Aleena had sent, then back, and noticed for the first time the timestamp in the corner of each one, well before midnight, hours before she had even opened them. Dadi refilled her own cup and said, in a voice that suggested nothing and knew everything, "More tea, or are you finished?"

Layla picked up her pencil and turned to a fresh page.

The vending machine on the fourth floor took Jesse's dollar and gave him nothing, which felt about right for the day. His grandfather had died at 6:40 in the morning, before the snow on the parking lot had even melted, and Jesse had been sitting in this corridor since eight, refusing the coffee his mother offered and the granola bar Dario's mother packed. He kicked the machine once, then again, until a nurse passing with a chart gave him a look he understood as an injunction against kicking hospital property, so he stopped.

"He was ninety-one," Dario said from the bench behind him. "That's not even sad, statistically." Dario talked like this when he didn't know what to do, turning everything into numbers, and usually it made Jesse laugh. Today it made him want to break something small, like the vending machine's glass.

"You don't get it. I don't feel anything." Jesse said it quietly, because his mother was down the hall and grief was supposed to be loud, or at least visible, and instead there was just this flat gray quiet in him, like a TV tuned to no channel. "The counselor gave us a handout in tenth grade. The five stages. Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. I keep checking, like a checklist, and I'm not on any of them. Am I broken?"

Mr. Fischer, who taught world history and coached the debate team, was in the family waiting room when Jesse went in to find the bathroom and instead sat down. Mr. Fischer's wife had been on the fourth floor since Tuesday, which was why he was there, and he had a styrofoam cup of terrible coffee and the kind of tired face that made honesty easier. Jesse asked him about the stages, mostly to fill the air, and was surprised when Mr. Fischer frowned.

"You know where those came from?" He didn't wait for an answer. "Kübler-Ross. 1969, a book called On Death and Dying. She was writing about terminally ill patients facing their own deaths. Not mourners. Everybody gets that backwards." He turned the cup in his hands. "Doesn't mean it can't apply to you. Just means nobody's grading you against it."

Jesse sat with that. The stages had felt like an assignment with a rubric, and now the rubric turned out to be for a different class entirely. Somewhere in him, something loosened, though he still couldn't name what he felt, and he was starting to think that was allowed, that the unnamed thing might be its own stage, or no stage, or just the ordinary texture of loving a person who used to sneak him licorice and enthralled him, at age six, with card tricks he later figured out were terrible. That was the part nobody's handout covered: the dead keep enthralling you after they're gone, from memory instead of a kitchen chair.

Down the hall, his grandfather's room was being packed up. An ancillary staff member with a laundry cart had already taken the bedding, and the bed was stripped to a plastic mattress, and this, more than the morning phone call, was what finally did it. Not the stages. The stripped bed. Jesse stood in the doorway and cried hard and briefly, like weather passing, while Dario hovered behind him holding, for some reason, a get-well card he'd never gotten to give, because he'd planned to visit next week and next week had arrived early and empty.

"I changed my mind," Dario said afterward, in the corridor, when Jesse had washed his face. "About it not being sad." He turned the card over in his hands. "You think they'd let me leave this somewhere? Like with his stuff? I wrote a joke in it. About chess. He always beat me at chess and I need him to have the joke before the stuff gets, you know, distributed." That was Dario's want, suddenly and plainly: not to be statistical, but to be remembered as someone who'd shown up.

Jesse took the card and went to find his mother, who was signing papers at the nurses' station with a pen that kept skipping. He asked, and she asked, and a nurse said family could put a card with the personal effects. So Jesse walked back down the corridor and set the envelope on the folded sweater in the plastic bag, the gray one his grandfather wore to Jesse's debate final in February, and smoothed it flat with his hand.

On the third morning in Lyon, Sophia taped her note cards to the mirror of the hotel bathroom and spoke French at her own reflection until her throat hurt. In two days she was supposed to stand in front of a classroom of French teenagers and argue, for five minutes, about whether cities should make public transit free. Her accent was decent. Her grammar held. What she had written, though, was five minutes of facts, and reading it aloud she felt the presentiment that something in it would not survive contact with an actual audience.

"You sound like a vending machine," said her brother from the doorway, in English, and she slammed the door on him.

That afternoon her host sister took her to a café where two classmates were already waiting, a boy named Kareem and a girl named Frances. They had agreed to be her practice audience. Frances pushed her coffee aside and said, "Beginne. Vas-y."

Sophia began. Free transit reduced congestion; a study in one city showed ridership rising. Free transit cut emissions. Free transit helped low-income workers. She finished in four minutes and some seconds, having used every card, and the table was quiet in a way that felt like weather.

"You had evidence," Kareem said carefully, in his lurching English, switching to help her. "But you were like a report. Nobody's heart moved. Nobody thought, this girl, I trust her."

Frances tapped the table. "In philosophy class we learned Aristotle. He named three means of persuasion. Ethos, pathos, logos." She counted them on her fingers. "Ethos, the speaker's credibility. Pathos, the audience's emotions. Logos, the logic of the argument. You brought only the last one."

Sophia looked at her cards, fanned on the table between the sugar and the ashtray, and understood that they were impermeable. Nothing warm could get in, and nothing warm could get out. Every point was a wall, and behind every wall was another wall.

Two winters ago, at her grandmother's kitchen table in Ohio, Sophia had watched her grandmother argue with an insurance adjuster on the phone for forty minutes about a claim. Her grandmother had no documents in front of her, no figures, no studies. She told the story of the pipe bursting on Christmas Eve, and how she had stood in six inches of water in her slippers, and by the end of it the adjuster's voice had changed, had gone soft and human, and the check came the next week. Twelve-year-old Sophia had thought her grandmother was just lucky. Now, in the café, she could see that her grandmother had known exactly what she was doing, that ethos and pathos were crafts you could learn, that the old woman had spent forty minutes building a person the adjuster could believe in.

"All right," Sophia said, and she turned her cards face down. "Again. In French."

She started over, slower. She talked about the woman she had seen that morning at the tram stop, counting coins in her palm while the doors closed. She admitted that free transit would cost the city money, that she didn't have all the answers, that she was a visitor arguing about someone else's home. When she stumbled on a word, she let the stumble stand instead of freezing. Kareem leaned forward. Frances had stopped checking her phone.

Afterward, walking back along the Rhône with the light going copper on the water, Sophia practiced under her breath, not the facts now but the opening she was trying to build, an opening that would preempt the room's first objection by naming it herself. Two approaches, her cards and her grandmother, and her position somewhere between them, holding both, certain of neither.

The morning of the debate, Ms. Pelletier, the teacher who had arranged the exchange, caught her in the corridor. "You have your notes?"

"I have them," Sophia said. "I might not use them."

Ms. Pelletier looked at her a moment, then held open the classroom door. Inside, thirty faces turned. Sophia walked to the front, set the cards on the desk without looking at them, and said, "Je veux vous parler d'une femme que j'ai vue hier."

Kareem, in the second row, nodded once.

The community sports field had been converted for the afternoon into something between a stadium and a living room, folding chairs in ragged rows facing the big screen the rec department had borrowed from the high school. Taylor arrived early with her father, who carried two camp chairs and a cooler, and claimed a spot near the middle where the sound cables wouldn't trip anyone. The Olympic opening ceremony was being streamed, and half the neighbourhood had turned out for it, kids dribbling a soccer ball behind the last row, Ms. Bekele from the rec department testing the microphone she would use only once, to say welcome.

Taylor had a private project for the day. Her mother was from a country whose flag was green, yellow and red; her father's flag was blue, white and orange; and at school she had been telling people for a week that the Olympic rings contained the colors of every flag on earth, a claim she had picked up somewhere and never checked. She wanted it to be true. If it was true, then the rings on the screen were, in some quiet way, hers twice over, and the argument she kept having with herself about which box to tick on forms that asked for one background could be preempted by a symbol that refused to choose.

Kayne and Rose-Marie showed up before the ceremony started, Kayne carrying a bag of chips he guarded like contraband and Rose-Marie with a printed flag of her own country taped to a stick. They sat down on either side of Taylor, and Kayne immediately began narrating the athletes' outfits, doing a bad French accent, until Rose-Marie elbowed him into something closer to silence.

"Look at the rings," Taylor said, pointing at the screen, where the ceremony had paused on an aerial shot of the stadium. "Every color of every flag. That's the whole point of them."

"Every flag?" Kayne said. "Every single one?"

"Every single one," Taylor said, though she heard the small falseness in her voice, the way you hear a floorboard shift under your own weight.

Rose-Marie held up her little flag and began checking it against the frozen image, blue, yellow, red, a methodical girl even at parties. "Mine works," she announced. "All three."

Kayne, naturally, made it a game. He started naming flags and demanding verification. Japan, white and red, fine. Brazil, green and yellow, fine, but there was blue in the globe and Taylor said so before he could pounce. Then he said Portugal, red and green, and Taylor hesitated, because neither of those was a ring color, and the black ring suddenly looked like a stranger. She laughed it off, said she'd look it up, and did not look it up, because the phone was in her father's cooler bag and the moment was moving on.

Her father, overhearing, leaned in from the next chair. "The rings are about unity, Tay. That's what matters. Not a checklist." He said it the way he said most things, warmly and as though the conversation were already over. It was his way of thinking: symbols were affective, they worked on you from a distance, and picking them apart was missing the point. Kayne, Taylor knew, thought the opposite, that anything you believed should survive being checked, or you should stop believing it. Both positions seemed true to her in the moment and neither seemed sufficient, and she sat with that discomfort while the parade of athletes began.

She did get the phone, eventually, using the pretense of photographing Rose-Marie's flag, a small subterfuge that fooled nobody, and looked it up with the screen tilted away from the sun. What she found rearranged the afternoon. The rings had been designed in 1913 by a French baron, Pierre de Coubertin, and he had chosen the colors deliberately, so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them. She read it twice. Every national flag of the time. And there, in the same paragraph, was the part that undid her whole argument in the most satisfying way: the white background counted too.

"Kayne," she said, and waited until he lowered his commentary. "Portugal. The rings don't have red or green. But the flag has white in the shield. And the white background of the rings counts, that's part of the design, it's one of the colors."

"So my flag's color is, what, the empty part?"

"Every flag of the time," Taylor said. "Designed in 1913, by a guy named Coubertin. He picked the colors so that at least one would be in every flag, and the white background is included."

Rose-Marie considered this with her flag still in her hand. "So mine is in the yellow and red and blue. Yours is in the green and the white. Kayne's is in the black."

"Mine's the orange and white," her father said from the next chair, having apparently been listening the whole time. He said it lightly, but Taylor noticed he had abandoned his unity speech, that he was now playing the checklist game too, and that the two ways of thinking had folded into each other without anyone conceding anything.

The ceremony moved on, fireworks over the stadium mirrored, faintly, in the windows of the apartments beyond the field, and Taylor found she was less sure than before, not more, though the uncertainty felt different. The rings held every flag from 1913, but 1913 was not now, and she didn't know what happened to the claim when new countries arrived, and she didn't ask, because she suspected the answer would be another afternoon of checking. What she had was a rule that was true once and mostly true now and beautiful either way, and a father who cared about the feeling of it and a friend who cared about the facts of it, and she sat between them with both.

When the torch finally reached the top of the stadium, the whole field stood up without being asked, kids on shoulders, Ms. Bekele on her folding chair, the soccer ball abandoned in the grass. Rose-Marie raised her little flag higher, and Taylor, without deciding to, raised the phone with the five rings still on the screen, and held it there against the darkening sky.

Olivia arrived at the community garden before anyone else, mostly to avoid her mother, who had spent the whole week rehearsing the phrase "responsible summer" as if saying it enough times would make it true. The garden occupied a scraped lot behind the laundromat, forty plots of fencing and tomato stakes, and it had a waiting list three years long, which was the only reason Olivia's application essay mattered. Ms. Warsame, who ran it, had told her the committee wanted to see "engagement." Olivia had written three hundred words about engagement and suspected every one of them was circumlocution, a fence of words around the simple fact that she wanted a plot because she was tired of the apartment, the parking lot, the whole gray geometry of her days.

Patience was already there, actually, crouched over the communal herb bed, which corrected Olivia's sense of priority immediately. "You're early," Patience said, without looking up.

"I'm avoiding my house."

"Cool. Hold this." Patience handed her a trowel and kept pinching off bolted cilantro, which had gone to flower because nobody had harvested it. "Karl's coming at ten with his thing about the water bill."

Karl's thing turned out to be the water bill. The garden's metered rate had jumped, the city was repricing usage after the reservoir dropped two feet, and Ms. Warsame had called a meeting of plot holders at the picnic table under the mulberry. Karl arrived on a bike with a folder of printouts, which he distributed like a man running for office. "If they raise the rate," he said, "half these plots go fallow. Mrs. Otero already said she can't do it."

"Then we do a shared fund," Patience said. "The people with money cover the people without."

"That's charity," Karl said. "Charity dries up."

"Being poor dries up faster."

Ms. Warsame rapped the table once. "One at a time. Olivia, you've been quiet, which is rare and suspicious."

Olivia had been quiet because she was reading Karl's printout, which was not about the reservoir at all. Page three was a case study from his geography elective, photocopied crooked, about the Aral Sea. She read it twice. "This says the Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea lost a fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people." She looked up. "Forty thousand."

"It's famous," Karl said. "It's like the textbook example."

"So the cotton farmers got water," Olivia said slowly, "and the fishermen got a desert. And it wasn't weather. It was a decision. Somebody chose which side of the pipe to stand on." She tapped the page. "That's the water bill. That's us, at the dumbest possible scale. When the reservoir drops, the price rises, and the price doesn't fall on everybody equally. It lands on Mrs. Otero, because she's downstream of money instead of downstream of a river."

Patience pointed at her. "See, that's the fund argument."

"Sort of," Olivia said, though she could feel the argument bending in her hands. "But Karl's right that a fund is a patch. The actual system is that water gets priced like it's private and used like it's shared, and nobody upstream of the decision ever sees the downstream." She paused. "I don't know the fix. I know the shape of the break."

"You sound sagacious," Karl said. "I hate it."

"You sound like a folder," Olivia said, and even Ms. Warsame laughed into her coffee.

The meeting ended without a vote, because the committee had not actually raised the rate yet, only floated it, which Ms. Warsame called "governance by weather balloon." People drifted back to their plots. Olivia took the printout home, read the rest of the case study on the bus, and read it again in the kitchen while her mother asked whether she had thought more about a real job. She had not. She was thinking about Mrs. Otero's tomatoes, which would die not from drought but from arithmetic.

The twist came on Thursday. Olivia stopped by the laundromat to drop off the folder Karl had left in her bag and found Mrs. Otero at the counter, feeding quarters into a dryer she did not need, because the machine's exhaust vented warm air and her apartment ran cold and the utility rate had gone up too. "Everything rises together," Mrs. Otero said, cheerful in a way that eviscerated Olivia a little, the way a person can be cheerful about being cornered. "Water, gas, bread. You young people plot your vegetables. In my day we plotted revolutions." She laughed at her own joke and pulled the last warm towel out.

Olivia stood there holding the folder, understanding something she could not yet say cleanly: that the garden was not separate from the laundromat, that Karl's bill and Mrs. Otero's dryer and a dried-up sea on another continent were all one machine with many dials, and that she had spent her essay talking about engagement as if caring were a hobby. She walked back to the lot, past the fence, and found Patience and Karl arguing at the herb bed over whether to rip out the bolted cilantro or let it reseed for free.

"Let it reseed," Olivia said. "Free water, free seed. Then we take the fund idea to Ms. Warsame, and we make the fund buy a rain barrel."

Karl squinted. "A rain barrel won't fix a reservoir."

"No," Olivia said. "But it keeps Mrs. Otero's plot alive while we figure out what will." She knelt down beside the cilantro, which had gone lanky and stubborn and was flowering anyway, and began to weed around it, her hands in the dirt, the flowers leaning toward whatever sun the mulberry left them.

Elliot had the printout flat on Ms. Traoré's desk before the bell finished ringing, one finger holding down the corner as though the paper might bolt. "Six hundred and twelve respondents," he said. "It's the survey. The one I told you about. Simeon wants to run it Thursday with the number in the headline."

Ms. Traoré looked at the page but kept her hands in her lap. "And you want my permission, or my blessing?"

"Neither. I want to know if it's right." He had known her for three years, since algebra, and he knew the difference between her silences. This was the silence that meant she was waiting for him to answer his own question. He straightened up anyway and waited it out.

The survey was real. The student newspaper had emailed it to every family on the district list, and six hundred and twelve people had answered the question about later start times for the high school. Fifty-three percent said yes. Simeon, who was co-editor, had written the headline already: MAJORITY OF FAMILIES BACK LATER START. He had shown it to Elliot at lunch with the particular confidence of someone holding a proof, and Cayden had leaned across the table and said, "Six hundred people out of how many? The district has like four thousand families. Isn't that basically nothing?" Simeon had waved him off. "It's more than professional polls use." Elliot had said nothing, which was unusual for him, and had spent the afternoon feeling like he'd swallowed a stone.

At lunch the next day, Cayden brought his laptop to the table and turned it so the others could see. "Okay, so I looked it up. A simple random sample of about a thousand people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus three percentage points." He said it flatly, reading. "For the whole sample's results."

"Margin of error," Simeon repeated, the way he repeated things he intended to dismiss.

"It's the wiggle room," Cayden said. "How much the number could be off by." He scrolled. "But here's the thing. Ours wasn't random. It was whoever opened the email."

Elliot took a bite of his sandwich and chewed slowly. The cafeteria smelled like bleach and hamburger grease; a sophomore at the next table was trying to balance a milk carton on its edge. "So the thousand thing doesn't even apply," he said finally. "That's for a simple random sample. Everyone has the same chance of being picked."

"Which we don't have," said Cayden.

"Right. But it's still the only number we know." Elliot pulled the printout from his binder, the same one he'd shown Ms. Traoré, and turned it over to the blank side. He wrote 53 at the top. Below it, out to either side, he wrote 50 and 56. "If a thousand people would give us plus or minus three, and we have six hundred, the honest wiggle room is even bigger than that. And on top of that, who answers a school email? My mom answers school emails. She'd answer that survey four times if it let her." He tapped the 50. "Fifty-three could be half. It could be under half."

Simeon leaned back with his arms crossed. The vitriolic tone that had won him two arguments at the editorial board meeting last month was in his voice when he said, "So we just don't report anything. We have six hundred people telling us something and we sit on it because of your mom." His milieu, Elliot thought, was exactly this: a cafeteria table converted into a courtroom, with Cayden as the jury and Elliot as whoever was losing. But that wasn't fair, and Elliot made himself pull the thought back. Simeon wasn't wrong to want the paper to matter. The paper had spent two years abrogating its own authority, running mood-board content and horoscopes, and this survey was the first real thing it had produced.

"That's not what I'm saying," Elliot said. "We report it. We just don't say 'majority.' We say what it is. Six hundred and twelve respondents, fifty-three percent, and we say the method, that it was whoever answered an email. Then people can decide." He looked at the numbers on the back of the printout. "If we had a thousand, randomly picked, we'd get plus or minus three, and even then fifty-three would only mean probably more than half. We're way past the point where a headline is honest."

Cayden pulled the laptop back toward himself. "There's a stats teacher here. Mr. Something. He posts the response rates for his own polls on his door."

Simeon was quiet for a moment, working a tater tot apart with his thumb. "Fifty-three," he said. "It's a good number. It feels true."

"That's the problem," Elliot said. He capped his pen.

Thursday was still two days away. Simeon took the printout from the table, folded it once, and put it in his back pocket without agreeing to anything. Then he stood, gathered his tray, and walked toward the drop-off window, and Cayden closed the laptop and watched him go.

The truck's passenger seat had a crack running through it, and Alexia kept her thumb pressed into the vinyl as the highway markers slid past. Her father drove with both hands on the wheel, saying nothing, which was its own kind of conversation. Behind them, in the box, were forty boxes and her mattress and a bicycle she hadn't ridden in a year. Two hundred and thirty miles behind them, or nearly, were Teegan and Kade and the parking lot where they'd all sat on Kade's hood the night before, until the streetlight clicked off and nobody moved for a while.

She had expected to feel something large. What she felt instead was a small, persistent tiredness, the kind that made her blink too slowly, and it annoyed her, because nothing had actually happened to her. Nobody had died. She wasn't sick. Her father had a job offer, and they had packed, and here they were. "I don't get why I'm so wiped," she said to the windshield. Her father glanced over. "It's a lot," he offered, and she thought that was too easy an answer, so she took out her phone.

Teegan had sent her a photograph an hour ago: the stress scale from some psychology thing, screenshotted from a website with a gray background and clip-art borders, the kind of site that looked like it hadn't been updated since Alexia was in kindergarten, almost obsolescent. She scrolled down the list, waiting for the numbers to load in chunks. Marriage, 50 points. Divorce, 50. She kept scrolling, curious now despite herself, the way she got when a system was involved, some hidden arithmetic underneath a feeling.

There it was. A change in residence, 20 points. She read the line twice, then looked at the entry just below it, because the numbers matched, and she sat forward against the seatbelt. A change in schools, also 20. The same. She'd been telling herself all summer that the school part was the hard part, the real part, and that the house, the town, the move itself was just logistics, boxes and a rental truck. But the scale counted them equally, as if leaving a bedroom and leaving a hallway were the same weight of event. And she was doing both at once, which meant, if the arithmetic meant anything, she was carrying forty points of it before the summer had even properly ended.

"Teegan found something," she said, and turned the phone toward her father at a red light. He squinted at it. "Holmes and Rahe," she said. "1967. Psychologists. They made a scale of stressful life events and gave each one points." He read for a moment, then said, "Huh," which from him was a speech. "Twenty for moving," she said. "Same as changing schools. Exactly the same." He pulled forward as the light changed. "So it's not just me being dramatic." He said it gently, not as a question, and she didn't answer, because she was already wondering about the other side of it, whether a thing being countable made it smaller or larger.

Because here was what she couldn't decide. Part of her wanted the number to be an excuse, a permission slip: the scale said so, therefore the exhaustion was legitimate, therefore she could lie down in this truck and be tired without rectitude or self-judgment, without the little prosecutor in her head asking what exactly you've done to earn this fatigue. But another part of her suspected that weighing a thing was a way of putting it down, of filing it. Her grandmother's death was 63 points on that list, and a move was 20, and she trusted the difference between those, and yet she didn't quite trust that grief could sit on the same ruler as a truck full of boxes. Both ideas seemed true. She held them the way you hold two groceries in one hand.

They stopped for gas outside a town whose water tower she could see from the pump. Her father went inside to pay, and Alexia walked around the box of the truck, pressing her palm flat against the sun-warmed metal, listening to the tick of the engine cooling. Kade called while she stood there. "Did you see what Teegan sent?" he said. "I saw it. Twenty points. Same as a new school." There was a pause with road noise in it, his road or hers, she couldn't tell. "Does that make you feel better or worse?" he asked, and she laughed, because he'd landed on the exact question, as he tended to.

"Both," she said. "It makes me feel both." She told him the thing about the prosecutor in her head, and he said he had one of those too, though his mostly showed up during exams. She asked him whether he thought you could count a feeling without shrinking it, and he said he had no idea, but that it was a good question, and she liked that he didn't pretend otherwise. A hawk crossed over the water tower, unhurried. "Text me when you get there," he said. "I will. Teegan too." "Obviously Teegan too," he said, and she smiled at the blank side of the truck.

Her father came back with two bottles of water and a bag of gas-station candy she hadn't asked for, which was his way of saying things. They climbed in. The seat crack was still there, and she put her thumb in it again, an old habit already, four hours old. Somewhere ahead was a town she'd never acclimated to, a school that counted the same as everything in this truck, a bedroom that would smell like somebody else's paint for a while. She didn't know yet which idea she'd keep, the permission slip or the suspicion of it, and she found she could stand not knowing, for at least the length of one more highway.

"Twenty points," her father said suddenly, pulling back onto the road, as if he'd been doing the math the whole time. "And school's another twenty." She looked at him. "So I'm at forty," she said. He nodded at the mirrors, checking the merge, and said, "Buckle up for the rest."

The metronome stood on the corner of the piano like a small wooden sentry, its brass pendulum frozen mid-arc. Riley had noticed it on his first evening at his grandfather's house, three days into what his mother kept calling a sabbatical, though it was really just the summer between high school and everything after. His grandfather had left the piano to him for the season, along with a beginner's book and one instruction: play something by August.

He could not play anything by August. He could play the first eight bars of a waltz, badly, and he could find middle C without looking, which felt like less of an accomplishment every day. His grandfather sat in the next room with the radio on, pretending not to listen, and Riley pretended not to hear him pretending.

"You're rushing," his grandfather called through the doorway on the fourth day. "Every time. You start slow and then you run away from yourself."

Riley lifted his hands off the keys. He reached over and set the metronome going, and the room filled with its dry, patient tick. "Who even invented this thing?" he asked, half to the room, half to the doorway.

His grandfather came in, wiping his hands on a dish towel, and looked at the little machine the way you look at someone you've known a long time. "Johann Maelzel patented it in 1815," he said. "Though the design wasn't really his. He drew on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel." He tapped the wooden case once. "Winkel got the idea and Maelzel got the patent. Decide for yourself which one mattered."

Riley thought about that while he practiced, the tick dividing the afternoon into equal pieces. At home he had learned everything the opposite way: fast, loose, by feel. His friend Jaeden played guitar like that, all instinct and swagger, and Riley had always envied it, the way Jaeden could pick up an instrument at a party and enthrall a whole room without seeming to try. Riley had once recorded himself playing the waltz and sent it to Jenna, who texted back "it's cute that you're doing this," a sentence he had read maybe forty times.

He worked at the metronome anyway. Sixty beats a minute, then sixty-four, the numbers marked on the plate in small stamped figures. When he matched it, the music sounded mechanical. When he ignored it, it fell apart. He began to suspect the machine was a kind of trick, that the point wasn't the tick itself but the argument it forced him to have with his own hands, and he kept losing that argument.

On the sixth day he got angry at it. He pushed the sliding weight up the pendulum, let it fly, and played as fast as he could, wild and crashing, until his grandfather appeared in the doorway with an expression Riley couldn't read. "That sounded vitriolic," his grandfather said. "The piano didn't do anything to you." Riley laughed before he meant to, and the anger went out of him the way air goes out of a cushion, all at once and without dignity.

That evening Jenna and Jaeden drove out to visit, and Riley showed them the metronome because it was the most interesting thing in the house. Jaeden picked it up, set the weight somewhere arbitrary, and let it clatter. "It's a cage," he said. "Music shouldn't be a cage." Jenna turned the case over in her hands, read the faded label, and set it back exactly where it had been. "Winkel invented it and Maelzel took it," she said. "That's the actual cage." Riley looked at the two of them, then at the piano, and understood that he agreed with both of them and couldn't say why that didn't feel like a contradiction.

After they left he played the waltz once more, slowly, with the metronome ticking beside him. Partway through he stopped watching the pendulum and just listened, and for eight bars, maybe ten, his hands and the machine arrived at the same place at the same time, neither one leading. Then he lost it, and the ticking went on without him, patient as ever, and he set his fingers back at the beginning.

Natalie had chosen the bank on Delmore Street because it was empty at four in the afternoon, and she wanted a counter to herself. She carried two things in her backpack: a bank envelope with four hundred dollars in birthday and graduation money, and her first credit card statement, which had arrived on Saturday and which she had read three times on her bed with a growing sense that she had missed something.

At the teller window she deposited the cash into a savings account she had opened online two weeks before. The teller, a man with reading glasses pushed up into his hair, pointed at a small printed slip. "Your rate is variable," he said. "It changes, but right now it's four point one five percent. Left alone, the money grows." Natalie nodded and folded the slip into her wallet, next to the statement she had not yet mentioned.

She found Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya at the desk nearest the window. He had been her neighbour for eleven years before he retired from the bank, and he still came in on Tuesdays to help people with paperwork, a folding sign on his desk that read GENERAL QUESTIONS. She sat down across from him and unfolded the statement on the blotter.

"I bought a laptop," she said. "Six hundred forty dollars. Books too. I start at Fairhaven in the fall and my mom's hours got cut." She turned the page toward him and put her finger under a box in the fine print, below the payment table. "This part. It says if I make only the minimum payment, it'll take me some number of years to pay it off. I counted the number twice. Is that real?"

Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya read the box, then turned the paper around so it faced her again. "That's the law," he said. "Under the CARD Act, statements have to tell you that. How long it takes if you only pay the minimum." He did not say more. He slid the statement back and waited, which was his way.

She counted on her fingers, though the box had already done the arithmetic for her. The laptop, which she had thought of as six hundred forty dollars, would cost more than that, and the years in the box were years she would still be paying for a machine she might have replaced by then. Meanwhile the four hundred across the lobby, doing nothing, would sit and grow at four point one five percent, small numbers becoming slightly less small, without her touching it. Money you owed worked against you over time; money you held worked for you. She had never had both facts in front of her on the same afternoon.

Kirsten arrived at five, shaking rain off her jacket, because they had planned to walk to the bus stop together. She dropped into the chair beside Natalie and read the statement upside down. "Just pay the minimum," she said. "Everyone does. Charles-Olivier's been doing it for a year on his card and he's fine." Then she squinted at the box, righted the page in Natalie's hands, and stopped talking.

"Charles-Olivier is a neophyte who thinks interest is something that happens to other people," Natalie said. "He was facetious about my deposit this morning. He said watching savings grow is like watching paint dry, and I should subsume my budget under one word, fun." She looked at the box again. The paint did dry slowly. That was the point of it. But the years in the box were also slow, and they were slow in the other direction, and she had assumed until this afternoon that the two things were the same thing. They were not.

Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya asked whether she wanted to set up an automatic payment above the minimum. She said she did, and he turned his keyboard toward her and showed her the screen where she could choose the amount. Kirsten leaned over her shoulder. Natalie typed a number, deleted it, typed a larger one, and paused with her finger above the enter key.

"Mom gets paid Friday," she said to Kirsten. "I'll ask her before I do this. If she can cover half this month, I can pay more than I thought."

"Text her now," Kirsten said.

Natalie pulled out her phone, typed "can you help with the card this month, I'll explain at dinner," and pressed send.

Kayla's father had cleared the coffee table of everything except the dip bowl, which meant he was serious. By six o'clock the living room held her parents, her uncle, Eliott sprawled on the rug with his phone, and Charles-Edouard, who had never watched a full soccer match in his life and kept asking questions at the exact moment someone was about to shoot. The semi-final started at seven, and the house rule, unwritten but iron, was that nobody spoke during the anthem.

"There's more teams this year, isn't there?" Charles-Edouard said, wedging chips into the dip like a man testing its solvency, as if the bowl might declare bankruptcy. "Eliott says forty-eight. That can't be right."

"It's right," Eliott said without looking up. "Forty-eight. First time ever."

Her uncle snorted from the armchair. "First time for a lot of things this year. Three countries hosting. Never been done. Canada, Mexico, us. You kids realize this is historic?"

"You've said that four times," Kayla said.

"Because it's true four times."

She let it go and went to the kitchen for ice, and that was where her mother cornered her, or seemed to; her mother never actually cornered anyone, she just stood where you were already going. "Your grandmother's not coming," she said quietly. "Your father hasn't mentioned it. Don't bring it up before the match."

Kayla had suspected as much. Gran had promised to come for the semi-final weeks ago, had talked about it on the phone with the specific enthusiasm she reserved for things she wasn't sure she could do. Her knee had been bad since spring, the kind of pain that didn't debilitate exactly, but made stairs a negotiation. Kayla carried the ice back in and sat on the floor beside Eliott, holding the new knowledge like a stone in her cheek.

The pregame show was doing a montage of the three host cities, drone shots of stadiums, and Charles-Edouard leaned forward. "So it's the first World Cup with forty-eight teams and the first with three countries hosting," he recited, as if memorizing it for later. "Is that in the rules now? Forty-eight forever?"

"Nothing's forever," Eliott's mother's boyfriend had apparently told him, because Eliott quoted people nobody in the room knew. "FIFA changes things when it suits them."

"It suits the small countries," the uncle said. "More teams, more chances. Cape Verde qualified this year. You know what that means to a country that size?"

"It means the group stage is bloated," Kayla's father said, his first complete sentence since kickoff approached. "It dilutes the tournament. An anachronistic purist like me remembers when sixteen teams meant every match mattered."

"Every match still matters," Charles-Edouard said.

"You've watched four matches in your life."

"Four very good ones."

Kayla watched her father, not the screen. He was checking his phone in the dark, the glow climbing his face, and she could see it was Gran, a message about her knee and the stairs and maybe next time. He put the phone face down on his knee and did not say anything, and when the whistle blew he stood up like a man answering a summons.

The first half was tense and low on goals, which suited nobody's nerves. At halftime her mother brought out the tray of sandwiches and her father disappeared into the garage, and Eliott nudged Kayla's shoulder. "Your dad okay?"

"Gran's not coming," Kayla said. "Don't say anything."

"I wasn't going to."

"I know. I just needed to say it out loud once, to somebody under fifty."

She sat with it through the second half. She understood her father's version of the game, the small perfect tournament where scarcity made everything precious, because it was the same instinct that made him scrub the coffee table before guests arrived, that made him keep a landline he never used. But she understood the uncle too, and even Charles-Edouard, memorizing the numbers of the thing like a password to a larger world. Forty-eight teams meant someone's tiny country in the montage, someone's grandmother staying up past midnight. Both things were true and they rubbed against each other like the halves of the same match, and she couldn't make them agree, and maybe didn't want to. What she did know, watching her father's stillness, was that a man could love a version of a thing so much he forgot to enjoy the thing itself, and she didn't intend to do that tonight.

The goal came in the eighty-fourth minute, a scramble off a corner, and the room detonated. Her father burst back in from the garage mid-celebration, swept her mother off her feet, and for a second Kayla saw his phone on the counter where he'd left it, still face down, Gran's unread follow-up waiting. He was laughing now, shouting at the replay, entirely here. He could call after. He would call after.

"Kayla," Charles-Edouard said over the noise, "who do we want in the final?"

She picked up her father's phone and held it out to him across the chaos. "Dad. Call Gran before the highlights."

The roast chicken was half eaten and Stella's grandmother was already crying, quietly, into her napkin, when Alexane texted a photo from the parking lot of the restaurant asking if she could come in. Stella excused herself from the table and stood by the hostess stand in her graduation dress, which was starting to itch.

"You said family only," Piper had warned her that afternoon, pinning the tassel back onto Stella's cap. "Your grandmother counts the chairs."

But Alexane had driven forty minutes because Stella had left the ceremony early, before the mortarboards went up, and everyone knew why even though nobody had said it. Stella's father had been in the hospital in March and April and most of May, and the family had adjudicated his attendance like a panel of judges, weighing oxygen tanks against wheelchair ramps against the May heat, and in the end he had watched the livestream from his recliner while everyone else sat in the bleachers. He was at the dinner now, pale, folded into the corner chair, and that was supposed to be the whole victory.

Alexane came in carrying a bakery box. "You left before they threw the caps," she said, hugging Stella hard enough to wrinkle the dress. "So I stole one."

The box held a single black cap, slightly dented, Piper's name still inked inside the band. The whole table turned, and Stella's mother made room and Alexane got squeezed in between two cousins, and for a while the dinner was loud again, Piper's mother Facetiming from the restaurant across town so Piper could wave at Stella, her aunts shouting congratulations into the phone.

Stella was quieter than the table deserved. She kept looking at her father's plate, at how he moved the food around with the patience of a man conserving strength, and she kept thinking that this was the last dinner that would ever be arranged around all of them in this configuration, the last time her grandmother would cry over her in a restaurant in their town. Everyone kept saying congratulations and it sounded like a door closing. When her uncle proposed a toast to the graduate, she raised her glass and felt the sadness arrive in a somatic wave, her throat tight, her hands cold around the stem, the body announcing what the mouth wouldn't.

Alexane leaned across the cousins. "You're doing the face."

"What face."

"The one from the debate tournament, when you lose on a technicality and pretend you're fine." Alexane took a roll from the basket, buttered it with unnecessary care. "You keep saying goodbye to everything like it's already gone."

"It is gone. That's what graduation is."

"It's called commencement," Alexane said. "The word means beginning."

Stella blinked at her. "It does not."

"It does. That's why they used it for the ceremonies, because graduates begin a new status. Like becoming a bachelor, or a master. Look it up." She held out her phone, screen already lit, and Stella read the entry twice under the table while her uncles argued about parking. She had walked across a stage that morning under a word she had never once thought about, a word that had been standing in the program the whole time, patiently insisting on itself.

She didn't feel converted, exactly. The grief was still real; the town and the schedule and the eleven friends she'd eaten lunch with every day since sophomore year were genuinely ending, and no etymology could adjudicate that away, and she didn't want it to. But she could hold both, she thought, turning the phone off. She could be sad about the closing door and curious about the hallway behind it, and the two didn't cancel out; they sat in her chest together, uncomfortably, like two relatives at the same wedding. College was in September, four hours north, and she had been dreading it and craving it in equal measure since the acceptance letter, and now she understood that the ceremony she'd fled had actually been named for the craving.

Her father caught her eye across the table. He looked tired but present, upright in his chair, and he lifted his water glass an inch, a private toast meant for no one else.

"Come outside with me for a second," Stella said to Alexane and Piper's pixelated face on the phone. In the parking lot the evening had cooled, and the asphalt still held the day's heat through her thin shoes. She took the stolen cap out of the box, set it on her head, and pulled the tassel across from right to left, the way they'd been taught. Piper, on the screen, whooped.

"Throw it," Alexane said.

Stella looked up at the sky, at the first pale stars over the strip mall, at her family visible through the restaurant window laughing at something her uncle had said, and she thought about keeping the cap somewhere safe, boxed, finished. Then she threw it. It went higher than she expected, wobbling against the dark, and Alexane caught it on the second bounce off a parked sedan.

John had been at his grandfather's house for two days, and the essay was due in five, and all he had was John Lewis Gaddis and a feeling that one historian was not enough. His grandfather's study smelled of pipe tobacco he was no longer allowed to smoke and held a wall of books nobody had opened since roughly the fall of the Berlin Wall, which John thought was fitting, since the fall of the Berlin Wall was more or less his topic.

"You look like a boy being digested," his grandfather said from the doorway, holding two mugs of tea.

"I need a second historian. If I only use Gaddis I'm basically writing his book report with extra steps."

"Then find one who disagrees with him." His grandfather set a mug down on a coaster shaped like a trout. "Disagreement is how the discipline stays honest."

John texted Brandon, who had already finished his essay and would not stop mentioning it. The reply came fast: "check leffler. melvyn leffler, A Preponderance of Power. it won the 1993 bancroft prize. it argued us leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world. you owe me a milkshake." Then a second message: "chocolate. large. i keep receipts."

John found the book at the public library the next morning, checked out under his grandfather's card because John had left his at home, which his grandfather found hilarious. He carried it back through the July heat and spread it on the kitchen table beside Gaddis, a historian on either side of the salt shaker, facing each other like duelists. Maina came over in the afternoon because her family was visiting relatives three doors down and she claimed exile.

"So one says the Soviets started it," she said, flipping a fork between her fingers, "and the other says?"

"The other says look at what America actually did, not what it said. Leffler's whole thing is preponderance. Power piled up until nobody could touch us."

"That sounds like a biome," Maina said. "One big dominant species and everything else adapting around it."

"That is a much better metaphor than anything in my draft," John said, and wrote it on his hand.

His grandfather interposed himself at the counter, pouring more tea, pretending not to listen in the way of grandfathers everywhere. "You know what Bancroft Prize means?" he asked.

"Brandon says it's a big deal."

"It is a big deal. It means his peers thought the argument was worth taking seriously, even the ones who hated it."

John spent the evening in the study with the lamp on, doing what Mr. Rao had told their class to do in the spring: test the explanation against the evidence. If Gaddis was right about Soviet expansionism driving everything, then American moves should look reactive, hesitant, dragged into commitments. He read the Marshall Plan documents twice. They did not look hesitant. They looked like men who had decided the shape of the postwar world before the war had quite finished, and who were building it the way you build a fence, generously, around everyone else.

But when he tried to write Leffler down as the winner, his pen stopped. Dominance explained the Marshall Plan and NATO and the bases. It explained less, he thought, why the Americans kept missing what the Soviets were actually doing, why the fear kept outrunning the facts. He wrote a paragraph arguing Leffler, crossed out the last sentence, and wrote in the margin, honest but unproven, which he suspected was not the kind of margin note that got full marks.

At dinner his grandfather asked how the duel was going. "You've reached the part where nobody wins," he said, ladling soup.

"That's the worst part," John said. "The assignment says compare and evaluate, and I want there to be an answer."

"There is an answer. The answer is you read the evidence and it fits Leffler better on some days and Gaddis better on others, and you say so. That's not a failure, that's the job." He pointed his spoon at John. "Also you owe Brandon a milkshake, and I'd like to be driven there when you go, since he chose a good book."

Maina, who had stayed for soup, reached over and tapped the back of John's hand. "Your note's sweating off. What's it say?"

John turned his hand over. BIOME, it read, smudged but legible.

"That," he said, "is my second paragraph."

The fish arrived still cold from the market, wrapped in newspaper that smelled of ink and riverwater, and Carson's grandmother set it on the counter with the authority of someone depositing a diplomatic pouch. "Whole fish," she said. "Head on. Tail on. Do not argue with me about this."

"I wasn't going to argue," Carson said, though he had been composing an argument in his head for two blocks, something about how fillets were easier to steam and nobody at the table wanted to look a dead fish in the eye. He was seventeen and this was the year he had been assigned the reunion dinner, start to finish, which meant the menu, the timing, the order of dishes, the little speeches. His grandmother had led it for as long as he could remember; his mother had led it the year after his grandmother's stroke; and now, apparently, it was him, because, as his mother put it, "you're the one who cares about food and nobody else in this family can be trusted with a calendar."

Michela was perched on a stool by the window with her phone out, ostensibly helping, actually narrating. "He's holding the fish like it's evidence," she reported to the room. "Exhibit A, one sea bass, deceased."

"Scale it," his grandmother said, handing him the back of a knife, and while he worked, his phone buzzed with the menu draft he'd texted to his mother, now returned with one line deleted and replaced in caps: THE FISH STAYS. He had cut it because it was fussy, because the steaming timing collided with the dumplings, because he had planned something modern and clean, and a whole fish with its head on did not feel modern or clean.

"You look like a lawyer who lost a case," Michela said.

"Everything in this menu is a symbol," Carson said, rinsing scales off his forearms. "The dumplings look like old money. The noodles are longevity, you can't cut them. There's a green vegetable because green sounds like money in Cantonese. I planned all that. And I still almost cut the one thing that actually matters, and I don't know how I missed it."

"Maybe ask the person who's glaring at you," Michela said.

His grandmother was glaring at him, though it was her ordinary glare, the one she used for unswept floors and karaoke. "Yu," she said, tapping the fish. "That is the word for fish. It sounds like the word for surplus. Abundance. You serve fish at the reunion dinner so there is something left over at the end of the year." She said it flat, the way she recited bus schedules, and then went back to lecturing the scallions.

"Wait," Michela said. "The entire dinner is a pun?"

"The entire dinner is a pun," Carson confirmed. "A very old, very serious pun. You can't laugh."

"I would never."

"You're laughing right now."

"I'm laughing incipiently. It hasn't fully arrived yet."

His grandmother snorted, which from her was roughly a standing ovation, and Carson found himself laughing too, scales in his hair, the fish staring up at him with its one dead sincere eye. He had been thinking about the menu all wrong, he realized, not as a list of dishes but as a sentence he was writing for the whole family, and he had nearly written an incoherent one. The modern clean thing, the dumplings shaped like ingots, the uncut noodles, and then no fish, no surplus, nothing carried over into the new year. It would have been like ending a toast halfway through.

"Okay," he said. "Fish stays. Steamed, ginger and scallion, done last so it comes out when everyone's seated. We titrate the soy sauce at the table instead of in the kitchen, so if it's too salty we can still fix it."

"Now he cooks like a chemist," Michela said. "Verrry careful. Add a little, taste, add a little."

"Titrate is the actual word for it," Carson said. "We did it in lab. You add until the color changes."

"Your veracity is overwhelming but your fish is drying out."

He moved the fish to the steamer rack and rearranged the rest of the timeline in his head, pushing the dumplings earlier, the vegetables later, the noodles at the very end so nobody would be too full to finish them. His grandmother watched him renumber the menu taped to the fridge, and when he offered her the pen to check it, she waved it off. "Your dinner," she said, which was either a compliment or a sentence, and left the kitchen.

By seven the relatives were due within the hour and the kitchen smelled like a banquet had detonated in it. Michela had been promoted from narrator to dumpling pleater, badly. Carson set the whole fish, steamed and glistening, on the oval platter in the center of the table, head pointing toward his grandmother's seat because she had told him twice which direction mattered and once that it didn't, and he had decided to believe the version where it did.

The doorbell rang, and the first aunts spilled in with plastic bags of oranges and complaints about parking, and his grandmother took her seat and looked at the fish and then at him, a long inspection.

"Yu," she said.

"Yu," Carson said back, and carried the platter the last inch toward her.

Anna had promised Mr. Ma a painting of his bakery window by Saturday, and by Thursday evening the shop itself had come out fine, the croissants stacked like little crescent moons, but the light coming through the glass refused to be yellow. It kept looking like margarine. She wanted it to look like morning.

She sat at the kitchen table with her tray of gouache open in front of her, a jar of rinse water going gray beside her elbow. Tenzin had come over to study for the chemistry final and had instead drifted into the kitchen, drawn, as he always was, by other people's projects.

"Add white," he said. "That's what my sister does."

Anna squeezed white into the yellow pool on her palette and stirred. The color went pale and chalky, like a school hallway at three o'clock, and the morning light was gone from it entirely.

"That's worse. That's a dentist's office."

"You could just leave it white," Tenzin said. "The canvas is white. Paper, whatever."

"The paper is white but it isn't light. Light is warm. The whole painting dies if the window looks like a hole." She frowned at the palette. She reached for orange, added a little, then more, then a touch of red for warmth, then some white to lift it back up, then more yellow because the red had dragged it toward brick. She stirred with the back of her brush, and the pool on the palette went a deep, disappointed brown.

"Oh no," Tenzin said, and laughed.

"It's mud." Anna held up the brush and let the mud drip back into the mud. "I added every good color. Orange, red, yellow, white. How is that not the best color? How is the best colors mixed together mud?"

"It's like your locker," Tenzin said. "Everything you like is in there and none of it works together."

Anna laughed despite herself, then stopped laughing, because something was turning over in her head. She remembered Mr. Ma complaining once, querulous and half-joking, about the flour delivery being late: everything piled on everything, he'd said, and somehow you end up with less bread, not more. She looked at the brown pool again. Each paint was doing its own thing, taking something away, and together they took away everything.

"Wait," she said slowly. "Light is the opposite. If you mix lights, colors, like on a screen, they add up brighter. But paint isn't light. Paint is the pigment absorbing stuff. Every pigment I add absorbs more, so mixing a bunch of pigments gets darker and muddier, not whiter. It's going toward brown, not toward light."

"That sounds like a chemistry thing," Tenzin said, "which means it's probably true and also probably on the final."

"It's called subtractive," Anna said. "Paint mixing. I remember Ms. Alper mentioned it in art, like, in passing, and I thought it was a fact for other people." She rinsed her brush and watched the water swirl. "So I can't get to morning by adding. I have to take away."

She got a fresh sheet of palette paper and squeezed out a single clean yellow, bright as an egg yolk, and let it sit there unblended. Then, instead of mixing the window color on the palette, she laid thin strokes side by side on the painting itself, yellow and a whisper of orange, letting the eye of whoever looked at it do the mixing from a distance. The window began to glow. Not like a photograph of morning, but like the memory of one, which was better.

"Two minds," Tenzin said, pointing at the painting and then at her chemistry notes, still open and ignored on the corner of the table. "Art brain and science brain."

"I used to think I had to choose," Anna said. "Like painting was going to emancipate me from school, or school was going to rescue me from being broke. Pick a lane. But the answer was literally sitting in the middle of the palette being brown."

"Deep," said Tenzin. "Also, we have learned nothing for the final."

"We learned one thing for the final. You owe me an hour of quizzing." She wiped her hands on the rag and looked at the finished window for a long moment. "I still don't know if he'll like it. I'm honest about that. He wanted a window, and I gave him an argument about light. That part stays uncertain."

"Then make reparations with a croissant," Tenzin said. "Buy two Friday morning. One for the mistake, one for the masterpiece."

Anna laughed and turned the painting around on the table so the window faced them both, the little strokes of yellow still catching the actual kitchen light, which was, she noticed, nothing like the painted one, and beautiful in an entirely different way.

"Two croissants," she said. "And we tell him nothing about the brown."

Mia had read the handbook twice on the bus, and the page she remembered was the one about following distance, though she could not have said why it had stuck. At the licensing office she waited in a line that smelled of wet coats and hand sanitizer, clutching her learner's permit the way other people clutched their phones. Nina was ahead of her, half-turned, whispering about the written test she'd just failed on her second try.

"You passed?" Nina said, seeing the paper.

"Barely."

"Malek passed with a hundred. He's an affectation, that's what he is." Nina said it fondly, the way she said everything, and Mia laughed even though she was still shaking a little.

Outside, a gray sedan idled at the curb with a plastic sign on the roof. Mr. Friedman got out. He was the neighbor who had offered the lesson, a retired mail carrier with a flat, unhurried voice, and he had told Mia's mother he would take her out on the quiet streets behind the office before they attempted anything with traffic lights. He walked around the car once, checked the mirrors, and got into the passenger seat. Mia settled behind the wheel and adjusted the seat three times before her feet found the pedals.

The first fifteen minutes went well, or well enough. She turned when he said turn, stopped when he said stop. The trouble came on the straight stretch along the frontage road, where a delivery van sat in front of them doing exactly the speed limit. Mia crept closer. She noticed herself doing it, eased back, and then crept again, as if the van were pulling her on a string. Mr. Friedman said nothing, which was worse than anything he could have said.

"Too close?" she asked.

"How far back do you think you are?"

She looked at the van's bumper, large in the windshield now. "A car length?"

"Watch when the van passes that lamppost ahead. Say 'now' when it does."

She watched, and said "now," and counted, and reached the lamppost almost before she got to two. She hadn't realized. She dropped back, tried again with the next sign, and this time counted a slow one and two that felt like holding her breath. She remembered the handbook then, the page that had stuck, the name for what she was doing. "The two-second rule," she said. "It was on my test." Mr. Friedman grunted, which she took for approval.

The van turned off, and Mia held the gap behind a hatchback instead, counting from mailboxes, from a fire hydrant, from a crack in the pavement where no fixed point should rightly have existed but did. She found she could think while counting, which surprised her. Nina would have said she was being obsessive. Malek would have said something pithy about spatial reasoning and then gotten it wrong himself. Both of them were partly right about her, she thought, and neither was exactly.

Mr. Friedman watched her settle into the distance like someone finding the right volume on a radio. He had taught his daughter thirty years ago, before the arthritis in his hands made him hand over the keys permanently, and he had learned that you could remonstrate with a student or you could give them a lamppost and let the lamppost do the arguing.
