She was laughing at something, a kid in a dinosaur helmet who had fallen in a perfect slow spiral, and she clamped his forearm to steady herself. It hurt in a small, specific way, like a blood pressure cuff with a sense of humor. He filed it under enthusiasm.

In the stands, Pedro and Felix-Antoine were sharing a plate of nachos they had no business calling nachos, since the cheese had gone the consistency of caulk. They had come, officially, to "support the arts," and unofficially because neither had anything else to do on a Thursday.

"Watch," said Felix-Antoine, gesturing with a chip. "She keeps doing that. The arm thing."

"Doing what?"

"Grabbing him. Hard. That's the third time. Look at his face after."

Pedro watched. Mason's face did a little thing after each grab, a wince smoothed over fast, the way you'd react to a stone in your shoe mid-introduction. "Huh," said Pedro. He had spent the whole semester in a health elective nobody else wanted, and something surfaced in him now, the way a license plate number surfaces when the police ask. "We just did this unit. In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence." He said it flat, like he was reading it off the nachos.

"That's grim," said Felix-Antoine.

"That's one kid in every row of the bleachers, basically." Pedro set down the chip. "I'm not saying that's this. She might just be clingy on skates."

"Everything is clingy on skates. It's the whole business model of skating."

Down on the floor, Prue grabbed Mason's arm again, hauling herself around the turn, and this time he said, "Ow, actually," and she laughed and let go, and thirty seconds later did it again. He began, quietly, to keep his left side angled away from her, a maneuver that required more skating acumen than he possessed, and which resulted in his colliding gently with a support column.

He skated over to the boards near his friends, pretending to fix his laces.

"You good?" said Pedro.

"Great," said Mason. Then, lower: "Does she grab hard, or am I being a baby?"

Felix-Antoine opened his mouth with the confidence of a man about to be scathing, and Pedro elbowed him before he could deploy it. "You're not being a baby," Pedro said. "She's leaving marks on your arm. I have eyes and, unlike Felix, I use them."

"Okay, one time I ignored a stop sign."

"It was a roundabout."

Mason looked at his forearm, where four pink ovals were surfacing, fading, surfacing again like a poorly edited photograph. He had spent two weeks rehearsing conversation topics, among them whether soup was a beverage, and had somehow rehearsed nothing for this. On one hand: it was a first date, she was funny, the kid in the dinosaur helmet had waved at him. On the other: one in twelve. It wasn't a law of the universe, it was just a number some survey had found, and it didn't say whether this was that, or whether Prue was that, and a number couldn't tell you what to say to a girl holding your arm.

He went back out anyway. He waited until she reached for him, and then, as gently as he could manage at nine miles an hour, he said, "Hey, you can hold my hand. Just, the arm thing hurts a little. My arms are famously made of dough."

Prue blinked. She looked, for a second, like someone checking a map. "Oh," she said. "Sorry. I do that when I'm nervous. I didn't think."

"Okay," said Mason. "Well. Now you think."

"Now I think," she agreed, and took his hand instead, much more carefully, like it was something she was being trusted with, and the kid in the dinosaur helmet went by again, waving, still falling, completely unbothered.

"IS SOUP A BEVERAGE?" Mason called over the music, because he had rehearsed it, and because a moment ago the night could have gone anywhere.

"Obviously not," said Prue. "Rerack. Wrong question."

"Fine. IS A SMOOTHIE A SOUP?"

She squeezed his hand once, hard, and then remembered, and loosened it.

The garage smelled of motor oil and cold concrete, and Caleb had claimed the corner by the workbench because it was the one place in the house where nobody asked what he was doing. He had his phone propped against a coffee tin, a keyboard app glowing on the screen, and staff paper weighted down with his father's abandoned socket wrench set. Sixteen bars. Chord changes. Written notation. The assignment sheet from Mr. Leblanc sat beside his elbow, dog-eared already.

The trouble was that Caleb could hear music all day, whole cascades of it, but the moment he tried to trap a phrase on paper, it went stiff, like a beetle pinned in a display case. He had worked out four bars the night before, a simple melody over a repeated pattern, and by bar eight the whole thing wanted to stop. It sounded finished. That was the problem. It sounded finished at exactly the wrong moment, and he had ten more bars to fill.

Alistair arrived on his bike with the noiseless confidence of someone who had been told the garage door was open and never questioned it. He leaned over the staff paper, chewing the strap of his helmet. "It just quits," he said. "Like a sentence with no period. No, wait. Like a sentence with all periods."

Caleb played the eight bars again, slower, listening past his own fingers. The last chord had a settled, square-jawed quality, the sound of a door closing on a room nobody had entered yet. He kept circling it the way he circled a math problem he suspected had a cleaner solution than the one he'd found. What if the ending was the thing doing the damage? What if the phrase wanted to be left hanging?

Agatha appeared in the doorway with two cans of soda and an opinion, as usual, about both. She had taken music theory the year before, the year Caleb had dismissed as paperwork for people who couldn't actually play. He had since revised this position, quietly, without announcing the reversal. She set a can on the workbench, condensation already sweating onto the staff paper, and he moved it with the speed of someone rescuing a small animal.

"Play the end," she said. He played it. "Now instead of that last chord, put the five chord there. The one built on the fifth note." He tapped it into the keyboard app, and the garage changed temperature, or seemed to. The phrase stopped asking to be finished and started asking to be continued. "It's called a half cadence," Agatha said, cracking her soda. "Ends on the five chord. Sounds unfinished on purpose."

"A trap," Alistair said, delighted. "You're setting a trap for the listener."

Caleb wrote the chord in, then played all eight bars twice more, and the second time he felt the pull in his own chest, the leaning-forward feeling of wanting the next phrase. He had always thought of theory as a set of rules for propitiating some grim examiner, an offering of correct spellings and roman numerals, but this was something else, closer to chicanery in the best sense, a trick played openly, the audience invited in on it and fooled anyway. He wondered whether a whole piece could be built out of doors that opened onto more doors.

Mr. Leblanc found them there an hour later, having walked over from his house two doors down, ostensibly about the hedge that bordered both properties. He stood in the garage doorway with his hands in his pockets, noxious fumes from a neighboring yard's leaf blower drifting past him, and listened while Caleb played the eight bars, then the nine, then the twelve he had started sketching in pencil so light it was almost rumor.

"You left the eighth bar hanging," Mr. Leblanc said. It wasn't a question.

Caleb looked at the paper. "I did it on purpose," he said, and heard how it came out, half defiant, half asking to be believed. He was not entirely sure which half was true. He had done it on purpose, and he also suspected he would not have thought of it if the melody had not stopped on its own first, and he could not separate those two things no matter how he turned them over. Some discoveries you made and some made you, and the middle of the Venn diagram was where he seemed to live.

"Then write the next phrase like you mean to pay it off," Mr. Leblanc said, and nodded at the hedge as though resuming a conversation that had never stopped. "It leans on the fence between our yards, you know. Yours can lean too."

Caleb picked up the pencil. Alistair leaned in over his shoulder, and Agatha pulled the second chair around, and the garage light hummed its one long note above them while Caleb wrote bar thirteen.

The envelope from Aldersgate College had arrived on a Tuesday, and by Thursday Dominic had been summoned to the guidance office, which smelled like instant coffee and the fake pine of December. He sat across from Mr. Adebayo with the letter folded in his back pocket, its crease already soft from handling. On the desk between them lay a scatter of transcript printouts and a half-eaten clementine, its peel curled like a ribbon.

"Congratulations," Mr. Adebayo said, though Dominic had not yet said the word accepted out loud. "Early Action. You applied in the fall, they answered in December, and now you have an answer before most people have even finished their forms." He slid a form across the desk, the one for the regular decision applications to Hartwell and Cass Technical and the state school, the ones whose deadlines were still two weeks away.

"I was thinking I'd just not do these," Dominic said. He tried to verbalize the feeling behind it, the way the letter had made everything feel finished, decided, over. "Like, I got in. Why keep writing essays about a challenge I overcame?"

"It's not binding," said a voice from the doorway. Maira stood there holding a folder someone had sent her to deliver, and she did not leave, because Maira never left anywhere quickly. "Early Action. You get an early decision but you can still say no. My sister did it. She got admitted in December and enrolled somewhere else entirely in April, and nobody revoked anything."

Dominic looked at her, then at Mr. Adebayo, who had leaned back with the particular stillness of a man letting two sixteen-year-olds work something out. The letter in his pocket felt suddenly less like an ending and more like a floor, something to stand on rather than a ceiling he had hit.

"So I could go anywhere," he said slowly. "Or I could go there."

"You could," Maira said. She set the folder on the corner of the desk, straightening it against the edge, an old habit of hers from three years of shelving books at the library. "That's what my sister said was the worst part, actually. Having the choice."

Mr. Adebayo watched the two of them while pretending to review the transcript printouts. He had been doing this job long enough to know that second-semester juniors and first-semester seniors occupied different taxonomies entirely, and Dominic had migrated between them in the space of one letter. He had also learned that the urge to rescue a student from a decision was endemic to his profession, an impulse he had to fight the way a doctor resists prescribing antibiotics for a cold. The boy did not need rescuing. He needed a deadline and a sandwich, probably.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," Dominic said. He had pulled the letter out now, holding it flat on his knee like a card he might play. "If Aldersgate is good, and it is good, then finishing the other applications is just work for no reason. But if I don't finish them, then Aldersgate stops being a choice and becomes the only thing. And I liked it better when it was a choice." He paused. "I don't know if that makes sense."

"It makes sense," Maira said. "It's just not a reason. It's a feeling wearing a reason's clothes."

Mr. Adebayo laughed despite himself, and the clementine peel rolled off the desk, and Maira bent to pick it up before it hit the floor, dropping it into the trash can by the filing cabinet without comment. She took the empty plate with her when she left, carrying it like it was the folder she'd originally come for, and the door sighed shut behind her.

Dominic sat for another minute in the quiet she had left. Then he picked up the Hartwell form, clicked Mr. Adebayo's pen twice out of habit, and at the top of the line where it asked for his intended major, he wrote undecided.

"Both of them?" Mr. Adebayo asked, nodding at the Cass Technical form still waiting.

"Both of them," Dominic said, and started the second essay.

The permission slip had said Family Meal Night, and Nolan had read it three times on the bus, because in his house nobody needed a permission slip to eat. His mother worked the evening shift at the hospital, his father sent a remittance from the job up north every second Friday, and his little brother, Dev, mostly lived on cereal. So the idea of cooking an actual dinner for them, in Mr. Bennett's room with its six stoves and hanging steel pans, had seemed at first like something borrowed from a different family. He had signed the slip anyway, and chosen roast chicken, because that was the dish his father used to make on Sundays before the job took him away.

He was not alone in the room. Haley had claimed the station beside his and was assembling a lasagna with the confidence of someone who had already litigated the question of ricotta versus béchamel with Carlo, who sat on the counter eating raw mushrooms and offering verdicts. The families would arrive at six. The clock above the door said five-forty, which Nolan tried not to look at, and then looked at anyway.

He unwrapped the chicken, set it in the sink, and turned on the tap. It was what his father did. He could still see it: the deliberate rinse, the water running pale over the pale skin, the shake, the paper towels, as though the bird arrived dirty, the way anything from a market arrived dirty. Dev, who had come early because the middle school let out first and he had nowhere else to go, grabbed his arm before the water touched it.

"Don't," Dev said. "The CDC says not to wash raw chicken. The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the counters. It's on the wall over there."

Nolan looked. Taped beside the handwashing poster was a printed page, the blue logo of the CDC at the top, and the same words Dev had said, plus a few he hadn't: nearby surfaces, not just the sink. He turned off the tap with two fingers. "Then how does it get clean?"

"It gets clean when you cook it," Dev said, in the tone of a person who had read the page twice and intended to enjoy this for the rest of the year.

Nolan stood there with a raw chicken and a problem. His father's method was not just a method; it was a kind of grammar, the way the man did everything, rinsed and dried and salted as if care itself were the point. But his father was four hundred miles away, and the evidence was on the wall, and Dev was watching him with his chin up, waiting to see which authority his older brother would obey.

He did both, in a way. He patted the chicken dry with paper towels, salted it the way his father did, sliding his thumb under the skin over the breast, and set it in the pan his father would have chosen. Then he took out his phone.

He typed: Doing the chicken for Family Meal Night. Did you know you're not supposed to wash it? CDC says the splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the nearby surfaces. I'm not washing it. Still doing the thing under the skin with the butter and the thyme.

The reply came while the chicken was going into the oven, and it was longer than his father's messages usually were. His father wrote like a man paying by the word. This one said: Your grandmother washed it and her mother before her. Never made anyone sick that I heard of. But they didn't have the science, and I don't either, so if the CDC says the water spreads it around the kitchen, do what they say. The rest, the butter, keep that. That part isn't science. It's just ours.

Nolan read it twice and put the phone face down on the steel counter, and Haley looked over and said, "Bad news?" and he said, "No," and found that he meant it.

The families arrived at six, and his mother came in her scrub top with her hair still damp, and his father came in behind her, which was the twist Nolan had not been told to expect, a Friday visit nobody had mentioned, and for a second Nolan stood very still at his station with the carving knife in his hand. Then Dev bolted across the room and their father caught him, and over Dev's shoulder he looked at the oven, at the browning skin, at the two of them.

"Did you wash it?" his father asked, coming over, not touching anything, the way he never touched anything in kitchens that weren't his.

"No," Nolan said. "The water splashes and spreads bacteria. To the sink, the counters, everything nearby. It's a CDC thing." He opened the oven and pulled the pan out, and the steam came up between them, smelling of thyme and butter and the exact Sundays Nolan had been afraid he was losing. "Everything else I did your way."

His father leaned in over the steam, closed his eyes for a moment, and said, "Then carve it, and don't give your brother the wing, he complains."

The nurse's office had been converted into a screening station for the health fair, and Luke stood at the second table with a cuff in his hands, waiting for Ms. Gill to finish with the student before him. She was the biology teacher who had organized the whole thing, and she had drafted six seniors to run the tables after a single afternoon of training. The cuff was heavier than he expected. It smelled like the inside of a doctor's waiting room, that faint powder and plastic smell, and when he squeezed the bulb it gave back nothing, just air moving through a tube.

Luke's job was simple on paper. Wrap the cuff, rest the person's arm on the table, inflate until the gauge climbed past one-forty, then ease the pressure down and listen. Two numbers. He wrote them on a card and handed it over. The hard part, Ms. Gill had said, was what came after the numbers, because people would ask what they meant, and he was supposed to say, "That's a question for your doctor," unless they pressed, and then he could tell them what the numbers measured without pretending to know more than he did. She had made them practice that sentence until it sounded bored instead of defensive.

He got through the morning on routine. Walter took a turn in the chair and let the cuff hiss against his arm while Maddex read out the gauge for him, and they argued about whether the fifth sound or the disappearance of it was the lower number, and Luke told them to check the card Ms. Gill had laminated, which said the disappearance, and they checked, and it did. Around eleven the parents started arriving for the open house portion, and the tables got busier, and the questions got harder.

A man in a gray jacket sat down at Luke's table a little after noon and pushed up his sleeve without being asked. He said he was somebody's father, gesturing vaguely toward the gymnasium doors, and that he hadn't had a reading in years because he didn't like what doctors had to say. Luke wrapped the cuff the way he'd been taught, two fingers of slack, the arrow over the artery, and pumped. The needle swung up and came down, and he listened, and wrote the numbers on the card and turned it around.

The man looked at the card for a long moment and asked if it was bad.

Luke said it was high, and that a doctor was the one to say how high, and the man said that was exactly the kind of answer that let people like him go home and forget about it. He said it without heat, more tired than anything, and Luke found he couldn't retreat behind the laminated sentence. He said the two numbers were pressure in the arteries, the higher one when the heart beat, the lower one between beats, and that the man's were above where they should sit.

"So what do I do," the man said. "Am I supposed to take a pill and eat like a rabbit."

Luke had a page of notes from the training folded in his pocket, and he took it out, and the relevant line was one Ms. Gill had underlined twice, about exercise. He read it once to himself and then put the notes away, because reading to a man's face felt like hiding. "Regular aerobic exercise lowers blood pressure in a lot of people," he said. "Brisk walking, or cycling, on most days. Even people who already have hypertension." The word felt strange in his mouth, formal, but the man nodded like it was a word he'd heard before in other rooms.

"You mean like walking around the block."

"Like walking fast enough that you couldn't sing but you could still talk," Luke said, and the man almost smiled at that, said his wife had been saying the same thing in different words for a decade.

Walter drifted over during the lull and leaned on the table, and when the man went to find his son, Walter said Luke had just prescribed exercise to a stranger. Luke said he hadn't prescribed anything, he'd read a line off a card, and Walter said it hadn't sounded like a card, it had sounded like Luke meant it. That stopped Luke for a second. He had meant it. Somewhere between reading the line and saying it, the sentence had become his, and he was circumspect about that, because the training had been clear about where his knowledge ended and a clinic's began, and yet the ending felt thinner than the middle.

He tried to compartmentalize it on the walk to the cafeteria, filing the man's face under finished business, but it wouldn't file. What stayed was the man's question, "Am I supposed to take a pill and eat like a rabbit," and the way it assumed the only choices were drastic ones, and how the alternative Luke had offered was almost insultingly small, most days, a brisk walk, and yet small was the whole point. He didn't know whether the man would do it. He didn't know whether one reading on a folded table in a hallway meant anything at all, or whether it was an indictment of the whole setup, six seniors with an afternoon of training telling parents things that deserved a follow-up appointment nobody would schedule.

After school Ms. Gill found him stacking chairs and asked how the day had gone. He told her about the man, the numbers, the line about walking. She listened with her arms crossed, and when he finished she didn't correct him or praise him, she just asked whether he'd told the man to see a doctor. He said he had, twice, and the man had said sure, and Luke hadn't believed him. Ms. Gill considered that, and said the reading they didn't measure was whether anything changed afterward, and no table at any health fair could take it.

On his way out through the side doors, Luke saw the man again, across the parking lot, standing beside a sedan with a boy who had to be his son, the two of them not talking, just waiting for the lot to clear. The man had the card in his hand, turning it over. Luke stood by the doors with his bag on his shoulder, and after a moment the man folded the card once and put it in the pocket of the gray jacket, and unlocked the car.

Jessica had spread her books across the long table by the library window before Isaiah arrived, two of them open to the same decade and disagreeing about it. One historian, Gaddis, wrote that the Cold War grew mostly out of Soviet expansion, that Stalin pushed and the West pushed back. The other, a revisionist whose name Jessica kept forgetting to write down, argued that American power had provoked the conflict as much as any Russian ambition did, that the United States needed markets and made enemies where it might have made partners. Ms. Zhang had refused to tell the class which one was right. "The evidence," she had said, "does not line up behind a single door. Your job is to weigh, not to pick a side and decorate it."

"You look like you're mad at the books," Isaiah said, dropping into the chair across from her with his own stack, all of it for the same essay. He turned one of her volumes around and scanned the page she'd flagged with a sticky note. She watched his eyes move the way they did when he was actually reading rather than performing it, and she felt briefly less alone in the problem.

"I keep finding that each of them sounds completely convincing until I read the other one," she said. "Gaddis makes the Soviets look like the aggressor, and then the next chapter has the Americans announcing their whole doctrine to Congress like they're proud of it. It's like two lawyers with the same discovery file." She had liked that comparison when it occurred to her on the bus, the idea that history was a trial where the evidence had to be cross-examined before anyone deserved an acquittal.

Ayva came over from the biography aisle holding a thick book with a black and white photograph on the cover. "Okay, so I found the speech everyone quotes," she said, pulling out a chair. "You know how the guide at the memorial last week kept going on about it? He made it sound like Churchill stood up somewhere in Europe and just declared the continent split in half." She flipped to the page she'd marked with a receipt. "But look where it actually happened. Fulton, Missouri. March 5, 1946." She read a few lines aloud, her voice dropping into a faint, borrowed gravitas. "From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent."

"Wait," Isaiah said. "Missouri? He said that in Missouri?" He leaned over the table as though the book might physically extrude the answer, and Jessica noticed something small and strange assembling in her mind, the way a paragraph she'd already read twice suddenly meant something different. Churchill had not been standing behind that curtain when he named it. He had been standing in the middle of the United States, at a small college in the middle of the country, telling Americans what Europe had become. She hadn't thought about where a speech happens before, only what it said.

"That matters," she said slowly, writing it down. "Missouri, March 1946. It's barely a year after the war ended, and he's already describing Europe as divided in two. So both historians can use this same moment and make it say opposite things." She pulled the Gaddis book back toward her. "If you think the Soviets closed the curtain, then Churchill is a witness, an early one, telling the truth before anyone else would. But if you think the West drew the line first, then the speech isn't a description at all, it's a move. It's a man standing in America telling Americans there's an enemy, three years before NATO exists."

Ms. Zhang passed their table on her way to the reference desk and paused, clocking the spread of books, the receipt marking the speech, Isaiah hovering. "You've found the Fulton address," she said, not a question. "It's a good one to sit with." She didn't say anything further, just tapped the cover once and kept walking, and Jessica was oddly grateful for it, the way you're grateful when someone lets you finish a thought you haven't finished yet.

Ayva was less sanguine about the whole project. "So which is it, then?" she asked. "Who started it?" She wanted verdicts; she wanted history to behave like a math problem with a circled answer at the end. Jessica looked at the speech, at the two books, at her notes, which now had a question mark in the margin where a conclusion was supposed to go. The evidence didn't acquit either country, and it didn't convict only one of them, and she was beginning to suspect that the honest essay was the one that said so out loud.

"Maybe the answer is that the curtain was real either way," Jessica said, "and the question is who had an interest in naming it first." She squared her notes, wrote Fulton, Missouri, March 5, 1946 at the top of a fresh page, and underlined the date twice. "Pass me that other book," she said. "I want to see what he was doing the month before."

The robotics club kept its member list in a battered blue binder, and by October the binder had one hundred and six names in it, which was why Ms. Dela Cruz gave them fifteen minutes at the start of Tuesday's meeting to find out who had actually paid their dues. "Check each name against the ledger," she said, "before you touch a single motor." Beckham went first, flipping from page one, running his finger down every line while Ana timed him with theatrical cruelty. Six minutes and forty seconds, and he'd found only the names through F. Ana then took over, starting from the back, which she insisted was a superior strategy because "the deadbeats are always the people who joined last." Alexia watched them and felt the particular itch of knowing there was a better way and not yet knowing what it was.

She'd been carrying the library's copy of an algorithms book in her backpack for two weeks, reading it on the bus in guilty fifteen-minute installments the way other people read things they weren't supposed to. Chapter Three had a diagram she'd traced onto her hand during precalculus: a list, a midpoint, a line slicing the page in half. She understood the shape of it but not the mechanics, the way she understood the shape of a college campus from the brochures stacking up in her guidance counselor's office.

"Give me the binder," she said. "And the list of who's paid."

"You don't get to be in charge," Ana said, but she slid the binder across the table anyway.

Alexia found herself at the whiteboard before she'd decided to stand up. "Okay. Say the names were in order. Alphabetical. A hundred and six names. I open to the middle." She tapped a spot in the air. "Say the middle name is Moreno. If the name I want comes before Moreno, alphabetically, then everything after Moreno, the whole second half, is useless to me. It can't be in there. I just throw it away." She drew a stroke through an invisible half of the board. "Then the half that's left, I take its middle, and I do it again."

"Throw away half the list," Beckham said. "Every time."

"That's the part I'm still working on," Alexia said. "Why it's allowed. Why throwing half away isn't cheating."

"Because the list is sorted," Ana said, in the tone of someone explaining that water is wet. Then she paused. "Wait. Is our list sorted?"

Beckham went very still. He turned to the binder, flipped to a random page, and found Nguyen wedged between Cortez and Diaz. Nobody said anything for a second. Then Ana laughed so hard she knocked over the cup of screws.

The plan fell apart and reassembled within the hour. Ms. Dela Cruz offered them the choice of sorting the binder by hand or running a search that actually matched the data they had, and Beckham, who had spent six minutes and forty seconds losing his afternoon to the unsorted version, volunteered to alphabetize all one hundred and six names with a violence that suggested each index card had personally wronged him. Alexia stayed after to help, or to supervise, or possibly just to sit near the problem until it confessed.

Later, walking home, she kept testing the idea against her own skepticism, because her father had raised her on the platitude that if something sounds too good to be true, it is, and halving a hundred things into fifty and fifty into twenty-five sounded exactly that good. But the trick didn't predicate anything on luck or on the good behavior of the data. It demanded one honest thing, sortedness, and one decisive act, throwing away the half that couldn't hold the answer, and then it demanded you trust that act. Flipping page by page through the binder, the way Beckham had, treated every name as equally likely to be anywhere. That was the equivocal position, respectful of all possibilities and loyal to none. The other way took a side. It said: this answer is not in that half, and I'm not looking there.

She tried to explain it to Beckham the next morning before first period, and the telling was where it got hard. "It's not just that it's faster," she said, holding two halves of a torn worksheet. "It's faster because of the order. If the list weren't sorted, the middle name would tell me nothing. Moreno in the middle doesn't mean anything unless everything before it actually comes before it." He nodded slowly, the nod of someone who half had it, and she realized she half had it too, that she could make the machine halve a list all day and still not be sure she could say why in a sentence that would survive a stranger's questions.

At Thursday's meeting they ran it for real. Sorted binder, dues list, Beckham calling out names, Alexia opening to the middle each time, comparing, cutting. Ana, who had bet a granola bar that it wouldn't beat her back-to-front method, watched the finds land in three and four checks apiece and slid the granola bar across the table with the face of a woman paying a debt to history. Ms. Dela Cruz stood at the door with her coffee and said nothing, which was her way of approving.

"Again," Ana said, flipping the binder shut and shuffling the cards like a magician. "And this time I sort them."

Taylor spread her geography homework across her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled of tea and the radiator's dusty heat. The assignment was due Monday: choose a country, analyse its population pyramid, and predict whether it would need more schools or more nursing homes in twenty years. Her grandmother set a mug down beside the laptop and looked over her shoulder at the chart on the screen, two stacked columns of horizontal bars narrowing toward the bottom.

"That's us," her grandmother said, tapping the screen with a bent finger. "Our whole country, in a picture." The bars at the base, the youngest ages, were thinner than the fat middle where her grandmother's own generation sat, and Taylor noticed the shape for the first time, really noticed it. She had skimmed the diagram a dozen times for other assignments without once thinking about what the narrowing meant.

"Can I use this?" she asked, mostly to herself, and pulled the chart closer. The base narrower than the middle. She copied the outline onto a napkin with a pencil, and her grandmother watched her draw as though she were mapping weather. "Fewer kids than there are people my age," her grandmother said. "I could have told them that. There were forty in my class and eight in your mother's."

Taylor's phone buzzed. Reuben had sent a photo of his own pyramid, Japan's, with the caption "this one looks like an upside down tree, what do i even write." She typed back that she hadn't figured it out yet, which was true, and then sat with the napkin. If the base was narrower, birth rates were falling, and the fat middle would keep moving upward into old age. She wrote at the bottom of her page: nursing homes, not schools. Then she crossed it out, because crossing things out felt like thinking, and wrote it again.

Her grandmother had gone to the counter to cut bread, moving carefully, one hand on her hip. Taylor watched her and felt the assignment shift under her, the way a lake shifts when you realize how deep it goes. "Grandma," she said, "who's going to work at those nursing homes? In twenty years, I mean. If there are more old people and fewer young ones." The question had not been on the sheet Mr. Sok handed out, but once she had asked it aloud she could not unask it.

Her grandmother laughed, a short sound. "You'll be working at one, dear, changing my hypothetical sheets." But Taylor kept looking at the chart, at the middle bars inching toward the top of the graph where the numbers thinned to nothing. "I'm being serious. It's the actual question. The pyramid says one thing, care, homes, all of it, but it doesn't say who does the caring." Her grandmother was quiet then, slicing the bread evenly, and the kitchen held only the knife's small rhythm.

Taylor opened a new document and typed two paragraphs. In the first she laid out the shape as evidence: a base narrower than its middle meant falling birth rates and an aging population, which pointed to rising demand for nursing homes and elder care rather than schools. She let that stand clean and definite, because the data was definite. In the second paragraph she wrote about the uncertainty the data could not circumscribe, the question of staffing, of migration, of whether young people like her would stay in the country at all. She was honest in that paragraph, perhaps more honest than Mr. Sok wanted, writing that she could predict the buildings a country would need but not the hands that would fill them. Entropy, she typed, then deleted, then typed again in a smaller sentence: the chart showed a kind of entropy, a system running down toward fewer, older lives, and no pyramid could show you the push against it.

Reuben texted again. "maddox says just write 'old people' and move on." Taylor smiled at the screen, aware that Maddox's answer was the mercurial one, easy today, gone tomorrow, and that her own answer would cost her something to defend in class. She wrote back, "I'm writing that we'll need the homes. And then I'm writing the question about who staffs them. He can mark it however he wants."

Her grandmother brought two plates of bread and cheese to the table and sat down across from the napkin drawing, turning it to face herself. She studied the narrowing base the way one studies a face, and Taylor watched her look at her own generation bulging in the middle of the page. "You know," her grandmother said, "when I was your age, I thought the hardest thing would be having children. Turns out the hard part is everything after." She slid the napkin back across the table, and Taylor tucked it into her binder, between the pages, evidence.

Clara had been drawing the school hallway for two days and it refused to become a hallway. On paper it was a corridor the way a diagram of a whale is a whale: doors in a row, lockers in a row, floor tiles like graph paper, everything obedient and dead flat. She sat at the long table by the window in Mr. Morales's art classroom, third period, pressing her pencil harder as if pressure could push the drawing backward into space.

"You're poking at it," Halle said from across the table, not looking up from her clay coil pot. "You do that when you're stuck. It's a mannerism, like my mom checking the stove three times." Clara looked down and realized her pencil was indeed jabbing the paper in small irritated strokes, so she set it on the table and put both hands in her lap.

The assignment was simple, which was the problem. Mr. Morales had asked for a drawing of a place you walk through every day, due Friday, and he had said almost nothing else, which was either laziness or something munificent Clara hadn't figured out yet, a gift of silence she didn't know how to spend. Other kids had chosen their bedrooms, the bus stop, the gym. Clara had chosen the east hallway because she had art in this room and chemistry at the far end of it, and she had walked it maybe four hundred times without once looking at it.

She did look now, or tried to. What made a hallway a hallway, when you stood in one? The walls were parallel. The floor was parallel to the ceiling. But when she held up her pencil at arm's length and sighted along the wall, squinting one eye, the baseboard line ran downhill toward the far door, and the top of the lockers ran downhill too, the two lines leaning toward each other like people sharing an umbrella. Her drawing had them parallel and level. That was the flatness. That was the corpse of the hallway lying on the page.

Domenico slid into the seat beside her, late as always, smelling of the parking lot. He looked at her drawing for a long, theatrical moment. "That's a hallway for ants," he said. "A flat hallway. A hallway drawn by someone who has never been in a hallway."

"Thank you, Domenico."

"I mean it as a diagnosis." He leaned over her shoulder. "Where's the vanishing point?"

She stared at him. "The what?"

"The vanishing point. Where all the lines run together and disappear." He took a scrap paper and sketched a fast box of a street, the building edges all sliding toward a single dot near the middle, and suddenly the scrap had depth, suddenly you could walk into it. "Some Renaissance guy did this," he said. "Filippo Brunelleschi. Around 1420, in Florence. He demonstrated it to everybody, linear perspective, drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point so a flat surface shows depth. Mr. Morales went on about him last year when I had him for studio. I mostly remembered the dot."

Clara took the scrap and held it beside her drawing. Her hallway had no dot. It had no place where anything ran together. It had four hundred walks' worth of nothing.

That night she wrote to her brother, who was doing a design degree two states away and answered faster when she claimed to be desperate. She texted: "Is it cheating if I mark a point on my paper and make every line in the hallway aim at it? It feels like cheating. Like the hallway isn't really like that, the lines aren't really converging, the walls are parallel, I measured." His reply came while she was eating cereal: "They're parallel in the world. They converge in your eye. The drawing is a picture of your eye, not of the world. Also it's not cheating, it's five hundred years old." She read it four times, then folded it into a wondering question she carried to sleep: if the drawing was a picture of her eye, then every drawing anyone had ever made was secretly a self-portrait of looking.

The next morning she did not draw the hallway. She drew a dot. She put it in the center of the page, lightly, apologetically, like a trespasser marking a claim. Then she ruled lines from the dot outward: floor, ceiling, both baseboards, the top edges of the lockers, the lintels of the doors marching away. She worked the doors in one at a time, each smaller and higher in the picture than the last, each fitting between the converging lines like beads on a string. When she placed the floor tiles she stopped drawing squares and drew receding lines toward the dot crossed by slowly flattening horizontals, and the tiles tipped away from her, row after row, and her stomach did something odd, as though she were actually standing there, actually walking in.

Halle came over with wet clay hands held away from her body. She looked a long time without speaking. "It's deep," she said finally, with some surprise, as if Clara had performed a surgery.

"It's borrowed," Clara said. "It's a trick from 1420. I don't fully get whether it's the truth about hallways or a lie we all agreed to believe." She wasn't sure, and she said so, and found that saying it didn't spoil the drawing. Domenico was right about the dot. Her brother was right about the eye. Somewhere between the two, the hallway existed, and she had put it on paper, and both things could be true, the parallel walls and the converging lines, and she could hold them without either one calcifying into a rule.

Mr. Morales walked the room slowly during the last fifteen minutes. When he reached her table he stopped, tilted his head, and looked down the drawing like a man sighting along a wall.

"Stand here a second," he said. "Where's the dot?"

She touched the pencil mark, still faint, at the center of the corridor. "Right there."

He nodded once. "Keep it visible."

"Visible? I was going to erase it."

"Don't." He moved on down the row of tables, and Clara leaned close, shading a tile, the lines running away from her toward the small gray point where everything met.

The pasta was still steaming when Alexandra's phone buzzed against the water glass, and she read the message twice before she let herself look up. "We have a problem," Branden had written. "West Council passed their version. Eleven to four. Ours passed ours on Monday. They're not the same." Her father was saying something about the diurnal rhythm of his new shift schedule, days collapsing into nights, and she nodded at him while her thumb typed a reply under the table.

"What's urgent enough to ignore my riveting account of sleep deprivation?" her mother asked. She taught twelfth-grade government at the school across town, and she had a way of asking questions that were already answerable.

"The book-locker bill," Alexandra said. "The two student councils were supposed to pass the same rule. Free periods, no locked shared lockers, something like that. But West cut out the appeals process we wrote in, and they added a fine. Monday is the deadline, and the principal won't sign off on two versions of one rule." She turned her fork in the sauce without eating. "Branden thinks we should just push our version through again and dare them."

Her mother demurred, tilting her hand as if weighing something invisible. "And what happened when Congress tried that?" It was her mother's habit to answer questions with questions, which used to infuriate Alexandra and now mostly trained her. Alexandra started to say that Congress had nothing to do with lockers, and then stopped, because the analogy was already assembling itself somewhere behind her eyes.

"Wait," she said. Branden, who wanted their version to win outright, believed the answer was force. Adriel, who had texted earlier, believed the answer was surrender, drop the bill, try again next year. Alexandra had been holding both messages in her head like two hands pulling the same rope. But there was a third thing, something from her mother's classroom, from the posters she'd stared at during conferences. "When the House and the Senate pass different versions of a bill," she said slowly, watching her mother's face for confirmation, "a conference committee of members from both chambers writes a compromise."

"Which both chambers then have to pass," her mother said, and went back to her plate.

Alexandra was already calling Branden. The connection crackled in the quiet kitchen, and his voice came through half-swallowed by hallway noise, a leitmotif of locker doors slamming behind him. "We can't make them take our version," she said. "We pick people from each council, sit down with West's people tonight, write one compromise, and then both councils have to vote on it. That's the whole mechanism. It's not winning. It's not losing. It's the only thing that gets the bill to the principal as one rule instead of two."

"West will never agree by Monday," Branden said, but she could hear him turning it over, the way his voice dropped when he stopped arguing and started thinking. "Who picks the committee?"

"You, me, and one more from ours. Three from theirs. And I think Adriel should be our third." There was a silence on the line long enough for Alexandra to notice her father had stopped pretending to eat and was watching her the way he watched weather coming in. Adriel had wanted to drop the bill. Adriel would walk into that room already convinced compromise meant defeat, and Alexandra wanted him there anyway, because a compromise built only by people who already agreed was just her version wearing a borrowed coat.

"Fine," Branden said. "Library at seven. If West shows up."

They showed up, all three of them, arms crossed in the corner carrel where the light was worst, and for the first twenty minutes it went exactly as badly as Alexandra had privately feared. The West delegate, a senior with a lanyard and no patience, kept sliding their fine back across the table like a stone he was unwilling to lose. Adriel sat with his chin in his hand, unhelpful on purpose. It was Branden, of all people, who leaned forward and said, "Take the fine out and we'll give up the appeals board. Written warning first, then the principal." Adriel lifted his head.

Alexandra wrote the sentence down, word by word, and read it aloud. Around midnight, both councils voted by message, and the counts crawled in one by one on her cracked screen while she sat very still at the cleared dinner table. Hers passed first. Then West's tally filled in, and she read the last name on the list, and pushed her chair back from the table.

The laminated sheet appeared on the pool door on Tuesday, taped at eye level where the usual schedule hung, and by Wednesday morning half the team had decided it was a punishment. Daniel read it while waiting for the chlorine smell to stop being the first thing he noticed every morning, which it never did. Fifteen minutes of on-deck work before anyone touched the water: single-leg balances, hop-and-stick landings, cutting drills between cones. Below the list, in smaller print, a sentence about neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique reducing the risk of knee ligament injuries.

Katrina slapped the sheet with the back of her hand. "Fifteen minutes. Do you know what I could do with fifteen minutes? Sleep. Eat a croissant. Live my life."

"We're in the water for two hours anyway," Daniel said. "What's fifteen more?"

"That's not the point. The point is the principle." She externalized everything, Katrina did, every small grievance dragged out into daylight and given a name, and the team loved her for it, mostly.

Ms. Wijaya, who coached the water polo squad and had apparently taped the sheet, said only that the routine started Thursday and the first match was Saturday, so there would be exactly two sessions to get it right before it counted. Then she went into her office and closed the door, which everyone agreed was suspicious. Coaches who believed in something usually lectured you about it until your ears bled.

Thursday, Sara-Maude balanced on one leg at the edge of the deep end like a heron with a grudge, arms out, wobbling. "This is dignity," she announced to the echoey room. "This is what dignity looks like. Take a photo for my mother."

"Hop and stick," Daniel called, reading off the sheet he'd borrowed from the door, because someone had to keep track and he'd been volunteered by not objecting fast enough. "Two hops forward, land soft, hold it."

"Why soft?"

The honest answer was that he didn't know, so he said, "Because the sheet says so," and Sara-Maude hopped, landed with a sound like a dropped melon, and swore at the ceiling. Behind her, Katrina did the cutting drill, sprinting between the cones with sudden changes of direction, and afterward stood with her hands on her knees breathing hard. "Okay," she admitted. "That one's actually terrible in a useful way. My legs feel like lawsuits."

Daniel had his own theory forming, and it was not yet a good one. His theory was that Ms. Wijaya had simply found a new way to fill the dead time before the pool opened, that the routine was busywork with a scientific varnish, and that the small print on the sheet was decoration. He held this theory loosely, the way you hold a suspicion about a friend, and he tested it the way you test that too, by watching for evidence.

The evidence arrived Friday at the second session, in the person of the trainer, a wiry woman who came in with a bag of cones and stayed to watch Katrina do the cutting drill. "Knees tracking over your toes," she said. "Good. When you planted that last one, you were a centimeter from caving inward." Katrina, who could not let a statement pass without commentary, said, "And if it caves inward, what happens, exactly?" The trainer shrugged. "Ask your knee ligament. Actually, don't. You'll want it intact."

That night Daniel typed the small print into his phone, word for word, and the sentence came back at him from a dozen places, the same claim in every one: neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. He sat on his bed in the blue light and felt the two theories grind against each other, busywork and prevention, and he noticed something slightly embarrassing, which was that it had never occurred to him that warm-ups were for anything other than feeling warm. You jumped in, you got loose, you played. The idea that you could rehearse the exact movements that broke people, the landing and the cutting, and get better at not being broken, seemed almost like cheating, except that it was the opposite of cheating, it was the most legitimate thing in the world.

Saturday morning the natatorium was loud, the other team shouting in the corridor, and the pool lying flat and pale under the skylights like something diurnal that had gotten up early against its will. Fifteen minutes before the whistle, Ms. Wijaya pointed at the deck. The team groaned in harmony, a practiced, musical groan, and then did it anyway, balances and hops and cuts, Sara-Maude wobbling less than Thursday, Katrina's lawsuits apparently settled out of court.

"You've converted," Katrina said, watching Daniel tape the cones down with unusual care.

"Half converted. I'm keeping the other half in reserve in case it turns out to be a scam."

"You're incapable of a full opinion. It's your tragedy."

In the third quarter a girl on the other team planted her foot to change direction and went down clutching her knee, and the pool went quiet in stages, whistle first, then shouting, then even the water seeming to hush. She was helped up and off to the bench, and the game restarted, and Daniel scored once and got beaten twice and swallowed half the pool, as usual. But between plays he kept looking at the bench, at the girl with the ice pack, and then at Katrina carving through the water with her knees tracking neatly over her toes, and he held both images without deciding what they proved, because two sessions of hopping was not a fact and one bad landing was not a statistic, and he knew enough by now to know he didn't know.

Afterward, dripping in the corridor, he found Ms. Wijaya coiling a lane rope. "So is that why you put up the sheet," he said. "The knees."

She looked at him for a second longer than necessary. "Same time Monday," she said. "Bring your own cone."

Florence had pitched the table at the end of the driveway by nine, before the heat flattened everything, and by eleven the pitcher was half gone and she had made nine dollars toward the econ club's trip to the state competition. Sidney sat beside her in the folding chair, scrolling through the practice questions on a cracked phone, reading them aloud in a bored voice that made each one sound like a small insult. "Explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation," Sidney read. "Worth twenty points. We are going to lose."

"We are not going to lose," Florence said, though privately she had written and crossed out the same answer four times the night before. The difficulty was that she could recite it and did not believe it, and she suspected that the judges, like her, could hear the difference. Joaquin arrived on his bike then, freewheeling the last stretch, and put two dollars on the table without asking for lemonade, which was his way of joining the club treasury and also of stalling.

"Tell me this," Florence said. "When the central bank raises rates, why does that fix prices? I keep saying it and it sounds like magic."

Joaquin took the cup she poured him anyway. "It's not the whole answer, but there's a rule," he said. "The Taylor rule. This guy John Taylor proposed it. When inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point." He said it the way he said most things, as though handing over something he had found on the ground and did not much care about keeping.

Sidney looked up from the phone. "More than one? That's the part I got wrong on the practice set. I said match it. If prices go up one, raise the rate one. That seemed fair."

"That's what I would have said too," Florence said slowly. She was quiet for a moment, working the paper rim of her cup with her thumbnail. So the bank was not supposed to be fair. It was supposed to overshoot, deliberately, by some amount, and the whole argument of the policy lived inside that little gap between one and more than one. She thought of her mother saying you don't fight a fever by making the room exactly as warm as the fever, and then thought that her mother had never said that, that she was inventing the analogy and then crediting it, which was a habit she meant to break before college.

"Write it on the sign," Joaquin said. "People love rules."

So they did, or Florence did, in marker on the back of the cardboard price list, and the three of them argued about how to phrase it while a line of customers looked at the tennis balls and the cooler. A man from down the street, Mr. Hamdan, who coached debate at the middle school and bought lemonade every Saturday, read the sign over Florence's shoulder with his cup still raised partway to his mouth.

"Inflation up one, rate up by more than one," he read. "Whose idea?"

"John Taylor's," Sidney said. "There's a rule named after him."

"Careful with rules," Mr. Hamdan said, which was as close as he ever came to advice, and he paid his dollar and walked on. Florence watched him go and decided he meant that a rule was a starting place, not an answer, and also that she had no idea whether he meant that or something less generous.

The afternoon brought the harder question, which Sidney asked without looking up from the phone: who pays when the bank overshoots. Because somebody always pays. It was not, Florence understood, a thing that would appear on the score sheet, but once she had seen it she could not sequester it in some separate part of her mind where inconvenient questions went to wait. Raising rates by more than inflation rose meant loans that got expensive faster than paychecks grew, meant the kind of tectonic pressure that built quietly and then moved through people's mortgages and hiring decisions, meant someone like the cashier at the pharmacy where Florence's mother worked, whose hours were the first thing cut when business slowed. To stabilize prices was to lean on somebody, and the rule never said whom.

"Maybe that's why it's called a rule and not a law," Joaquin said. "It's a starting place. You still have to decide."

"That's not on the test," Sidney said.

"It should be," Florence said, and meant it, and also knew that at the competition she would write the clean version, the one with the gap between one and more than one rendered confidently in her neatest handwriting, and that she would feel a small complicity in the tidiness of it. She could hold both things now: the answer they needed and the answer she actually had, which was that the rule told you the size of the push and nothing about the people it pushed on. What she could not yet hold was whether knowing that made her better at economics or only sadder in a way that looked, from the outside, like understanding.

At five they poured the last of the pitcher into three cups and split the thirteen dollars, and Sidney counted it out twice, and Joaquin pocketed his share and said the trip was as good as funded if they sold cold brew next week. Florence copied the sign, the whole thing, rule and all, into her notebook before the ink could smear in the evening damp.

"Quinn," Sidney said, using the old nickname from middle school Spanish class, "you're going to write the sad version on Saturday, aren't you."

Florence capped the marker and looked down the street where Mr. Hamdan had gone.

"I'm going to write the true one," she said, "and then the one that scores."

The line outside the middle school gymnasium was longer than Jonathan expected, and slower, so that by the time he reached the folding tables near the doors he had read every poster about provisional ballots twice. It was his first election. He had turned eighteen in March, and the registration card had arrived in the mail like a small credential, less exciting than his acceptance letters but somehow more official. Behind him, Dalton was arguing with Yousef about whether their votes mattered at all, given the district.

"Statistically, one vote decides nothing," Dalton said. "It's a ritual. We reify the ritual by showing up, like that makes it real."

"It's not a ritual for my uncle," Yousef said. He held up his phone, screen tilted so they could both see. A livestream from another country, a chamber full of representatives, a Speaker calling a division. "This is happening right now. My dad's been watching since four in the morning."

Jonathan leaned in. The numbers were climbing on a board at the front of the chamber, green votes and red votes, and a banner along the bottom of the broadcast was cycling through a phrase in translation: motion of no confidence, motion of no confidence, motion of no confidence. The count finished. The government had lost. The chamber erupted, some members standing and applauding, others slumping, and the camera cut to the prime minister, who was gathering papers without looking at anyone.

"So what happens now?" Jonathan asked. "Do they impeach him? Is there a trial?"

"That's not how it works there," Yousef said. "It's a parliament. It's not like us." But he didn't say how it did work, and the line moved, and the three of them shuffled forward past a woman with a stroller and a man still wearing his work ID on a lanyard.

Jonathan kept turning it over while he waited. He had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that every country removed a leader roughly the way his did: a long process, an accusation, a chamber of judges, a threshold so high it had almost never been crossed. But the broadcast had shown something different, a single afternoon, a single vote, and a prime minister stacking his papers. Was the head of government just an employee of that chamber, hired and fired by it? The thought made the office seem smaller and stranger, or maybe larger, because it meant the majority in the lower house could reach up and take power back whenever it lost patience. And yet it also seemed to make the whole thing faster, almost casual. A prime minister could fall because of one bad Tuesday.

He was still holding his phone, watching the aftermath, when the anchor said it plainly, almost in passing: a government that lost such a vote in the lower house had to resign, or call a general election and put the question to the whole country. That was it. Two doors, and the fallen government itself chose which one to walk through. Jonathan read the closed caption twice. He pictured a president here losing a vote like that, and could not, and the failure of the picture told him more than any diagram in the civics textbook he had half-read senior year.

At the check-in table, Ms. Kobayashi, who had taught him world history and now apparently spent Election Day finding names in a binder, located him without looking up. "Jonathan Reyes. First time?" she said, and when he nodded, she handed him the marker to sign the line. He noticed she had a small television behind the table, muted, tuned to the same foreign channel.

"You're watching it too," he said. "The no confidence thing."

"It's called a vote of no confidence," she said, initialing his form and moving him along, already reaching for the binder again. "Third one this year over there."

In the booth, Jonathan slid his ballot out of its sleeve and looked at the names, the local ones, the ones he had researched in October and argued about with Dalton in the group chat. He found himself wondering whether any of the people on this paper, if they won, could be removed this quickly by anyone, or whether the machinery here was built the opposite way, heavy and slow on purpose, vestigial parts included, so that only the rarest crises could ever dislodge anyone. Or whether slowness just protected people nobody wanted to protect. He could argue it both ways, and he noticed that he wanted to argue it both ways, right there in the booth, with his marker hovering over the ballot.

He voted. Outside, the line had grown longer, and Yousef was holding his phone up over his head. "They're calling an election," Yousef called to him across the barrier. "Six weeks. The whole country votes again."

The card table wobbled on the second hinge, so Aiden folded a napkin into quarters and wedged it under the short leg while Avery counted the cash box for the third time that morning. Forty-one dollars and change. Avery wanted ninety by Sunday for the concert ticket, and had calculated that at a dollar a cup they needed two more good Saturdays, assuming weather held and the bike path stayed busy. Aiden's own stake was smaller, a vague promise of pizza money, but he had agreed to the whole of today's shift because Avery had a dentist appointment at eleven and because he was trying, for reasons he could not entirely codify, to be a more dependable person this summer.

The morning came on warm and slow. Sprinklers hissed across the lawns, and a man in an obsolescent walkman-era jogging suit passed twice without buying anything. At ten the radio they'd brought out on the back step, tuned to the news station because Avery's mother liked it, announced that the Federal Reserve had raised rates again to fight inflation. Aiden was pouring a cup when the customer at the table, a woman with a toddler on her hip, frowned at the radio and said, "Which rate is it they keep raising, do you know? My mortgage? Something else?"

Aiden opened his mouth and found nothing in it. He had half absorbed the phrase "the Fed raised rates" from a hundred headlines without ever asking which rates, or whose. "I think it's like the rate banks pay the government," he said, and heard the guessiness in his own voice and disliked it. The woman nodded the way people nod at weather, paid her dollar, and moved on, but the question stayed at the table with him like a wasp he couldn't leave alone.

When Meadow pedaled up at half past eleven with a backpack and an appetite for free lemonade, Aiden had his phone out and was reading with the concentration of an acolyte confronting a dense scripture. "Don't tell me you're doing homework at a lemonade stand," Meadow said, stealing a cup. "It's not homework," Aiden said. "That lady asked me a question and I made something up. Sort of. I want to actually know." Meadow leaned over his shoulder, slurping. "Know what, exactly?"

"Okay," Aiden said slowly, reading, then reading again. "So the Fed's main policy rate, the one they move when you hear 'the Fed raised rates,' is called the federal funds rate. And it's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." He said it out loud twice, testing the weight of it. "Not the government lending to banks. Banks lending to banks, overnight." Meadow raised an eyebrow. "Why would banks lend to each other overnight?" "I genuinely don't know yet," Aiden admitted. "But at least now I know what the thing is."

The hard part, he discovered over the next hour, was not the knowing but the saying. He tried out an explanation on Meadow, who had appointed herself a skeptical audience. His first attempt collapsed into jargon halfway through. His second was so vague it could have described anything. Meadow kept one condition on her refills: he had to make it plain enough that she, who claimed to find all economics a form of arithmetic gossip, could repeat it back. Between customers he scribbled on the inside of the poster board, crossing out sentences, hunting for the shape of the idea rather than its costume.

By two o'clock the path had thinned and the sprinklers had gone quiet. Aiden had settled, provisionally, on this: the Fed moves the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves, and that rate ripples outward until borrowing costs more everywhere, and when borrowing costs more, people and businesses spend more slowly, and prices stop climbing so fast. He could feel the seams in it, the places where he was repeating rather than understanding, the word "reserves" still slightly opaque to him. He told Meadow that too. "I can say it," he said, "but I can't defend every step of it yet. If someone asked why slowing spending tames prices, I'd probably improvise, and I saw today where improvising gets me."

At quarter to three Avery came back with a numb cheek and a revised forecast, down to one more Saturday instead of two because a neighbor had promised to buy two pitchers for a block party. While Avery recounted this, the woman from the morning reappeared on the return leg of her walk, toddler now asleep in a stroller. "You figured out that rate thing?" she asked, half smiling. Aiden wiped his hands on the towel and stood up straighter behind the table. "It's called the federal funds rate," he said. "It's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." She looked at him for a moment, then at the radio, then back. "Huh," she said. "So what does that have to do with my grocery bill?" Aiden reached for a fresh cup, filled it slowly, and began.

The practice rooms off the band hallway smelled of valve oil and old carpet, and Elizabeth had claimed the one with the working piano every Tuesday and Thursday since September. Ms. Zhou had posted the assignment on Monday: sixteen bars, a melody with chord changes, written out by hand in standard notation, due in three weeks. Elizabeth wanted it to be good, not passable, and the difference between those two things was taking up all the space in her head.

The trouble was the seventh bar. She could hear it, the melody stepping up and then holding, filling the space before it turned and came down again, but when she wrote it out the bar came up short. One beat, gone. She counted the sixteenth notes twice, tapped the pulse against the piano's closed lid, and still the bar ended a beat too early, leaving a hole where the held note should have been.

Alyvia knocked on the door with her knuckles the way they had agreed on in September, two quick and one slow. She had her theory notebook under her arm and a granola bar in her teeth. "Are you hiding or working," she said around it.

"Working. Come look at this." Elizabeth slid over on the bench. Alyvia leaned in, chewing, and read the stave with her finger hovering above it without touching the page. The radiator under the window ticked, and somewhere down the hall a trumpet worked through a scale badly, the same missed note three times.

"Your melody is right," Alyvia said. "I can hear it. But the bar's short."

"I know it's short. I don't know how to fix it without chopping the tune into pieces."

Alyvia tapped the half note in question. "What if you just make it longer?" She took the pencil from behind her own ear, and before Elizabeth could object she added a small dot after the note, then sat back on the floor with her knees up. "A dot after a note adds half the note's value. So a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4."

Elizabeth looked at the mark, so small on the page, so consequential. She counted it through under her breath, one-two-three, and the bar closed like a door swinging shut. "Three beats," she said. "That's exactly the hole." She played it, and the melody finally sounded the way it had sounded in her head, the held note suspending the line before it turned.

"It's funny," Alyvia said, unwrapping a second granola bar she had apparently been sitting on. "Violette got so mad about this exact thing last week. She said notation is a virulent conspiracy to make simple music complicated. She used those words. Virulent."

"She said conspiracy?"

"She was having a day." Alyvia shrugged. "I told her the symbols are just the cheapest way to get the sound out of your head and into somebody else's. She said that was too optimistic for a Tuesday."

Elizabeth copied the bar onto a fresh sheet, dot and all, then played the whole sixteen bars through. In places it worked. In the ninth bar the chord change she had chosen, a minor chord where she had first wanted major, made the melody sound sadder than she had intended, and she could not decide whether that was a discovery or a mistake. Both readings felt true. She played it twice more, once believing each one, and the music seemed to change under her hands, though the notes on the page stayed identical.

When Ms. Zhou came by during the last fifteen minutes of the period, she stood in the doorway with her arms crossed, listening without commenting. Elizabeth finished and kept her hands in her lap. She wanted to say that the piece was finished and she wanted to say that it was not finished, and both statements felt like lies from certain angles.

"The seventh bar," Ms. Zhou said. "Good solution."

"I almost didn't find it," Elizabeth said. "Alyvia showed me the dot."

"Then you'll know where to look next time." Ms. Zhou glanced at the page. "Bring the ninth bar to class on Thursday. I'm curious what you decide."

After she left, Alyvia stood and brushed cracker dust off her jeans. "What are you going to decide?"

Elizabeth played the ninth bar once, major, and once, minor. She had wanted, all along, for the assignment to be something she could control completely, every choice deliberate, arrived at by her own volition, and this was the part nobody had warned her about: that the music had wants too, or seemed to, and that following them felt less like deciding and more like negotiating. She could not prove the minor chord was better. She could only play it and feel the room tilt.

"I don't know yet," she said. "That's allowed, right?"

Alyvia zipped her notebook into her bag. "Probably. You're the one who has to hand it in."

They walked out together past the practice rooms, one of which had gone quiet, and the hallway lights hummed overhead. Elizabeth held the folder against her chest with both hands. In the ninth bar the melody went up into the minor chord and then, in the tenth, came down by step, and she caught herself walking in that rhythm, three beats and a turn, all the way to the parking lot.

The thermometer read 150 exactly, and Camille pulled the roast out of the oven with a confidence she did not entirely feel. Behind her, the screen door banged twice, once for Megan and once for Hamzah, who had promised to help and had so far only helped themselves to the lemonade her mother had left in the fridge.

"Is that it?" Megan asked, peering over her shoulder at the pan. "That's the whole dinner?"

"That's the whole dinner. My parents get home at seven, and I said I'd handle it." Camille had said it in a moment of ambition, on the phone, after her mother had worked three doubles in a row and sounded tired in a new way. She had imagined herself calm at the stove, the backyard smelling of rosemary, everyone impressed. The imagining had not included the part where she stood in the kitchen alone with a slab of beef and a phone with nine percent battery.

Hamzah leaned against the counter and studied the roast like it was a problem set. "So it's done? A hundred fifty is done?"

"That's the number the recipe said. Medium well." She had the page printed out, actually printed, because her phone was dying and she distrusted herself enough to want paper. The recipe had a strange sentence near the bottom, something about resting the meat, which she'd skimmed and moved past. Now she read it again while Megan set three glasses on the picnic table on the back porch.

The sentence said the temperature would keep climbing while the roast rested.

"Keep climbing," she said out loud. "How would it keep climbing? It's out of the oven."

"Maybe they mean it stays hot," Hamzah offered.

"It says rises. It says it can rise by several degrees." She looked at the roast, glossy and brown, and felt the first thin thread of doubt. Several degrees of what, though. How many. The recipe was generous with adjectives and stingy with numbers.

Megan came back in. "Table's set. What's wrong?"

"Nothing. Maybe nothing." Camille typed carryover cooking into her phone before it could die, and the search results loaded in a slow crawl. She read with her finger on the screen. Carryover cooking, it said, means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast can rise by several degrees internally while it rests. She read it twice. "So if I pulled it at 150 because I wanted 150," she said slowly, "then by the time everyone eats it, it's not 150 anymore. It's past it."

"Past it meaning what?" Megan asked.

"Meaning overcooked. Meaning dry." Camille set the phone face down on the counter as if it were suddenly an unreliable witness. The clock over the stove said 6:12. Her parents were due at seven, which was less a deadline than a wall she was walking toward. She couldn't put the roast back in to un-cook it. That was the thing about heat, she thought; it only moved in one direction, like time, which was a comparison she would have rolled her eyes at in an essay but which felt true here in the kitchen with the oven ticking as it cooled.

Hamzah, who was less a gourmand than a person who regarded food as fuel, still understood the shape of the problem. "So next time you take it out early. Like at 145, and it walks itself up to 150 sitting on the counter."

"That's the idea. Carryover cooking. But this time I didn't, so." She covered the roast loosely with foil and stood there in the yellow light of the kitchen window, listening to the cicadas start up in the backyard. Through the screen she could see the picnic table Megan had laid out, the cloth her mother only used in summer, three glasses catching the last of the sun.

"Next time," Megan said, "test it on us first. Practice roast."

Camille almost laughed. She had wanted this dinner to be a kind of proof, that she could be trusted with the household for one evening, that she was already the version of herself she kept planning to become in college. And now the centerpiece of the proof was going to come to the table slightly over the line she'd aimed for, through no carelessness of her own, or maybe exactly through a carelessness of her own, since she'd skimmed the part of the recipe that mattered. She couldn't decide which, and she found she could hold both at once, the way you can know you did your best and also know your best had a hole in it.

She carried the roast out to the picnic table while it was still too hot to carve, and set it down on a folded towel, and the three of them stood around it in the backyard with the light going amber at the edges of the fence. The tomatoes and bread were fine; the salad was actually good; the roast was the question. When her parents' car pulled into the driveway at ten to seven, she still hadn't cut into it.

Her mother came through the side gate first, still in her work shirt, and stopped at the sight of the table. "You did all this?"

"Most of it. The roast might be a little more done than I meant." Camille picked up the knife. "I took it out at the right temperature, but it turned out the temperature keeps going after the oven. It rises while it rests. Several degrees, for a big roast. I didn't know that this morning."

Her father was already pulling a chair around. "So carve it, and we'll see."

She cut the first slice, and everyone at the table leaned in to look.

The wind came off the fields the way it always did in March, boreal and thin, flattening the grass inside the track oval until the white lines looked like seams on a pressed sheet. Charlie stood at the edge with a clipboard she had borrowed from her mother's office and watched the under-twelves run their scrimmage, which was what they ran every practice, every week, all season. The ball travelled in long hopeful punts. Nobody passed to anyone who wasn't already shouting for the ball. She had been put in charge because the regular coach was on leave, and because she was seventeen and had played since she was eight, and because nobody else had volunteered.

The losing was not the problem, exactly. It was the sameness of the losing.
