Ms. Paquette, the instructor her mother had hired, sat in the passenger seat with a clipboard she never once wrote on, which Lily chose to interpret as confidence rather than indifference.

Two weeks earlier, waiting for her permit test, Lily had stood in that beige office and read a poster on the wall because Jana's texts had stopped coming and there was nothing else to look at. Drivers aged sixteen to nineteen, the poster said, had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven. She had read it twice. A boy beside her, maybe fifteen, was quizzing his mother on road signs and getting them wrong with total serenity, and Lily had thought, not kindly, that the poster was really about him.

That night Jana had texted her a long message about why she hadn't gone through with signing up for the permit test herself, and Lily had read it under her covers with the screen brightness turned low, the way you read anything important. "I'm not saying I'm scared," Jana wrote, "I'm saying the numbers are the numbers, and you don't get to opt out of being a statistic by being special. My cousin rolled a car at seventeen and everyone still calls him the lucky one. Maybe I'll do it next year. Maybe the risk per mile goes down when you're twenty and I'll just wait it out. Anyway tell me how the Kmart lot is, you said that's where they teach you, that's so grim, I love it."

Lily had typed back a joke about the ghost of retail past and then deleted it, because it wasn't what she meant, and what she meant was harder to say: that she had taken the test anyway, and that she wasn't sure whether that made her brave or merely lucky in a way that hadn't resolved yet. She settled on "it's next week, I'll bring you a slushie after," which underwrote the whole arrangement between them, the promise standing in for the reassurance she couldn't manufacture.

"Gentle on the gas," Ms. Paquette said now, in the tone of someone describing weather. Lily's foot had been, in her own accounting, gentle. The car lurched and stalled, and the silence afterward had a texture to it. "Again. Turn the key. This time imagine you're pouring something you don't want to spill."

"That's a nice image," Lily said, restarting the engine. "My friend Jana thinks nobody our age should drive at all. She read the same poster I did."

"She's not entirely wrong," Ms. Paquette said, which Lily felt was a betrayal of the entire transaction. "Almost three times the fatal crash rate of anyone twenty or older, per mile. It's on the poster because it's on the data. Doesn't mean you stay home. Means you pay attention." She adjusted the mirror on her side, the way people do when they've decided the conversation is over.

They practiced turns between the faded lines, and Lily found she could do two things at once only if she stopped narrating them to herself, which was its own kind of quiet. On her fifth attempt at a three-point turn she thought of Saad, who had gotten his license at seventeen and driven everyone everywhere with an air of destiny, and how she'd once told him he drove like a lawsuit waiting to be filed. He'd laughed. She'd meant it, mostly. There was a small casuistry she'd been running for a year, telling herself that her caution was principle while his confidence was recklessness, when honestly she had just been afraid, and dressing fear up as judgment felt, in the empty lot, with the wheel warm under her hands, like the one thing she'd done that was genuinely dishonest.

The car crawled through the turn. She checked her mirror, checked it again, completed the maneuver without stalling, and Ms. Paquette said "adequate," which from her appeared to be a decoration for valor. Lily laughed, surprising herself, a short sound in the closed car.

"You can pull up by the cart corral and set the brake," Ms. Paquette said, checking her phone. "That's our hour."

Lily eased the car toward the corral, where a single shopping cart stood abandoned against the rail, listing slightly, and she brought the car to a stop a careful three feet from it, then, after a moment's thought, another foot closer. She pulled the handbrake and let her hands rest on the wheel, and outside the windshield the cart shifted in the wind, rolled a half-turn, and stopped.

"You'll book the next one?" Ms. Paquette asked, already gathering her clipboard.

"I'll text my friend first," Lily said, and reached for her phone on the passenger seat behind the instructor's bag.

The departures board turned over three times before the gate agent announced that the flight to Lisbon would be at least four hours late, and Payton sat down on the cold tile beside the window and opened her laptop on her knees. Mr. Tran had assigned the population profiles before winter break, one page per student, hers due by midnight no matter where in the world she happened to be. She had Portugal. She had meant to finish it on the plane.

Beside her, Moses was reading a guidebook with his feet stretched across their shared duffel bag, and Alexy had gone to buy sandwiches. The three of them were going to visit Alexy's grandmother for the holidays, an arrangement their parents had codified in a group email with rules about curfews and spending money, rules that Moses had already printed and annotated with jokes.

Payton's page needed one thing: a decision. Would Portugal in thirty years need more schools or more nursing homes? She had a printed copy of the country's profile chart folded into the front pocket of her backpack, and she spread it now on the tile, smoothing the creases with the heel of her hand. The chart looked like two towers standing back to back, bars of different lengths, numbers along the sides. She had assumed, from the first glance on the bus to the airport, that the left side showed females, because she was used to reading left to right and thinking of herself first. So she had started drafting a paragraph claiming the profile was bottom-heavy, wide at the base, young.

"The bars," Moses said, leaning over without invitation. "That's a population pyramid, right? My sister did one." He pointed at the stacked rows of ages. "Youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top, like a building."

"I know that part," Payton said. But she didn't know which side was which, and now she was worried she had it backwards, and the paragraph on her screen was built on a guess.

Alexy came back with sandwiches and dropped into the third chair. "Gate's a zoo," she said. "Some man tried to board with a fish tank." She looked at the chart. "What's the assignment?"

"Predict what the country needs. Schools or nursing homes." Payton turned the paper sideways, as if the problem would rearrange itself. The longer bars, the wide part, whichever sex that was, sat in the middle ranges, the forties and fifties, and the bottom of the chart was narrow. She knew what a narrow base meant if she let herself say it. Fewer young people. But if she had the sexes flipped, her whole reading of the imbalance flipped too.

Mr. Tran had told them, on the last day of term, that the assignment was less about Portugal than about how they reasoned. "Anybody can look up an answer," he had said. "I want to see the seeing." Payton had thought this was a teacher's way of making things harder than necessary. Now, with four hours of delay and a midnight deadline, she thought it might be the only useful thing he had said all semester.

She searched on her phone, holding it low so the screen glare wouldn't wash out, and found a page from a geography text with a caption underneath a similar chart. Males on the left, females on the right. She read it twice, then set the phone face down. So the left tower was males, the right females, and the ages stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top, exactly as Moses had said, and her draft paragraph had the sexes reversed. The asymmetry she had noticed, one side bulging more than the other in the middle years, belonged to the men, not the women. That mattered for the nursing homes question, she supposed, since women in most countries lived longer, and the chart showed that too, in the thin pale rows at the top where the female side stretched further.

She deleted the paragraph and started over. The wide middle, the narrow base, the long female tail at the top: put together, they pointed toward an older country, one that would be stocking pharmacies and building wards before it broke ground on primary schools. But she made herself write the counterweight as well, the honest part. A narrow base could recover; people moved; policies changed. A prediction was not a law of physics, more like a guess about a system trying to hold its own homeostasis, a population adjusting itself over decades in ways no single chart could codify. She wrote that she was confident about the direction and uncertain about the speed, and left it there.

"Done?" Moses asked, when she hit send at 9:40 p.m., one minute after the boarding call finally crackled through the terminal.

"Done enough." She folded the chart along its old creases and put it back in the front pocket. Alexy shouldered the duffel and Moses picked up the sandwich wrappers, and the three of them joined the slow, turbid line snaking toward the jet bridge, and Payton kept her boarding pass in her hand the whole way, uncreased.

The gray came out of the tube the same way it always did, a plain slab of nothing, and Faith pushed it across the canvas in two long strokes before she noticed that the strokes did not match. On the left, where she had underpainted a field of raw orange, the gray sat warm, almost fleshy, like cement on a summer sidewalk. On the right, over a patch of scraped blue, the same paint went cold and steely, the color of a January morning. She held the brush above the canvas and did not move it. She had squeezed from one tube. She was sure of that, because she had squeezed it herself, ten minutes ago, in this room that smelled of turpentine and burnt coffee.

The community studio occupied the back half of a shuttered plumbing supply shop, and on Thursday evenings it belonged to whoever showed up with five dollars and a willingness to sweep at the end. Curtis had claimed the easel beside hers in September and never given it up, though he mostly painted girls he had no intention of speaking to. Tonight he was hunched over a portrait with the chin wrong again, and Hugh was at the window doing what Hugh always did, which was three careful marks and then twenty minutes of staring, as if the painting might confess something if he waited long enough.

"Come look at this," Faith said. "Tell me if I'm losing it."

Curtis leaned over, chewing the plastic end of a pen. "The gray's different. Did you mix two batches?"

"One tube. One squeeze. Watch." She dragged a fresh stroke across the boundary so that it crossed from the orange into the blue, and the stroke changed temperature in the middle like a road crossing a county line. Curtis made a low sound through his teeth. Hugh came over, looked for a long moment, and said, "It's the underpainting doing that. It has to be."

Faith wanted a better word than "has to be." She had wanted a better word all autumn, ever since her interview at the art school in the city, where a woman with gray-streaked hair had flipped through her portfolio and said it was promising but undisciplined, that she relied on accident and called it intuition. The sentence had catalyzed something in Faith that she still could not name, a stubbornness that made her want to prove the woman wrong and, in weaker moments, made her suspect the woman was right. The letter from the school was due any day now. She had stopped checking the mailbox because checking made her insufferable, her mother said, and her mother was not incorrect.

Mr. Banerjee, who ran the studio and had run it since before the plumbing shop closed, kept a shelf of warped art books by the sink. Faith went to it while Curtis and Hugh argued about whether the phenomenon had something to do with the lamp. Most of the books were water-damaged monographs, but one, fat and cloth-bound, had a spine she could read: Principles of color. She carried it to the folding table and let it fall open where it wanted.

There it was, in a chapter on a chemist named Michel Eugène Chevreul, who had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839. The page said that a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, mouthing it. Her gray had not changed at all. It had only done what a gray does beside orange and beside blue, pushed this way and that by its neighbors, faithful and deceptive at once.

"Simultaneous contrast," she said aloud, carrying the book back to the easel. "That's what it's called. A chemist figured it out. He published it in 1839."

"Wait, the color moves?" Curtis said.

"No. It looks like it moves. Toward the complement of whatever's beside it." She set the book down open on the stool. "So my gray isn't two grays. It's one gray getting pushed around."

Hugh peered at the page. "So you could plan it," he said slowly. "You could pick the underpainting to make the gray do whatever you wanted."

That was the turn of it, and Faith felt the turn happen in her chest. All term she had let the accidents stand, calling them happy, and part of her had known that the woman in the city was talking about exactly this. But the book said something more complicated than either accident or control. The gray was honest and the gray was a liar and both were true depending on the company it kept. She did not know yet what to paint with that knowledge, only that she had it now and could not give it back.

She worked until nine, laying a new ground of green under a strip of gray she had scraped clean, watching it flush faintly red as it dried. Curtis packed up his travesty of a chin and left without goodnight, which meant he was still angry about the portfolio review, where the visiting critic had praised Faith's accident and said nothing about his portrait. She let him go. It cost her something to let him go, and she paid it.

At the door, in her coat, she stopped and looked at the half-finished strip, green pushing the gray somewhere she had not predicted, her plan already drifting off its rails in a way she could not yet tell was failure. She took out her phone and photographed it, then photographed the open book beside it, Chevreul's name and the date and her one gray becoming many.

"Tomorrow," she said to the empty studio, "the mailbox."

Peyton counted the thumbnails on her laptop screen for the third time, and the number stayed stubbornly at ten. She was sitting on the porch of the art cabin at Camp Windrow, mosquitos ticking against the porch light, her sketchbook balanced on her knees. Ten pieces. She had planned for ten all summer, a tidy arc around the theme of houses left behind, drawings of doorways and peeled wallpaper and the hollow where a porch swing used to hang. The plan had felt complete in June. Now, in the last week of July, it felt like a house with a missing wall.

She had heard about the AP portfolio from Kayden, who was already a senior and had a stack of college brochures on her bunk like playing cards. Kayden had mentioned it offhandedly over dish duty, scraping macaroni into the compost bin, and Peyton had filed it away and then, tonight, looked it up on the camp's one spotty computer. What she found made her sit very still.

"Sustained Investigation," Kayden said the next morning, when Peyton showed her the screen by the canoe rack. Kayden was wringing out a towel, and she squinted at the page. "That's the section they score. Fifteen digital images. Sixty percent of the whole thing." She tossed the towel over the rack. "You're doing ten."

"I was doing ten." Peyton looked down at the lake, where Talon was trying to teach a cluster of eleven-year-olds to paddle in something resembling a line. "Ten seemed like a real number. Enough to say something."

"Fifteen is the number that counts, apparently." Kayden picked at a splinter on the rack. "Anyway, you've got a year."

The morning passed in its ordinary rhythms, but Peyton kept doing the arithmetic in her head. Five more pieces. Five more doorways, five more empty rooms, and the ten she had already made would have to stretch further, mean more, sit beside five strangers she hadn't planned for. She found herself being petulant about it, snapping at Talon when he splashed lake water near her sketchbook, and then apologizing in a mutter while he looked at her like she'd grown a second head. She took her lunch to the far end of the dock and ate it slowly, letting the fact settle instead of fighting it.

That afternoon, Ms. Kerr, the ceramics teacher who came up from the town on Thursdays, was unloading the kiln in the shed behind the cabin. Peyton watched her lift the finished bowls with tongs, each one wrapped in newspaper, and set them on the shelf like sleeping animals. Ms. Kerr did not ask why Peyton was there. She let her watch, and after a while Peyton found she was able to say it out loud.

"I had it all figured out. Ten pieces, one idea. Now I find out the whole thing is bigger than I built it for."

Ms. Kerr set down a bowl with a hairline crack running through its glaze, a piece she did not discard but placed apart from the others, on its own corner of the shelf. "That one opened in the fire," she said. "I like it better now." She peeled off her gloves. "When I was your age I thought a plan was a kind of promise. It's not. It's a first draft of a promise." Then she went back to the kiln, because she was the kind of adult who knew when to stop talking.

Peyton walked back along the shoreline, past the canoe rack, past Talon's shouting paddlers, and turned the problem over the way she turned a pencil in her hand. One way of thinking said the plan was sacred: ten pieces chosen with intention, each one necessary, nothing padded. Another way said the theme itself was the real thing, and the theme was not finished; the empty houses she drew were about absence, and absence kept generating more rooms the longer she looked. She had been treating the number as the frame. Maybe the investigation was the frame, and the number was just the door you walked through.

She also had to admit, standing on the dock while the sun went copper over the water, that she did not know yet whether the five new pieces would deepen the work or dilute it. That part stayed uncertain, and she let it stay. Entropy was the word that came to her from physics class, the way things drift toward disorder unless you keep feeding energy in. Maybe that was what a portfolio was: not a finished house but a decision to keep paying the energy, image after image, until the disorder agreed to mean something.

She sat down on the dock with her sketchbook and started a list, not of drawings but of questions she hadn't asked yet about the houses. What was behind the wallpaper. Who had left the porch swing. What the rooms looked like at night. Beside the list she wrote, in small letters, fifteen, and underlined nothing.

Kayden found her there at dusk with two cups of cocoa from the mess hall. She sat down, looked at the sketchbook open on Peyton's knees, and read the questions without asking permission, which was the kind of friend Kayden was.

"So you're doing it," she said.

"I'm doing it." Peyton closed the sketchbook and held it against her chest, the cover still warm from the day. Out on the water, Talon's last canoe was coming in, and the paddlers were singing something off-key. "Hand me the cocoa," she said.

Logan stacked the last crate of tomatoes and checked his phone again. Dana was ten minutes late, which meant he would be alone with Mr. De Vries for ten more minutes, and Mr. De Vries liked to talk.

"You're the one doing that economics thing," Mr. De Vries said, weighing peppers for a woman in a sun hat. "The presentation." He said it the way people said the word homework, kindly but without much hope for it.

"Tuesday," Logan said. "Explaining how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation." He wiped the scale with a cloth. The market smelled of cut cantaloupe and hot plastic tablecloths; somewhere behind them a guitar case lay open with a few coins in it. "I've got the first half down. Rates go up, borrowing costs more, people buy less, prices stop climbing so fast. It's the second half I can't get right."

Mr. De Vries handed the woman her change and watched her walk away before he answered. "And what's the second half?"

"The part nobody puts on the poster." Logan turned a peach that was bruising where it touched the wood. "My grandfather loves telling it, actually. Last Sunday, at his kitchen table, he started on Volcker. Grandpa kept a newspaper clipping from when the rate hikes finally beat inflation, and he called it the cleanest thing the government ever did. And then my uncle put his coffee down and said, easy for you, you weren't in the unemployment line in eighty-two. I hadn't known that. My uncle lost his job that year. He said unemployment went above ten percent during that recession, ten percent, and he made me say the number back to him twice." The kitchen had gone quiet except for the clock over the stove, and his grandfather had looked at the clipping for a long moment before saying that he still thought it had to be done.

Mr. De Vries had stopped wiping the scale. "What did you say to your uncle?"

"That I was sorry. He said don't be sorry, be accurate." Logan could still see his uncle's hands around the mug, the small tremor of it. "That's the second half. Slowing inflation by raising rates usually costs jobs. It's not a footnote. It's the price."

Dana arrived then, ponytail damp, apologizing about a bus. She and Logan were doing the presentation together, and she slid behind the table beside him and started arranging sweet corn the way the market's ordinance required, husks on, stacked no higher than the crate rim. The city had passed it last spring; Mr. De Vries called it the most circumscribed pile of corn in the state. Dana had laughed at that for a full minute the first time she heard it.

"Okay, run it by me," she said. "Mr. De Vries, you be the teacher. Be merciless."

Mr. De Vries folded his arms. "Young man. You tell me the central bank raises rates. Tell me why I should care."

Logan took a breath that smelled like peaches. "When rates go up, loans get expensive, so people and businesses spend less, and when spending slows, prices stop rising so fast. That's how it tames inflation." He picked up a plum and put it back. "But it's not free. Slowing inflation this way usually costs jobs, because when people stop buying, companies cut workers. In the early eighties, when the Fed hiked rates hard to kill inflation, the recession it caused pushed unemployment above ten percent."

Dana was nodding, but Mr. De Vries wasn't. He was looking at the far end of the market, at the honey stall, and his jaw was working.

"You said your uncle," he said finally. "Eighty-two."

"Yeah. Why?"

Mr. De Vries untied his apron, retied it, untied it again. "Because I was there too. Machine shop outside Akron. Fourteen years, and one morning the foreman read a list of names and mine was on it." He set the apron on the crate of tomatoes. "I don't know if it was the rates or just the recession. Nobody ever told me that, and I've had forty years to wonder. That's the honest answer, and you can put that in your presentation if you want. Nobody ever tells you which part of it was you."

Nobody spoke for a moment. A customer came and Dana sold her a bag of green beans, weighing them with a steadiness that seemed, to Logan, like a kind of mercy.

"I keep wanting there to be a right answer," Logan said quietly, when the customer had gone. "Like, the hikes were good, or they were bad. But my grandfather's clipping and my uncle's unemployment line are both true."

"That's not a failure of your research," Mr. De Vries said. "That's the research." He put his apron back on, took a peach from the bruised pile, and handed it to Logan. "On the house. Eat it before it goes deleterious on me."

Dana laughed. Logan bit into the peach, which was sweeter for the bruise, and juice ran down his wrist and he didn't wipe it away.

The dealership smelled like new carpet and lemon polish, and Zachary had spent enough Saturdays behind the buffer to know that the smell was the most expensive thing on the lot. He worked the detailing bay three days a week, minimum wage plus tips whenever a salesman felt generous, and every dollar went into an envelope in his desk drawer at home. Six hundred and forty dollars. Nine months of weekends.

He'd been saving for a car since October, a notion that had transfigured his whole idea of the future: with a car he could take the shift at the grocery store in Fairview that paid three dollars more an hour, could drive himself to the winter tournaments instead of begging rides, could stop being a person whose plans had to be approved by somebody with keys. Then, three weeks ago, Coach had pulled him aside after practice and mentioned the summer showcase in the city, the one scouts attended. Registration was two hundred and fifty dollars, not counting the bus. The deadline was Monday.

Both were impossible together. That was the arithmetic he carried around the lot on Saturday mornings, wiping handprints off hoods, and no amount of hoping made the envelope in his drawer grow.

"Did you hear that thing yesterday?" Draven asked him at lunch in the break room, phone propped against a sugar jar. Draven worked the phones at the front desk and listened to podcasts through one earbud all day. "The British and the French built this airliner, the Concorde, years back. Spent a fortune on it. And by the time they knew there was no economic case left for it, they kept pouring money in anyway. They'd already spent so much that quitting felt like losing everything." He tipped the earbud out. "It's called the Concorde fallacy. Throwing good money after bad because you can't stand walking away."

"That's stupid," Zachary said. "Once you know it's bad, you stop."

"Everybody says that," Draven said, "right up until they're the ones holding the ticket."

Zachary didn't think about it again until Tommy came in at four, morose in a way that had become his weather. Tommy had quit the detailing bay in January for a kitchen job at the steakhouse on Route 9, and he hated it, and he was still there. He sat down across from Zachary, unlaced his boots, and rotated his ankle like it ached, and the boots were the expensive non-slip kind he'd bought before his first shift, ninety dollars of his own money. "You still doing the showcase?" he asked. "My brother said the scouts actually show up to that one."

"I don't know yet. I've got to decide by Monday. What's it to you?"

"Nothing." Tommy relaced the boot, cinched it too tight. "I'm thinking about getting out of the kitchen. Six months of double shifts and I still want to quit every single day."

"So quit."

"I've got ninety dollars in boots, man. Plus the knife set, plus I already did the worst months, the training months. Leaving now means all that was for nothing."

Zachary opened his mouth to say it was already for nothing either way, then heard the shape of the sentence and shut it. He thought of the governments and the airliner, the money they knew was gone and kept spending anyway. He thought of Draven's line about the ticket, and how certain he himself had sounded at lunch, and how cheap certainty was when it wasn't your money in the boots.

It was Mr. Farah who brought things to a point. The sales manager had noticed Zachary lingering by the used lot on his breaks, had noticed which car he lingered by: a silver Civic, high miles, priced at eight hundred and driveable tomorrow. On Saturday, as Zachary was folding the last chamois, Mr. Farah came into the bay with his jacket already on, keys in hand. "I can do seven fifty on the Civic if your father co-signs," he said. "But I need to know tonight, because there's a man coming at ten tomorrow morning who wants it."

Seven hundred and fifty. Zachary had six hundred and forty and a fifty from his grandmother he'd been pretending wasn't there. The numbers fit. The car could be his by tomorrow afternoon, and Monday's deadline would take care of itself, the way impossibilities do.

He stood by the silver Civic while the lot lights buzzed on, moths beginning their slow circles above the sodium glow. He put his hand flat on the hood, still warm from the sun it had been sitting in all day, and it seemed to him that the showcase was a ticket too, one he couldn't appraise the way Mr. Farah could appraise a trade-in. If he passed on the car, he gave up the better job, the rides, the two years of being his own driver, and if he passed on the showcase he might be giving up something he couldn't even name yet, and no one would ever tell him the price of the thing he hadn't bought. That was the part nobody mentioned when they talked about choices, he thought, wiping a last smudge off the windshield with his sleeve. You never got to see what the other one would have become.

He took out his phone and typed a text to Mr. Farah, deleted it, typed it again, and stood there so long the moths had settled and the lot had gone quiet.

"I'll know by nine," he said finally, out loud, to nobody, and pressed send.

Cameron had drawn the graph four times and it was still wrong. Two axes, fish on one, lumber on the other, a curve bowing between them. Mr. Singh had assigned it on Friday: pick two countries, give each a production possibility frontier, then show what trade could do for them. Cameron's trade point sat stubbornly outside his curve, in blank space, like a plane flying past the edge of a map. He pressed the pencil down until the graph paper dimpled.

"You're wrecking that page," his mother said from the doorway. She set a mug of tea on his desk, close enough to reach but far enough from the ink. "Homework or art project?"

"Neither, apparently." He turned the page so she could see the point floating in the white. "The trade point lands out here. That can't be right. A country can't consume more than it can make."

She peered at it, shrugged with real apology, and told him she'd eviscerated her own economics notes years ago, sold the textbook back for eleven dollars. He thanked her for the tea and heard her pause at the top of the stairs, then go down softly, the way she did when she knew he needed quiet more than help.

He texted Marilou, who was better at graphs, and Bria, who was better at arguing. Both said they'd come. While he waited he redrew the curve one more time, slowly, checking each end. Norway, he had decided, could make either forty tons of fish or twenty of lumber if it put everything into one. Canada could make thirty of fish or thirty of lumber. He'd made up the numbers and now he was trapped by them.

Bria arrived first, dropped her bag on his bed, and bent over the desk with her hands on her knees. "This is a travesty of geometry," she said. "Your axes aren't even the same scale." She took the ruler out of his pencil case without asking, which was how they'd been since fourth grade. Marilou came in ten minutes later smelling of rain, shook out her umbrella, and pulled his desk chair around backward so she could straddle it beside them.

"Okay," Marilou said. "So Canada gives up one ton of fish for every ton of lumber it makes. Norway gives up two tons of fish for every ton of lumber. So Norway should do the fish and Canada should do the lumber. That's the whole thing, that's comparative advantage." She tapped the curve. "Norway has the lower opportunity cost in fish. So Norway makes only fish, Canada makes only lumber, and then they trade."

"But look." Cameron plotted the totals, then split them down a plausible deal, and the point for what each country got to consume landed outside its own curve again. He waited for one of them to laugh. Neither did. Bria leaned closer, and he watched her run it the same direction he had, Norway keeping thirty tons of fish and taking nine of lumber, ending up past the line it could never cross alone. "It's not a mistake," she said slowly. "That's the point of the assignment. By specializing and trading, each country ends up consuming a combination of goods that's beyond what it could produce on its own. Like, actually beyond the frontier. Off the graph's map."

"So what do I write, that everyone wins forever?" Cameron heard his own voice go bellicose, a defensive tone he hated in himself, and lowered it. "Sorry. It's just, someone has to lose, right? That's what my uncle says about trade."

Marilou rotated the page, studying the two curves side by side. "Maybe not the way you drew it," she said. "Maybe both get combinations they couldn't reach alone. That's what the math shows here." She hesitated, which was unlike her. "I don't know what it shows in the real world, with real countries. That part we're not going to settle tonight."

"That's honest, at least," Bria said. She slid the ruler back into the pencil case, then took it out again and set it beside the graph, aligned with the trade line, as if to hold it in place. Cameron copied the diagram onto a fresh sheet, careful and slow, and wrote his first sentence underneath. Outside his window the streetlight came on, and his mother called up that there were leftovers if they wanted them. He kept writing while Marilou and Bria argued pleasantly about the uncle, and the point outside the curve stayed exactly where it was, out past the frontier, in the blank space where nothing had been drawn yet.

Katherine had the display board under one arm and the folder of data in the other, and she had walked to the library because Reagan had texted that she owed Katherine an apology. She did not feel owed anything. She felt like the vinegar had gone warm in her hands, the way it did before something curdled.

The experiment had been simple, which was the problem. She had tested whether seedlings watered with diluted chamomile tea grew taller than seedlings given plain water, and after three weeks the chamomile trays had won by a margin she could see without measuring. She had measured anyway. Eleven millimetres. At the science fair, Keon had looked at her chart for exactly four seconds and asked whether she had repeated it, whether anyone else had repeated it, whether she had considered that her bedroom window faced east and her neighbor's maple had leafed out mid-trial and changed the light. She had not considered the maple. She had wanted to tell him that the maple was not her variable, that her variable was chamomile, that the whole point of controls was to isolate one thing. Instead she had said something short, and Keon had said "whatever" in the tone people use when they mean the opposite, and Reagan had laughed, and now Reagan was texting about apologies.

She found Reagan at the corner table by the periodicals, headphones half off, and set the board down across from her.

"I didn't laugh at you," Reagan said. "I laughed at the way he said repeat it. Like he's the FDA."

"He's not wrong, though." Katherine sat. "That's the part I can't stop thinking about. He's not wrong and it still felt like an attack."

Reagan pulled one headphone free entirely. "So what are you doing here?"

"Looking for why it felt like that. And whether I should redo it."

She left Reagan guarding the board and went into the stacks. The sociology section was two aisles she had never had reason to visit, shelved between psychology and something called methology before the label corrected itself to methodology. She was looking for anything about how science decides things, because the fair judge, a woman with a lanyard and a clipboard, had written one line on her evaluation card: claims are accepted by a community, not by an experiment. Katherine had read it eleven times on the bus and understood it less each time.

The book she pulled was about the sociology of science, and she stood in the aisle reading it the way you drink from a water fountain too long, bent and unwilling to stop. In 1942, she read, the sociologist Robert K. Merton had named a norm of science organized skepticism. The words sat on the page in that order. Claims, he argued, must survive critical scrutiny by the community before they are accepted. She read the sentence twice. Keon's four seconds and his question about the maple had not been cruelty, or not only. They had been the ordinary weather of the whole enterprise, something scientists were inured to the way sailors were inured to cold spray off a fjord, not because it was pleasant but because it was the climate the work happened in.

She carried the book back to the table and read the passage aloud, quietly, her finger under the line.

"Organized skepticism," Reagan said, when Katherine finished. "That's a great name for it. It sounds like a club you get drafted into."

"It kind of is. He wrote it in 1942, and it's a norm, not a law. Nobody forces it. The community just won't accept a claim until enough people have kicked it around, repeated it, tried to break it."

"So Keon was doing sociology at you without knowing it."

"Keon was doing science at me without knowing it." Katherine closed the book. "Which is almost worse, because I can't be angry and correct."

Ms. Demetriou passed with a cart of returns and paused at their table, her eyes going to the seedling chart. "Are you the chamomile girl? I judged near your aisle. Eleven millimeters, was it?"

"Eleven and a half, averaged."

"Are you redoing it?"

"That's the decision." Katherine looked at the board, at her neat bar graphs, which now seemed to her nascent rather than finished, a first word in a conversation she had mistaken for a verdict. "If I redo it, and it holds, it means more. If I redo it and it doesn't, then Keon caught something real. Either way I'd rather know than win."

Ms. Demetriou stacked two books on her cart that had nothing to do with anything and said, "The window in the study room faces north, if that helps," and rolled on.

That was the twist, though Katherine didn't recognize it as one until later: the library had a room for this. She gathered the board, asked Reagan to carry the folder, and went to claim the key. In the north-facing study room she found Keon already sitting there with three trays of soil and a bag of chamomile, headphones on, a ruler laid parallel to a notebook like an instrument waiting for a hand.

He pulled the headphones off. "I started without you. Same seeds. Your watering schedule's on the shared doc." He turned the notebook so she could read the first page, which was blank except for the date and a column headed plain water and a column headed tea. "I figure my window's different. That's the point, right? Different window, different person."

Katherine set her board against the wall, unopened. She pulled out the chair across from him, took the ruler, and drew her own columns beneath his.

"Take the north window," she said, and marked her first seed.

The playground behind the community center still had its toddler equipment, a plastic slide and a climbing frame shaped like a doomed spaceship, but for three weeks it had belonged to the summer frisbee league, whose members were seventeen and too proud to admit they were practicing on mulch. Chloe sat on top of the spaceship with her cleats dangling, holding the league's phone with the filmed match from Tuesday, because Tuesday was the match she could not stop replaying.

Teagan climbed up beside her, peeling a tangerine. "You've watched that four times. Mr. Goh is going to eulogize the frisbee at this rate. He gave a whole speech about effort at midfield today."

"He wasn't eulogizing anything. He was mad." Chloe tilted the screen. "Watch this part. Third point. Blake's wide open on the right and I don't throw to her, and then watch her face."

Teagan leaned in, squinting. "She looks like a seagull that got its chip stolen. That's just her concentration face."

"No, she goes flat after that. For the whole rest of the game she stops cutting hard. And I said nothing. I just let it sit there like a dead raccoon between us."

Teagan offered a tangerine segment, which Chloe took, because tangerine diplomacy could not be refused. "So say something to her."

"I tried yesterday. I said she should be more aggressive." Chloe pulled her knees up. "She said, and I quote, 'I am aggressive, you just never look at me.' Then she did a fake laugh and left. So now I have two problems instead of one."

Blake arrived at the base of the spaceship with a water bottle she was using as a microphone. "This just in, local girls scheming on a climbing frame, film at eleven."

Chloe looked down at her, and something in her chest performed a slow, unhelpful somersault. Blake was easy to tease and hard to correct, because Blake treated all criticism as either a joke or a declaration of war, with no middle country. Chloe had spent Thursday night reading, of all things, an article her cousin had sent about how workplaces trained their managers to give feedback, because that was the kind of person Chloe was when a friendship had a dead raccoon in it.

She climbed down to the mulch and turned the phone around. "Blake. Do you have two minutes? I filmed the game and I want to show you something, and I want to try saying it a different way than I did before."

Blake's eyebrows went up, but she sat on the bottom rung. "Is this an intervention? Is Teagan here to hold me down?"

"Teagan is here to eat tangerines and judge us," Chloe said. "Okay. I read this thing. It's a model from the Center for Creative Leadership called Situation-Behavior-Impact. You name when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. That's the whole thing. So instead of 'be more aggressive,' which means nothing and also sounds like an insult, I'm going to try the actual version."

Blake made a gesture of go on, but she had gone still in a way that was not unfriendly.

"Tuesday, third point, I had the disc and a look at the right side." Chloe held up one finger, then two. "You made three hard cuts toward the end zone, and each time you slowed down before I even started my windup, like you'd decided in advance I wouldn't throw. And the impact was that I stopped reading you as an option, and we lost the point, and honestly I felt like you didn't trust me, which made me play worse too." She heard her own voice shake slightly on the last clause and kept going anyway. "That's it. That's the whole thing."

Blake peeled the label off her water bottle in one long strip, which was what she did when she was actually thinking. "You counted my cuts?"

"I watched it four times."

"You watched it four times." Blake looked at the label, then at Chloe, then at the doomed spaceship as if it might offer a postulate superior to anything available on the ground. "Okay. Here's mine, then, same rules. Tuesday, fourth point, you had the disc, I was open for two full seconds, and you threw a hospital pass straight to the other team. Impact: I yelled 'CHLOE,' in a tone my grandmother would call unbecoming, and then I sulked for six points because I decided you were being malevolent, which, for the record, I no longer postulate. You were probably just scared of the wind."

"I was scared of the wind," Chloe admitted. "It was a very windy day."

"It's an outdoor league, Chloe."

"I'm aware it's an outdoor league."

Teagan dropped tangerine peel onto both their heads from above, and Blake scrambled up the frame after her, and the three of them ended up in a mulch-scuffling heap by the slide, which was not in any feedback model Chloe had read. Later, when the others had gone for slushies and Chloe was coiling the cones, she turned the thing over once more. She still did not know whether the model would hold on a day when the criticism was bigger than a frisbee throw, or whether naming an impact honestly was kindness or just a tidier way to wound someone. She only knew that Blake had stayed for the whole conversation, and that Thursday's rematch was supposed to be windy again.

She picked up the last cone and, at the edge of the field, heard Blake calling her name from the slushie line, holding up a cup the color of something radioactive.

Alexis had arranged the living room with the seriousness of a stage manager: chips in the auxiliary bowl, the good one reserved for later, chairs angled toward the screen, the good lamp turned off because Dylan insisted it created a glare. By the time the tip-off came, his father had claimed the armchair, Dylan was folded onto the rug, and Marie-Soleil sat on the arm of the couch with her phone face-down on her knee, a gesture of discipline she would not keep for long.

In the third quarter, the Raptors' shooting guard made his fifth consecutive basket, and Dylan rose from the rug like a man witnessing something religious. "He's on fire," Dylan said. "Feed him the ball every possession. He cannot miss tonight."

"Every possession," Alexis's father said, "is exactly how you lose a lead. He's due to miss."

Alexis felt the old argument unfold with the familiarity of furniture. One side believed in the fire, the other in the correction, and neither side ever conceded anything, which was maybe why they enjoyed it. Tonight, though, he wondered whether there was anything underneath the argument besides preference. Was a streak a real thing a player entered, like weather, or just a story people told about randomness after the fact? He took out his phone.

"He's heating up again," Marie-Soleil said, and indeed the guard had made two more, one of them from distance with a hand in his face. She turned her phone over and started typing, which meant she was having the same question, or betting on something, or telling her brother to turn the game on.

Alexis found it quickly, because the internet had already had this argument thousands of times. A study from 1985 by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky had looked at streak shooting and called the "hot hand" an illusion. That was the phrase the paper used, the exact word, and Dylan would not like it. The study had said, in essence, that what fans saw as fire was just the ordinary wobbling of chance, that a player's makes after makes were no more likely than his makes after misses. For thirty years that had been the settled answer, the one his father would have cited if his father cited anything.

Then, in 2018, two researchers named Miller and Sanjurjo went back over the old study and found a statistical flaw in how the streaks had been counted. When they corrected it, the evidence pointed the other way: streak shooting looked real. Alexis read the sentence twice, partly because he wanted it to be true and partly because he had learned to distrust that wanting. He liked the idea of fire, the idea that a person could catch something and carry it for a while, but liking an idea was not a reason.

"Alexis," his mother called from the kitchen, "the extra dip is in the fridge if you want it." He got up, carried out the small auxiliary errand, and came back to find the argument in full bloom. Dylan was enunciating each word with the exaggerated patience of someone who thought he was surrounded by fools: "You. Give. Him. The. Ball." Marie-Soleil was scrolling with her thumb and holding the phone so her eyes could do two things at once.

"I found something," Alexis said, and the room half-turned, the way a room does when the game goes to a timeout. "There was a study in 1985, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. They said the hot hand is an illusion. Streaks aren't real, just chance."

"See," his father said, gesturing with a chip.

"Wait," Alexis said. "In 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo redid it and found a flaw in the statistics. With that fixed, they found evidence of streak shooting." He heard his own voice get quicker, the way it did in seminar when a paper actually worked. "So the fire might be real. Or might not be, exactly. Two smart papers, thirty years apart, opposite answers."

Marie-Soleil had stopped scrolling. "So nobody knows?"

"Two groups of people with numbers think they know," Alexis said. "That might be different."

Dylan pointed at the screen, where the guard was standing in the corner waiting for the inbounds pass, sweat-dark, jaw set, five for five in the quarter or six, nobody in the room quite sure. "Tell your studies he doesn't exist," Dylan said. "Look at him."

Alexis looked. The guard caught the ball, dribbled once without looking down, and rose into his shot with the unhurried certainty of a man closing a door behind him. The whole room leaned forward, Alexis included, papers and flaws and thirty years of argument suspended somewhere above the couch.

It rattled once on the rim, soft, and dropped through.

Eli had parallel parked the family sedan between two recycling bins eleven times in the school parking lot, and on the twelfth attempt he clipped the one standing in for the front bumper. Ms. Romano, his neighbour three doors down, who had agreed to supervise his practice hours in exchange for his hauling her yard waste to the depot in June, watched from the curb with her thermos. She was a taciturn woman who graded his driving the way she graded everything, with a small nod or its absence. Today she gave the nod anyway, which he understood to mean the bins were not people and the sedan was not her car.

The problem was Saturday. Alec had tickets to a show two towns over, no transit after ten, and a mother who had announced she was done being a taxi service for boys old enough to vote. If Eli did not pass the road test on Friday afternoon, Alec's forty dollars would evaporate, and Alec had mentioned this, by Eli's count, every day since Sunday. Alec's older cousin had agreed to be backup driver, but the cousin worked Fridays and Saturdays and, in Alec's phrasing, "smelled like a bait shop," so this was less a plan than a threat.

"You're amortizing the lesson cost over my gratitude," Alec said on Wednesday, riding shotgun while Eli circled the school block for the fourth time. "Every hour you practise, the concert gets more likely. That's basic finance."

"That's not what amortize means."

"It's close enough."

Ms. Romano sat in the back out of some private principle, leaving the front to Alec, who narrated. Eli worked the wheel between the bins until the parking no longer required thought, until his hands did it and the rest of him was free to worry about the other thing, the on-ramp, which no amount of bins could simulate.

The other thing had a history. On Monday, at the ramp onto Route 9, Eli had frozen. He'd crept up the merging lane at forty while the traffic streamed past at highway speed, and a truck had braked behind him, and Ms. Romano had said, quietly, "Again tomorrow," which from her was a paragraph. He'd read the handbook that night under his blanket like contraband. The acceleration lane, it said, was for reaching a speed close to that of highway traffic before merging. Merging slowly, it said, forces others to brake. He had read it four times and still felt the two facts pulling against each other, because everything his body wanted at forty was to slow down, and everything the page wanted was for him to speed up.

Thursday after last period, he drove Alec and Channing, who had attached herself to the operation because her own test was next month and she claimed to learn by osmosis, out to Route 9. In biology they'd just finished a unit on homeostasis, how a system fights to hold its balance, and Channing kept using the word for everything, including the thermostat in the gym and Alec's mood. "This ramp is your homeostasis," she said from the back. "Highway's in equilibrium. You have to arrive already matching it, or you knock the whole thing out."

"That's actually not terrible," Alec said.

Eli signalled, checked the mirror, and entered the acceleration lane with his foot already moving. He brought the car up to a speed close to that of the highway traffic, closer than he had ever voluntarily gone, and looked over his shoulder into a gap that three seconds earlier had been a wall of metal and was now an open doorway. He merged. Nobody braked. The car settled into the lane as though it had always been there, and behind him Channing let out a breath she had apparently been holding since the school lot.

"There's the difference," Alec said. "Monday you made that truck slow down. Now nothing had to change for you."

"It felt like the wrong thing," Eli said. "Going fast to be safe. It still feels backwards."

"Physics doesn't care about your feelings," Channing said, and then, "I'm stealing the homeostasis line for my test."

They took the next exit and looped back so Eli could do it twice more, and both times the gap appeared, or he made it appear, which was possibly the same thing and possibly not, and he could not have said which. On the third pass Ms. Romano, from the back seat where she had sat saying nothing, leaned forward slightly.

"Tomorrow," she said, "the parallel parking comes first. Do it the way you do the bins."

The test was Friday at two. Alec waited in the parking lot with the tickets in his jacket, standing where the bins had stood, arms out like a man measuring a space that wasn't there yet.

Maelle had read the thermometer wrong the first time, and the chocolate had seized into a grainy gray slab, so on the second evening at the campsite she set the pot in the coals at the edge of the fire and watched the numbers like a hawk. She had brought the couverture in a cooler from home, two kilos of it, because the farmers' market on Saturday had a table for students and she intended to sell dipped apricots and small bark shards, and she refused to sell anything that bent instead of snapping.

Aiyana sat on an overturned crate beside her, sorting apricots by size. "You know it's chocolate," she said. "People will buy it either way."

"They'll buy it once," Maelle said. "Then they'll remember me as the girl with the waxy chocolate."

Jai came back from the washhouse with wet hands and a theory he'd been carrying since lunch, which was that Maelle was pathologizing a batch of candy. She let him have the joke. He was the one who had wandered past Mr. Francis's site that afternoon, and Mr. Francis, who kept an apiary and sold honey at the same market, had mentioned something offhand that Jai now delivered like a dispatch: that the chocolate on the market tables last summer had sat all day in the sun, solid on the table, and still melted the instant you put it in your mouth. Body temperature, he'd said. That was the whole trick. Chocolate set solid below the body and gave up above it.

Maelle stirred and thought about that. She had learned tempering as a procedure, cool it, seed it, warm it back, hold it steady, but she had never thought about what the procedure was for. The chocolate on the table could survive the sun because the crystals that mattered melted at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, a shade under body temperature, and that was why a properly tempered piece held its shape in a warm hand and still dissolved on the tongue. She said it out loud once, without the numbers, and Aiyana frowned and asked how a person could make something sit right on the edge like that, and Maelle said that was exactly what tempering was, as far as she could tell: persuading the fat into the one crystal form out of several that set shiny and snapped clean. She didn't say Form V, because she wasn't sure enough yet to name it. Later she would check her notes against the phone in the car, and the name would be there, and she would feel the small seismic shift of a procedure turning into an understanding, but that came after.

What she had instead was the thermometer reading 45 and falling, and the seed chocolate she'd chopped going in a handful at a time, and the shine beginning to come up on the surface like a steppe horizon at the end of rain, wide and level and sudden. Jai leaned over the pot with the flashlight. The marsh behind them was ticking with frogs. Somewhere down the loop a child was being called to bed in a patient, practiced voice.

"Test it," Aiyana said.

Maelle dipped the tip of a knife and laid the smear on a strip of foil on the cool stone table. They all watched it as though it might do something theatrical. It did nothing. It sat. Then, after a minute that felt longer, it dulled slightly and set with a dry edge, and when she pressed her fingernail to it, it resisted and then gave with a faint click.

"That's it," she said, though she kept the doubt in her voice on purpose, because a smear was not a shard and a cool stone was not a July table in direct sun.

They dipped apricots until the light failed, working fast, and set the tray inside the car with the windows cracked, which was a compromise between humidity and raccoons that Maelle was not entirely satisfied with. In the morning the chocolate had held its gloss, and she broke a corner off a shard and it snapped, cleanly, the sound more like a twig than a candy, and the broken face was matte and tight and looked like slate.

Aiyana put a piece in her mouth and closed her eyes. "It's gone already," she said. "It wasn't like that yesterday."

At the market, Mr. Francis came by near noon, when the sun was flat on the table and the samples had sat out for two hours without a bloom mark. He picked up a shard, held it in his closed fist for a slow count, then ate it. Maelle watched him, wanting the verdict and also not wanting it, because his fist was one test and a customer's mouth was another and she was beginning to suspect that the space between them, that degree and a half or so, was the whole art and not something she would ever fully own. He turned the remaining piece over in his fingers, unmarked by his hand.

"Solid in the fist," he said, "and it vanished the moment it touched my tongue. You held it right on the line."

Maelle looked at the tray, at the shine she could see her own face in, and reached for another apricot. "The next batch is on the table in ten minutes," she said.

The playground behind the middle school had one piece of equipment Anthony still visited: a rusted basketball hoop with no net, its backboard warped by some long-ago winter. He stood at the free-throw line with Siena's borrowed physics worksheet folded in his back pocket and a tennis ball in his hand, because the quiz was Monday and the problems might as well have been written in Sumerian.

"Mr. Wang says you split the velocity," Siena had told him on Friday, leaning across the aisle, her pencil tapping the diagram of a cannon on a cliff. "Horizontal and vertical. They don't talk to each other." Anthony had nodded the way he nodded in class, which was to externalize an understanding he did not have, a performance for the teacher's benefit and his own. He'd copied the equations. He'd copied the arrows. Nothing had stuck.

That was the night he remembered now, standing at the line in the cold. His father had been in the kitchen, and Anthony had taken a ball out to the driveway to time a throw with his phone, mostly to avoid the kitchen. His father had come to the doorway with a dish towel over his shoulder and watched without comment, and the silence between them had felt like a held breath. Anthony had thrown the ball straight up, caught it, thrown it again, and on the third throw he'd actually watched the numbers. The ball had left his hand fast. It had slowed, hung, fallen. He'd expected the fall to take longer than the rise, some instinct telling him that climbing is harder than descending. The timer said otherwise. Up and down had matched.

"Nine point eight," Siena said now, arriving with her bike, one wheel still spinning as she dropped it in the wood chips. "Metres per second. Every second." She held out her hand for the ball. "Vertical only. Mr. Wang said it twice and you were drawing that shark."

"I wasn't drawing a shark."

"You were drawing a shark."

He threw her the ball underhand, a lazy lob, and she caught it and launched it high over the hoop, higher than necessary, and they both watched it hang. "Same rate up as down," she said. "Whether it's rising or falling. Nine point eight each second." Then she looked at him sideways. "You didn't come to Oceanne's thing last night."

"I had this."

"Nobody has a worksheet on a Saturday."

He picked up a wood chip and split it with his thumbnail. Oceanne's thing had been a goodbye, he suspected, though nobody had said so. Her family was moving in March and she'd invited everyone from chemistry, and Anthony had chosen rust and numbers instead, and he hadn't decided yet whether that was cowardice or honesty. He suspected his father, also leaving, though nobody had said that either. The dish towel. The doorway. The not-commenting.

"Throw it at the hoop," Siena said. "But tell me where you're aiming before you do."

"Top of the square."

"That's your vertical. The distance is your horizontal. Time connects them. That's the whole quiz." She bounced the ball once, hard, and the sound cracked across the empty playground. "Go on. Aim wrong on purpose."

He aimed at the top of the square, which he would normally have done anyway, and the ball clanked off the front rim. He did it again, aiming higher than felt reasonable, and the ball dropped through the netless hoop, clean, nothing but a soft thud on the asphalt. Siena said nothing, which was louder than saying something. He retrieved the ball and stood there holding it, running the numbers in his head, the rising and the falling at the same relentless rate, the horizontal stroll of the ball across the sky, undisturbed, going its own way while everything vertical fought and surrendered.

"Here's the thing," he said. "I can do the problems now. I think I actually can. But I don't get why it's the same going up as coming down. Nobody's told me that and the book doesn't."

Siena shrugged. "Mr. Wang says that's next semester."

"Next semester," Anthony said. He looked past her at the hoop, at the square he'd aimed at, at the invisible arc he could now calculate but not quite believe in. "Everything important is next semester."

Siena held out her hand for the ball again. "Oceanne's still awake, probably. Her mom lets her have people over till eleven."

Anthony weighed the ball in his palm, its fuzz worn to shine on one side, the lineage of a hundred other hands on it, his father's probably, years ago, in this same yard. The putative excuse of the worksheet sat folded in his pocket, still available, still believable.

"Give me one more shot," he said. "Then we go."

He stepped to the line, aimed above what felt right, and let it go.

My grandfather says I have been practicing the blessing in the car for two weeks, which is a lie, because it has been nine days, and two of those days I was only mumbling. My mother says I have nothing to be nervous about, which is also a lie, because if I had nothing to be nervous about, my hands would not be sweating through my shirt cuffs on the drive to Aunt Rina's house. "You're going to be great," Jaxson said from the passenger seat, holding my phone with the recording of Grandpa's voice. "Although honestly, man, you've played this thing so many times I could say it myself." Colton, from the back, cleared his throat and recited the first four words with a truly offensive accent, and I told him that if he butchered it at the table tonight, my grandmother would never forgive him, which was not a lie at all.

Here is the situation, as I understand it. Kiddush is a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to begin Sabbath and Jewish festival meals, marking the day as holy. Grandpa has said it at every holiday table since before I was born, and this year, because his voice is going and because I am seventeen and apparently it is time, he asked me. He asked me in the kitchen in October, while washing his hands, without looking up, which is how he asks for things that matter. I said yes before I understood what I was agreeing to, which is a habit of mine.

The problem, which I discovered around day three of car practice, is that there are two ways to do this, and each person who cared enough to weigh in cared very loudly. Grandpa sings it, slow and ornamented, the tune his own father used, and when he finishes, the room hums like something struck. My cousin Danit's husband, who converted a few years ago and is more precise about ritual than anyone born into it, says it plainly, each word clean, because in his community the melody is a distraction from the meaning. "The words are the thing," he told me at Rosh Hashanah, tapping the table. "Sing them if you must, but know them first."

I had privately decided that the husband was wrong and Grandpa was right, because Grandpa is Grandpa. Then I spent an afternoon with my phone, listening to recordings from a synagogue I found online, and something shifted. The plain version, word by word, did something to me I did not expect. It slowed the meaning down until I could hear it: the blessing over the fruit of the vine, the blessing that sets the day apart. I had been singing sounds for years without ever once hearing sentences. But then I would put on Grandpa's recording and feel that other thing too, the way the tune carries the room, the way my grandmother closes her eyes at the same note every single time, like a boat finding a channel.

"Are you having a crisis?" Jaxson asked when I played him both versions in the parking lot before tonight's dinner. "Because this feels like a crisis."

"It's a synthesis," I said.

"You don't know what that word means."

"I looked it up."

I had, in fact, looked it up, and also read half of a philosophy forum thread at two in the morning, which either invigorated my thinking or ruined my sleep, possibly both. Somewhere in there I stopped trying to decide which way was correct and started thinking about what the blessing is actually for. It marks the day as holy. That is its whole job, whether it arrives on a melody or on plain words, and maybe the argument between Grandpa and the husband is less like a fight over right and wrong and more like two people building the same door out of different wood. I could not fully convince myself of this. Part of me still believes the tune is the door, and part of me still believes the words are, and I decided, somewhere between the parking lot and Aunt Rina's front steps, to hold both and stop pretending I had settled it.

Mr. Adeyemi from next door was already at the table when we came in, because Aunt Rina invites him every year and every year he brings his own bottle of sparkling juice and asks, with total seriousness, whether this is the one where he gets to hide the bread. "Different holiday," I told him, and he said, "They can't all have hiding, I suppose," with such sullen disappointment that my grandmother laughed into her napkin. He leaned over as I sat down. "So you're the one tonight. My grandmother made me lead the toast at every gathering from age twelve. My hands shook until I was twenty." He held his up, perfectly steady. "Then they shook again when she died. Different kind of shaking." He patted my wrist and turned back to his glass, and I did not know what to do with that, so I did nothing.

The table filled. My grandmother poured the wine and the grape juice, juice for the kids and for Mr. Adeyemi, who was driving. Grandpa sat at his place but the cup came to me, and everyone went quiet in that way that is somehow loud. I stood up. My prepared remarks, which I had rehearsed, evaporated. I looked at Grandpa, and I looked at the husband, and then I looked at the cup, which caught the light from the chandelier like a small bright lake, and I opened my mouth.

I said the words plainly, every one, the way the husband had taught the internet to teach me, clean and unhurried, and then, at the line where Grandpa's melody always lifts off the ground, I let it lift. Not the whole tune. Just enough of it that my grandmother's eyes closed at the right note, and Grandpa looked up at me with an expression I had never seen before and could not read at all.

"Well," Mr. Adeyemi said, raising his sparkling juice. "To the shakers."

"To the shakers," said Grandpa, and reached for the bread.

Connor had wanted to act in the spring one-acts, and when the cast list went up without his name on it, Mr. Nikolaidis called him aside in the hallway by the theatre doors and asked him to direct instead. He said it the way he said most things, briefly, already turning away, and Connor agreed before he had decided to. That was in March. By the second week of April he had learned that directing was mostly standing in the dark rows of the house while other people stood in the light, and asking them to move two steps to the left.

The play was a short one about two sisters arguing over a phone call neither of them had made. Salma played the older sister and she was voluble in rehearsal, generous with ideas, offering interpretations of her character that arrived faster than Connor could answer them. The other actor was quieter, a boy from his chemistry class who kept his hands in his pockets even when the script demanded otherwise. Between them, Connor tried to titrate his corrections the way he titrated acid into base in the lab, one drop at a time, watching for the moment the colour changed. Too much at once and Salma would defend herself for ten minutes; too little and the scene stayed flat.

Samira was the stage manager. She sat at a folding table just offstage with a thick binder, and at first Connor paid her no attention, assuming she was there for props and attendance. Then one afternoon he watched her work. Every time he set a movement, her pencil moved. "That's your cross," she said once, when Salma asked why she had to do it again. "Downstage left, three steps, then turn." She tapped the page, where a tiny diagram of the stage was marked with arrows and abbreviations. "It's in the prompt book now."

Connor leaned over the binder during a break. The pages were dense, not just with movements but with pauses, entrances, where the chair went, when the lamp switched on. He asked how she remembered all of it. "I don't remember it," she said. "I wrote it down." She said it plainly, the way you'd say water is wet, and he felt slightly foolish, as though he'd been carrying something heavy that had a handle he'd never noticed.

Still, he distrusted it a little. The arrows on the page were fixed and the actors were not. On the Thursday before opening, Salma decided her big monologue worked better delivered from the window instead of the table, and she was probably right, it was warmer there, more human, and Connor let it stand. He didn't tell Samira. He told himself the moment was alive and the page was not, and that a living thing beat a written one. Mr. Nikolaidis, passing through the theatre on his way out, said only, "You're the director. It's your call." He meant it as permission, but Connor heard the other half of it too.

Opening night, the little theatre was fuller than he expected. The first scene went well. Then, in the monologue, Salma walked to the table. Not the window. She was tired, or the nerves had pulled her back to the safe road, and she delivered the speech beautifully from a place he had stopped believing in. The monologue landed anyway, the audience leaned in, and after the curtain call Salma found him in the lobby, glowing, and asked how it went. "You were at the table," he said. She frowned. "Was I? I thought the window." They stood there a moment while the lobby emptied, and then Connor said, "Which do you want?"

In the green room after, Samira had the binder open. "The window's crossed out," she said, running her finger down the page. "Thursday's note. It says you approved the change and I never got it, so the book still has the table." That was the whole of it, laid out in pencil. The prompt book held the record so that the blocking could be repeated the same way at every performance, and the book said table, and Salma had done table, and there had been no argument to have. Connor realized he wasn't sure whether the record had saved them or merely settled a question that the performance itself had already answered differently.

He sat down next to Samira and took the pencil. There were two more performances. He drew a small arrow through the crossed-out note, then hesitated, because he honestly did not know which version he believed in, the one he had chosen or the one that had happened without him. He looked at Salma, who was pulling bobby pins from her hair, and then at the stage beyond the half-open door, still lit, the chair exactly where the diagram said it should be. Samira slid the binder closer and waited, pencil sharp, the page blank under the lamp.

The cuff hissed, beeped, and printed its verdict on the little screen: 142 over 88. Eva read it twice, then looked at her mother, who was peeling an orange at the counter as though the machine were merely a rude guest.

"That's not right," Eva said. "The bottom number's under 90. That's fine, isn't it?"

"The nurse didn't think so." Her mother separated another segment and offered it across the kitchen island, which was her way of changing the subject while appearing generous. "She said stage 2. Stage 2, Eva. It sounds like a play I would fall asleep in."

Eva took the orange segment anyway. She had a want now, sharp and specific: she wanted to understand what the machine had accused her mother of, because the accusation had landed on her too, the way family diagnoses always landed sideways. She carried the pamphlet from the doctor's office to the kitchen table, where Kacey was already sitting, ostensibly to help her study for the nursing assistant course they were both starting in the fall, actually to eat the orange.

"Look at this." Eva pushed the pamphlet across. The table was still sticky from that morning's maple syrup, an atavistic residue of the pancake era their household had supposedly outgrown, and the paper stuck, then released with a small kiss.

Kacey read with her mouth full. "Stage 2 hypertension means systolic 140 or higher, or diastolic 90 or higher."

"Or. It's or, not and." Eva sat back, feeling the click of it. "So 142 over 88. The bottom's under 90, but the top's over 140, and either one is enough. That's why the nurse said it. Either one. It's like a club with two doors."

"A very bad club," Kacey said. "The sort of club where the bouncer is a cardiologist."

Their neighbor Ms. Li knocked then, returning Eva's mother's measuring cups, which she had expropriated three weeks earlier for a batch of mooncakes and defended ever since with polite, immovable excuses. She set them by the sink, noticed the monitor on the counter, and raised an eyebrow at it.

"The machine has opinions," Eva's mother said.

"Are they going to take the good soy sauce next?" Ms. Li asked. "When they've finished with the salt?" But she said it lightly, and she sat down at the table without being asked, which meant she intended to stay for the interesting part.

Eva turned the pamphlet toward her. "Is this right? Either number high enough counts, even if the other one's fine?"

Ms. Li nodded once, unsurprised, and stole a piece of orange, which Kacey defended with a fork. Nobody explained further, because there was nothing further to explain; Eva had already worked it out herself, and that, she was discovering, was the whole difference between memorizing something and owning it.

"So what changes it?" she asked. "The pamphlet keeps saying diet and exercise, but it doesn't say how, exactly. It's like a recipe that says serves four."

"Then cook it and see," Ms. Li said. "That is what the recipe is for."

The next two weeks became a kitchen experiment with a sample size of one, which Kacey insisted on calling "a monomer study," because she had learned the word in chemistry and refused to let it go to waste. Eva rebuilt the grocery list around it: less of the instant noodles that had quietly colonized the top shelf, more of the vegetables Ms. Li brought over in exchange for continued access to the soy sauce. Her mother began walking the loop around the park with Ms. Li in the evenings, the two of them complaining about each other's pace in a way that was, Eva suspected, the actual point of the walks.

Every few days they took the reading together. 138 over 84. Then 135 over 82. Eva logged the numbers in a spiral notebook, drew a graph, and resisted the urge to draw conclusions from a line this short, this noisy, this full of evenings when her mother had walked and evenings when she had watched television instead. The trend was probably real. She could not prove it was, and she said so at dinner, which Kacey found hilarious.

"You're the only person who makes a success story sound like an apology."

"It's not a story yet," Eva said. "It's four data points and a wish."

The morning before her mother's follow-up appointment, they took one more reading in the kitchen, the cuff hissing its familiar breath over the same spot on the same arm, her mother holding still this time instead of arguing with the machine while it worked. The number came up on the screen and Eva copied it down, then sat looking at it while the orange sat unpeeled between them.

"Tell me the number," her mother said.

"I'll tell you after the doctor does," Eva said, and closed the notebook, and slid it across the sticky table toward her.

The rink had emptied an hour ago, but nobody in the lobby wanted to leave. A television had been wheeled out from the office and propped on two folding chairs, and around it sat Kayla's whole family plus half the neighbours, coats still on, watching the World Cup. The Zamboni had gone quiet in the background. Through the double doors Kayla could see the ice, pale and flawless, waiting for a public skate that would not start for another ninety minutes.

Peter had claimed the good couch by the vending machines. Genevieve sat cross-legged on the floor beside him, working through a bag of salt and vinegar chips, and Kayla's father stood at the back with his arms folded, radiating the particular tension of a man whose team was up by one with four minutes left. Kayla herself sat on the rubber mat by the skate rental counter, close enough to the TV to feel its warmth, far enough from her father that she could pretend not to watch his hands.

The equalizer came in the eighty-eighth minute. A corner, a scramble, a shin pad, and then the ball bulging the net while half the lobby roared and the other half groaned. Peter was on his feet with his jacket half off, spinning it over his head like a lasso, and Genevieve was laughing at him, and Kayla's father had turned away to face the dark rink as though the glass itself had personally betrayed him.

Then the referee made the box signal with his hands and pointed to his ear, and everything stopped.

"What's happening," Genevieve said. She said it flatly, the way she asked questions when she suspected the answer would be boring.

"They're checking the goal," Kayla said. "VAR. It's the first World Cup with it. They used video assistant referees in Russia this year." She had read an entire article about it on the bus that morning, partly because the article was there and partly because she had wanted something to hold in her mind other than the acceptance letter folded into her back pocket, the one she had not yet shown her father.

"So they can just take it back?"
