Grady came with her, because Grady came with everything Rebeka did, carrying a thermos he referred to as "the good coffee" and refusing to share it, which was his one consistent personality trait. The four of them arranged the crates under the canopy: squash, apples somebody's tree had overproduced, bread from the bakery that had gone out of business the month before, and, inexplicably, forty pounds of onions.

The bread was the problem. Rebeka, untying her paper hat, mentioned that her manager threw out three garbage bags of unsold buns every night, and Mr. Goh made a sound like a kettle. He asked whether her manager knew stores and restaurants could donate without being sued, and Rebeka said no, he thought if somebody got sick off an old bun, the restaurant would be finished. Mr. Goh said that was the whole point of the law, the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996, which gives food donors limited protection from liability, and that was why places donated surplus food at all.

"So he's just scared of nothing," Rebeka said.

"He's scared of the thing he imagines," Mr. Goh said, "which is heavier than any real thing."

Jonathan, sorting apples by bruise, felt something shift in him that he distrusted on principle. He had spent the morning privately ranking volunteers by probable college essays, the way he ranked everything, and had put himself near the top on irony. But the law thing snagged him. At lunch he looked it up on his phone behind the onion crates, scrolling with a thumb sticky from apple juice, and found the act described in a government database with all the gravity of a document that had never once been read for fun. His erudition on the subject now extended to one page of a .gov website, which was, he conceded, one page more than Rebeka's manager had.

"He could just call the food bank," Jonathan said, when the lunch crowd had thinned. "They'd pick it up. He doesn't have to do anything but say yes."

"My manager doesn't say yes to anything," Rebeka said. "Last week he said no to a second mop bucket."

"The buns are already in bags," Grady said, from inside his thermos. "It's not like he'd have to touch them again. He's basically throwing away pre-packaged charity."

Rebeka looked at them both with the expression she used when boys were being slow and also, occasionally, right. "I'll ask him Monday," she said. "If he says no, you two are coming with me and explaining the liability thing, because when I say legal words he hears a fire alarm."

The afternoon rush came and went, a retired couple who took squash and complimented the sunflower mural, a man with a wheeled cart who discussed onions at a length Jonathan would not have believed possible, a woman who worked at the library and traded them a stack of novels for a bag of apples. Jonathan found he was good at the table, better than he expected, mostly because he could carry two crates and did not lecture anyone about kale. He had assumed volunteering would be a performance of goodness for an audience of admissions officers. It turned out to mostly be logistics, and the logistics turned out to be satisfying in a way he had no category for, which annoyed him.

By five they were folding the canopy and fighting over who had to take the onion crates back to the shed. Jonathan lost, or won, depending on how you felt about forty pounds of onions, and carried them across the grass while Rebeka walked backward in front of him doing a dramatic monologue about her manager's fears, pausing only to say "limited protection from liability" in a courtroom voice until Grady laughed so hard he sat down on a raised bed.

"You know I'm doing this for my resume," Jonathan said, setting the crates inside the shed door.

"Sure," Rebeka said. "And I'm asking my manager about the buns because I love buns."

"And the buns," said a voice from the shed, "are not going to throw themselves at the hungry."

Mr. Goh emerged with a rake and the reading glasses now on the end of his nose, and pointed it at the last crate still in the grass.

The argument started over a throw-in, of all things. Alec wanted the short throw, Ashton had already turned upfield, and by the time the ball went out of bounds again they were shouting at each other in voices that carried across the whole pitch. Kelly-Anne stood between them with her hands up, saying their names like she was calling dogs off a scent. In the third row of the bleachers a couple of freshmen went quiet and watched.

It had been building for weeks. The team had started the season politely, almost shyly, everyone passing to everyone and apologizing for mistakes they hadn't made. Then somewhere in the middle of October the politeness curdled, and every frustration, every swallowed grievance about playing time and lazy recovering runs, coagulated into something you could practically see at practice, a gray weight sitting in the middle of the field.

At the end of that session Ms. Leung blew her whistle and made them sit on the balls. She was a chemistry teacher who coached soccer because nobody else would, and she had a way of looking at a group that made the group look at itself. "A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages," she said. "Forming, storming, norming, performing. You're storming. It's normal." Then she told them to run a cool-down lap and went to collect the cones.

Ashton ran the lap thinking about it. He hadn't known there was a word for what was happening to them, let alone a sequence, let alone someone who had thought about it in 1965 and decided it applied to more than soccer teams. That night he looked it up at the kitchen table while his mother washed dishes, and he read the stage names twice, forming, storming, norming, performing, and felt something loosen in his chest. It wasn't that they were falling apart. It was that they were on schedule.

The problem was Alec. Alec had done the reading too, or enough of it, and had decided that since the storming was normal, his part in it required no apology. "It's literally a stage," he said the next day, lacing his cleats on the bench. "I'm being a stage." Kelly-Anne said that was the stupidest thing she'd ever heard him say, which launched a fresh argument that Ashton, for once, watched from a distance, like a man standing in a doorway out of the rain.

He tried to think it through honestly. He liked the idea of stages because it promised an ending: storm, then norm, then perform, a line drawn forward through the season. But a sequence wasn't a guarantee, and nothing in what he'd read said a team had to reach the last stage at all. The etiology of their trouble wasn't mysterious, either. It was Alec wanting to be scouted, and Kelly-Anne wanting to win the district title her sister had never won, and Ashton wanting both of those people to still like him in November. A theory could name a stage. It couldn't make anyone pass the ball.

The semifinal came on a cold Tuesday, the kind of night when the floodlights made halos and breath hung over the field like something the grass was giving off. They were losing one to nothing at half, and in the huddle Kelly-Anne said, quietly, that she was done talking about Tuckman. Then, eleven minutes into the second half, Alec took the ball down the left side and, instead of shooting from an angle he'd been hogging all season, cut it back across the box. Ashton was there. The goal was almost silent, the net barely moving, and the lead they took three minutes later was evanescent, undone by a rebound before the crowd had finished celebrating the first.

They went to penalties, and Ashton, who had drawn the last kick out of the hat at practice that morning, stood over the ball with the whole gray weight of the season behind him. He thought, absurdly, of Ms. Leung stacking cones. He thought of the word norming, and how he still couldn't have said whether this was it, whether they had passed through anything at all or simply gotten tired of shouting. The keeper shifted his weight. Ashton exhaled and started his run.

Anais spread the pamphlets across the kitchen table at eleven minutes past eight, with Reanna due at half past and the presentation due first period tomorrow. Ms. Petrov had assigned it on Monday: fifteen minutes on consent, contraception, and where to get tested, delivered to the rest of the peer health class, and Anais had volunteered before she understood what volunteering would cost her.

She exhumed her notes from the bottom of her backpack, where they had spent four days under a gym shirt and a ruined pen. The top page was smeared. The second page held her only solid research, a clinic handout with a statistic highlighted in green, and she read it again while the kettle worked itself toward a whistle.

Reanna came in through the back door without knocking, which was the arrangement. "My mom's still at the courthouse," Anais said. "She's got a deposition tomorrow, so she's reading transcripts at the table like it's the end of the world. We're in the kitchen."

"Fine by me. The kitchen has food." Reanna pulled a stool to the counter and looked at the pamphlets. "So you actually have to say words out loud. To people. About this."

"Kaleb's coming too. He said he'd be the audience so I can practice on someone who won't laugh."

"Kaleb laughs at everything."

"He laughs after, not during. There's a difference."

Kaleb arrived at ten to nine with a bag of clementines and took the chair nearest the auxiliary door, the one that let a draft in whenever the wind came off the school field. Anais stood where the refrigerator handle wouldn't block her, held her smeared notes at an angle she could read, and began.

"Consent has to be freely given, and you can take it back at any point, even in the middle. If someone's been drinking, they can't give it. Silence isn't it. Going along with something because you're scared isn't it." She kept her eyes on the microwave clock. "That part's fine. That part I can say in my sleep."

"Say the pill part," Reanna said, peeling a clementine. "That's the part you keep skipping."

"I don't skip it. I say the pill exists and move on, because the pill part is where I sound like an idiot."

"You don't sound like an idiot. You sound like a person who's never taken it, which you are. So learn the numbers and say the numbers."

Anais put the notes down and picked up the clinic handout. "Fine. Here's what I've got. With typical use, about seven in a hundred people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy." She said it flat, the way the handout said it, and watched their faces to see if it landed. "Typical use. Not perfect use. Typical, meaning people like everybody actually is."

"Seven out of a hundred," Kaleb repeated. "That's more than I thought."

"That's why the nurse at the clinic kept saying set a phone reminder for the same time every day. I kept wondering why she hammered it so hard. Then I found this and it made sense, kind of. People miss doses." Anais paused. "I can't explain the biology of why missing doses matters. I asked my mom and she got weird about it and started talking about her deposition instead."

"You don't have to explain the biology," Reanna said. "You just have to say the number and say the reminder thing. Say: with typical use, about seven in a hundred people on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. Then say, so if someone's on it, a daily alarm isn't fussiness, it's the whole system working."

Anais wrote that on the back of the handout, word for word, because it was better than anything on her smeared pages.

"Now the clinic part," Kaleb said. "Where do people even go?"

"There's the health department on Corbett Street. You can walk in. Testing for infections is free, and it's confidential, which means they don't call your parents, even at sixteen." She had checked this twice by phone, disguising her voice slightly the first time and then not bothering the second. "You don't need money and you don't need a reason. You can just go once a year, like a checkup."

"Are you going to say that part from experience?" Reanna asked.

"No. I'm going to say it because I called and asked, and that's what I'll tell people if they ask. I'm not going to pretend I've done it. I'll say, here's the address, here's the hours, here's what happens when you walk in. And if someone asks me something I don't know, I'll say I don't know and write it down and find out."

Kaleb peeled another clementine and split it in three without being asked. "That's actually a better presentation than pretending," he said. "Half the adults who come talk to us pretend."

Anais ran the whole thing once more, start to finish, while Reanna acted out an audience member who asked annoying questions and Kaleb kept time. Eleven minutes. She cut nothing and added the phone reminder line in the contraception section, where it belonged, and her voice only caught once, on the word confidential.

At ten o'clock her mother came in for water, transcripts under her arm, and stood at the counter listening for a moment without saying anything.

"Seven in a hundred," her mother said finally. "With typical use?"

"That's what the clinic handout says."

Her mother filled her glass and went back down the hall, and Anais squared the pamphlets into a stack, put the handout with its green highlight on top, and set the phone alarm for six.

The Salazars' den smelled like burnt popcorn and jalapeño chips, and Addison had claimed the good beanbag chair before anyone else thought to, which was the kind of tactical achievement her brother would spend the whole night trying to reverse. Twelve people had squeezed in around the Huddens' television because the Huddens had the biggest screen on the block, and also because the Huddens had left for the weekend and given the key to Addison's father, who had opened the door and said, "Enter freely," in his Dracula voice, which never got less stupid and somehow never got old.

The game had been lopsided for three quarters, which was why nobody minded when Marissa started rooting for the away team's point guard, a lanky kid named Dawes who had hit two shots in a row and then, absurdly, a third. "He's heating up," Marissa announced, standing in front of the nachos. "Give him the ball. He's getting hot."

"Two threes," said Justine from the couch, without looking up from the score app on her phone. "That's a streak of two. My grandmother does better at the casino and we don't call her hot, we call her lucky."

"My grandmother is hot," Addison's brother said, and was pelted with popcorn, and the room settled into the comfortable murmur of a game where the outcome no longer mattered and the arguing could. Dawes missed a runner in the lane. Justine raised both fists like she'd won a debate. Marissa said the miss proved nothing because the shooter had been fouled, which the referee, a man both girls now held in personal contempt, had apparently not noticed.

Mr. Islam, the neighbor from two doors down who came to these things for the guacamole and stayed for the arguments, leaned back in the recliner. "The hot hand," he said, in the tone of a man laying down a card. "My father used to say the hot hand is the biggest lie in sports. He had a book of aphorisms. Feed a cold, starve a fever. Never trust a streak. That one was his."

Adisson had been half-listening, but the phrase snagged in her, the way a loose thread snags. Somewhere in the back of her mind there was a shelf, and on that shelf was a video she'd watched at one in the morning in October, recommended by an algorithm that knew her too well. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, 1985. They'd called the hot hand an illusion. That part she'd absorbed while brushing her teeth. But there was a second shelf, a lower one, and on it something about a flaw. "Wait," she said out loud, lifting a hand like she was in class. "Wait, wait. Don't fight yet."

The room looked at her. On the screen, Dawes hit another three, and the crowd noise swelled, transfiguring the den for a second into something almost religious, everyone's faces lit and yelling. Addison talked over it, fast, because she could feel the memory dissolving. "Okay. So there was this study, 1985, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, and they said the hot hand is an illusion. Like, just randomness, people seeing patterns. That's the classic thing, that's what everybody learned."

"Justine's side," her brother said, and Justine bowed.

"But," Addison said, and held up her second finger, "hold on, because I watched this whole video about it and I fell asleep during the boring part and then rewatched it, so I know it. In 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo reanalyzed it and found a statistical flaw in the original, and actual evidence of streak shooting. So the hot hand is real. Sort of. Partly." She paused, aware that she had reached the end of what she could defend. "The math part of the flaw I cannot explain, because the video lost me there, and I will not pretend otherwise."

Marissa made a sound like a courtroom lawyer who has just been handed the winning document. Justine made a sound like the other lawyer. Mr. Islam dipped a chip with great dignity and said, "Two sides of one coin, and the coin is still spinning," which Addison privately found less trenchant than he clearly did. Her father shouted that everyone under twenty had to surrender their phones to verify nothing, the whole point of a watch party being to argue from the heart.

By the fourth quarter Dawes had hit five of his last seven, and Marissa was insufferable, doing a small dance by the television, and Justine had gone quiet in a way that Addison recognized as recalculating rather than conceding. Addison sat in her beanbag with the nacho cheese cooling on her fingers and held both truths like two cards she refused to discard. The streak was probably partly real and partly luck and there was no clean line between them, and the boring part of the video was the part that would have told her where the line was, if she ever bothered to watch it a third time. She thought she might. She thought she might not.

With four seconds left and the game decided either way, Dawes took one more shot from somewhere near the logo, deep and unnecessary and gorgeous, and the whole den rose up off the furniture at once as it banked in.

"See," Marissa screamed over the buzzer. "SEE."

"Two out of three," Justine said grimly, and reached for the last chip.

Sara sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor the night before Eid, counting out envelopes while her mother measured rice into plastic bags. There were seven bags, one for each person in the house, and Sara wrote the names on little slips in her looping handwriting: Ammi, Abu, herself, her three little brothers, and Dadi, who was asleep already with the fan pointed at her feet. Her mother checked the measure twice, then a third time, because it had to be the same for everyone, a set amount, not what anyone felt like giving that day.

"It has to be given before the prayer tomorrow," her mother said, sealing the last bag. "Not after. If it comes after, it's just a gift."

Sara stacked the bags in a crate by the door. "What's it called again?"

"Zakat al-fitr," her mother said, already looking for the tape. "Per person, for every member of the family."

Sara had known about it her whole life without ever really holding it in her hands before. In previous years it had been a thing her parents did on their phones, a transfer made in the middle of cooking, an errand her father ran after the night prayer while she argued with her brothers over who got the good kurta pressed first. This year her mother had handed her the measuring cup and said, you're eighteen, you do it, and the weight of the rice in her palm had surprised her, the way a thing can be ordinary for years and then suddenly specific.

The Eid prayer was held in the big public park off Chandler Road, because the mosque three towns over couldn't hold everyone and the city granted a kind of informal clemency every year, waiving the usual permits so that blankets and prayer rugs could be laid out on the soccer field before the sun got high. Sara's family arrived early, the crate of rice bags riding on her hip. The grass was still wet and cold through her sandals, and men in white and women in pale colors were arranging themselves in rows near the treeline, and somewhere behind her a boy was shouting that he'd found a perfect spot by the swings.

That was where Payton and Kayleb found her. They had come to the park for entirely different reasons, Payton to run the trail loop and Kayleb because Payton had the car keys, and they'd wandered over when they saw the crowd. Payton worked at the smoothie shop near school and had once defended Sara's fasting to a customer who complained that Sara's slowness at the blender was proof of something. Kayleb was acerbic about nearly everything, and he did not make an exception for religion.

"So what's the rice for," he said, nodding at the crate. "Picnic?"

"It's zakat al-fitr," Sara said. "Before the Eid prayer, everyone who can afford it gives it, a set amount for each person in the family. So that poor families can celebrate Eid too." She said it plainly, the way her mother said it, and then felt the strange doubling of hearing her own voice carry the sentence, like the words had been sitting in her chest all night waiting for somewhere to go.

"An entry fee," Kayleb said. "Nice. The whole thing's a system to subjugate people into giving, and everyone just calls it beautiful."

"It's not to subjugate anyone," Sara said, and heard her own sharpness. "Nobody's making us. My mom measured it out three times because she wanted it to be right."

Payton was quiet, watching a man near the collection tables lifting a girl onto his shoulders so she could see over the crowd. Sara followed her gaze and saw that the tables were already piled with rice and flour and sealed envelopes, families streaming past them in their good clothes, each dropping something into the bins before finding their places in the rows. The whole field was doing it, hundreds of households, before the prayer, exactly as her mother had insisted, and she understood suddenly that the order wasn't a rule for its own sake, that it was timed so the food would arrive before the day of feasting began, so that whoever received it would have it on the day itself.

"I don't know," she said, more slowly, because Kayleb was looking at her like he wanted a fight and she didn't want to give him one that she'd lose by winning. "Maybe it can be a system and still be beautiful. Maybe the system is what makes sure the beautiful part actually reaches people instead of just being a feeling." She shifted the crate on her hip. "It doesn't fix anything permanent. It's one day. I don't know what the poor do the day after Eid, and I don't think anyone at that table knows either."

Kayleb shrugged, but he didn't answer, and Payton said the prayer was starting, and the three of them drifted toward the edge of the field where the non-praying could stand without being in the way. Sara carried the crate to the collection table and counted the bags into a volunteer's waiting arms, seven, and the volunteer, an older woman with henna to her wrists, touched each bag as though counting them back, as though the number mattered as much as the rice.

The prayer ended and the field broke apart into hugging and shouting and children racing toward the playground with coins in their fists. Sara's youngest brother barreled into her legs and demanded she come judge a race. She was halfway to the swings when she glanced back toward the collection tables, meaning only to find her mother in the crowd, and saw Kayleb standing at the end of the row of bins, alone, hastily dropping a folded bill through the slot of the box marked for cash donations, then shoving his hands in his pockets and walking off fast in the direction of the trail.

James's mother had volunteered him before she told him, which was how things usually worked. The Kwanzaa celebration had spilled out of the community hall onto Delancey Street, cordoned off between the shuttered laundromat and the arepa stand, and at six o'clock, when the sun was already gone, he was supposed to stand at the small stage near the kinara and explain the day's principle to the gathered families. He had said yes the way you say yes to a mother holding a tray of cassava, and then he had spent the walk over rehearsing what he thought he knew, which was that Kwanzaa was an old tradition, something carried from Africa across the ocean, older than anyone could remember.

Evan found him behind the stage, where James was pretending to straighten a folding table. Evan had come for the food, honestly, and said so, being voluble as ever about the plantains he'd already eaten two of and intended to eat six more of. When James told him what he was about to do, Evan pulled a creased flyer from his jacket pocket, the kind the woman at the welcome table had been handing out all evening, and held it under the string of lights.

"You should read this before you go up there," Evan said. "Seriously."

James read it standing in the cold, his breath fogging the paper. The words did not say what he had planned to say. Kwanzaa had been created in 1966, by a man named Maulana Karenga, and it ran from December 26 to January 1. It honored seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja. Not ancient. Not carried across any ocean. Invented in California within his own grandmother's lifetime, on purpose, the way someone builds a house on purpose.

"Wait," James said. "It's newer than my mom."

"Newer than my dad," Evan said. "Practically an affidavit, that flyer. It's got citations."

James sat down on an overturned milk crate. His speech, the one he had been rehearsing since Tuesday, was now a speech about something that did not exist. He could feel it dissolving, and underneath the panic something more uncomfortable: the question of whether it mattered. People at this festival had been lighting the candles for years, his family among them. His aunt made the necklaces. His little cousins argued over who got to place the ears of corn. If all of it had started in 1966, in a room with someone deciding, did that make it thinner? He had always quietly assumed that older meant truer, that people valorize whatever came before them simply because it came before, and now the ground under that assumption was moving.

Ariana appeared with two cups of ginger beer and gave him one without asking. She was better at this than he was; her family hosted the December 26 dinner every year, and she had recited principles in front of relatives since she was nine. When he told her about the flyer, she shrugged.

"So it was made," she said. "So what. Somebody made your jacket too and you still wear it."

"That's different."

"Why, because nobody gave a speech about your jacket?"

She said it lightly, but it landed somewhere serious. James looked out at the street, at the candles guttering in glass jars along the curb, at the drum circle starting up unevenly near the arepa stand, at Ms. Wiśniewski from the chemistry department at the college standing with her plate, nodding along though she surely didn't know the songs. Everyone here was keeping something alive on purpose. Maybe the purpose was the tradition. Maybe it didn't need to be old to be real, but he wasn't certain, and he didn't think pretending to be certain would help.

"Umoja," he said to Ariana, testing it. "That's tonight. Day one."

"Umoja means unity," she said. "You knew that."

He had known it and not known it, the way you know a word before you ever ask where it came from. His mother leaned around the stage curtain and pointed at her watch, and James stood, took the flyer with him, and folded it into his back pocket. He walked out past the curtain, and the little crowd turned toward him, maybe forty people, breath rising, the kinara behind him with one green candle waiting to be lit after the black one.

"Kwanzaa started in 1966," James said, and heard his own voice steadier than he expected. "A man named Maulana Karenga created it. It goes from December 26 to January 1, and every day has its own principle. Seven of them, one each day. Tonight is the first, and it's the one I was asked to talk about." He paused, and Ariana, in the second row, raised her cup an inch. "Umoja. Unity. Which is easy to say and harder to do, and I'm still working on what it's asking of us, but I think the working is part of it."

His mother lit the candle. Somewhere behind him the drum circle caught a rhythm and held it.

Jonathan had never seen Ms. Silva's living room so full. The whole block had migrated there for the championship because she had the biggest television and the only basement that didn't flood, and now the couch, the stairs, and the carpet were occupied by parents and kids shouting at the same screen. His father sat in the armchair with a paper plate balanced on his knee, and Isla had claimed the spot directly in front of the TV, arms crossed, wearing the opposing team's colors like a dare.

The fourth quarter was tied when the running back stretched for the end zone and the pile collapsed on top of him. The officials convened for a long time, and when the head referee raised both arms, the basement erupted. His father stood up so fast the plate went spinning onto the carpet. Jonathan joined the cheering because that was what you did, but he hadn't actually seen the ball. Nobody had. The camera angle had been blocked by three hundred pounds of tackler.

"Show it again," the coach from two doors down shouted at the screen, as if volume were a remote control. "They have to show it again. That's the whole point of television." Several people agreed loudly. Isla did not cheer; she stood with her hand over her mouth, and Jonathan understood that she had not seen the ball either, and that her silence was its own kind of honesty.

It came to him then, a fact he had picked up in Ms. Silva's media studies elective, of all places, buried in a unit he'd assumed would be boring. He had written it on an index card for a quiz and thrown the card away. Now it surfaced whole. "The first instant replay ever on TV was CBS, during the Army-Navy game, December 7, 1963," he said, and the room quieted enough that he kept going. "A director named Tony Verna devised the system." He hadn't planned to say it out loud; it just seemed important, suddenly, that people yelling for technology to settle their argument should know where the technology came from.

"1963," his father repeated, in the tone he used when he thought Jonathan was showing off. "Fascinating. Now can they show the play." On the screen, they did. The broadcast cut to a replay from the sideline, and the basement leaned forward as one consciousness, every separate opinion suddenly fused into a single held breath. The angle was clean this time. The ball was visible, and it was short of the goal line by what looked like half a football, and then the runner's knee was down.

For a moment nobody said anything. Then the referee appeared on screen and announced, almost apologetically, that the ruling on the field was reversed. Touchback. No touchdown. Ms. Silva's basement divided along its fault line with a speed that would have impressed a geologist: the home side groaning, Isla's small contingent suddenly alive, his father dropping back into the armchair like a man shot.

"The replay's rigged," the coach said. "They slow it down, they pick the angle, they make it look like whatever they want." He was already half out the door for the porch and his cigarettes, but Jonathan followed him, partly to get away from the noise and partly because the accusation bothered him in a way he couldn't immediately name. "It's the same footage," Jonathan said on the porch steps. "They just showed the one clean angle. It's not grandiose conspiracy stuff. The ball was short." The coach exhaled smoke and looked at him with something between affection and pity, the look adults give you when they've decided you'll understand when you're older. "The footage doesn't lie," he said. "The people choosing the footage aren't the footage."

Jonathan stood there while the cold worked into his jacket. He tried to dichotomize it in his head, the way he did for essays: replay good, human judgment bad, technology neutral, humans corrupt. But it kept refusing to sort. The machine had shown the truth and the truth had been reached through a director's choice, the same kind of choice Tony Verna had made in 1963 when he decided the moment was worth repeating. The tool and the hand holding the tool were tangled together, and Jonathan couldn't cleanly praise one and blame the other, and he wasn't sure anyone could.

Inside, the game went on without the touchdown, and the home team lost by a field goal as the clock ran out. Isla found him in the kitchen afterward, where he was helping Ms. Silva stack cups he didn't feel like stacking. "Nice history lesson," she said, and he braced for mockery. "Verna. December 7, 1963. That was actually kind of great." She took the cups from his hands and set them in the sink. "Of course, if the replay had gone the other way, you'd all be calling it the greatest invention in sports."

"That's the thing," Jonathan said. "I'd want to believe it was neutral. I just don't think it is." Isla considered this, drying her hands on her jeans, and Ms. Silva turned off the television in the other room so that the house went quiet except for the ice melting in the punch bowl. "Come on," Isla said finally, nodding toward the door where his father stood waiting, staring at the dark screen. "You can tell him the truth was short by half a football. See how far that gets you." Jonathan pulled on his jacket and followed her out into the cold.

The calculus room still smelled of the floor wax the custodian had put down over the weekend, and Samuel sat in the second row with the box problem in front of him, unsolved for three days. A rectangular sheet of cardboard, twenty centimeters by thirty, square corners cut out, folds up into an open box; find the size of the squares that maximizes the volume. He had written V equals x times the quantity thirty minus two x times the quantity twenty minus two x, multiplied it out into a cubic, and then stopped, because he did not yet know what to do with a cubic.

Mr. Ahmed had put the problem on the board Friday and said only, "You have everything you need." Samuel doubted this. He had pages in his notebook that argued otherwise.

Dakota slid into the seat beside him and looked at his page. "Still stuck on the box?"

"I can get the polynomial," Samuel said. "I can't get the peak of it. I could graph it and zoom in forever, but that's cheating. It's not an answer, it's an approximation of an answer."

"Graphing is how everybody did it for two hundred years," Dakota said. "Before the algebra, I mean."

"That's supposed to comfort me?"

Bruce arrived late, as always, garrulous even at eight in the morning, narrating his walk from the parking lot, the ice on the steps, the janitor who had waved at him with a mop. He dropped his bag and leaned over Samuel's other shoulder. "Oh, the box. I did the box. You want the derivative."

"I know I want the derivative. The section on derivatives is next week. That's the whole problem."

Bruce pulled the textbook from his bag, flipped ahead to a chapter they had not been assigned, and turned it so Samuel could see. The pages were dense with expressions Samuel half recognized: polynomials, then those same polynomials with something written beside them, something that looked like a fraction. d y over d x. The numerator and denominator sat apart, stacked like an actual ratio, and yet the text treated them as a single mark, one symbol with two floors.

"Why does the book write it like a fraction," Samuel asked, "if it isn't one? You can't cancel anything. You can't clear the denominator. It's just lying there."

"That's Leibniz," Bruce said. "The notation dy/dx comes from Gottfried Leibniz, and it's still the standard in mathematics today." He tapped the page. "Mr. Ahmed went on about it Tuesday, when you were at the orthodontist. He said other people invented the same ideas at the same time with different symbols, but this is the one that survived."

Samuel looked at the mark again. It behaved like a fraction and it didn't. It was a machine for stating how fast one thing changed against another, dressed in the costume of a ratio. He copied it into his notebook anyway, because whatever it was, it was the language the book spoke, and he could not afford to be an ideologue about notation when a problem was waiting.

Mr. Ahmed came in, set down his thermos, and saw the textbook open to the wrong chapter. He did not close it. He wrote Samuel's polynomial on the board, the cubic from the box, and said, "Who can tell me where this is biggest?"

Dakota said, "You graph it."

"You graph it. Good. What does the graph do at the top of the hill?" Mr. Ahmed put the chalk against the board and drew the curve with his hand, a long rise, a rounded crest, a fall. At the crest he stopped. "Here. What is the slope here, exactly?"

Nobody answered. Samuel looked at the flat instant at the top, that single moment where the climb had ended and the descent had not begun, and said, "Zero."

"Zero. The slope is zero. And the derivative tells you the slope. So if you can find the derivative of your polynomial, and find where it equals zero, you have found your maximum." He set the chalk down. "Now, the rules for finding it. There are three, and they are shorter than you expect."

He taught the power rule in eleven minutes. Bring the exponent down, reduce it by one, term by term, each term subsumed into the new expression without ceremony. Samuel followed the cubic through the transformation, watching it lose a degree, and came out with a quadratic. He set the quadratic equal to zero, factored it on his own paper, and got two answers: x equals three and x equals eleven.

"Two answers," he said to Dakota. "Two squares I could cut."

"Two flat spots," Dakota said. "The hill goes up, flattens, goes up again or goes down, flattens, goes down. Only one of them is the top."

"One of them is a valley." Samuel went back to the original polynomial and evaluated it, no derivative now, just arithmetic. At three, the volume came out to eighteen hundred and thirty-two. At eleven, the side lengths went negative, the volume came out negative, and a negative volume meant nothing you could fold out of cardboard. He wrote 3 beside the crest of his sketch and crossed out the eleven.

Mr. Ahmed was walking the rows. He stopped at Samuel's desk, looked at the factored quadratic, the two roots, the chosen one, and the volume checked by substitution. He put one finger on the page where Samuel had copied the stacked notation, the numerator over the denominator, the mark that was not a fraction.

"You asked why it looks like that," Mr. Ahmed said. It was not a question.

"It looks like something it isn't," Samuel said. "It looks like a fraction and it works like a rule. I don't know which one to trust."

"Trust what it does," Mr. Ahmed said. "You just did. The box has its maximum at three centimeters. Cut the corners at three." He moved on down the row.

Samuel squared his paper and wrote the answer at the top, then sat with the strange mark a moment longer, the d over the d, honest in the only way that mattered, which was that it got him to three. He still did not know why a fraction that wasn't a fraction had survived three centuries when cleaner symbols had not. He underlined the answer twice.

"Three centimeters," he said to Dakota, and drew the cardboard in his notebook, twenty by thirty, the little squares marked at each corner, waiting to be cut.

The interfaith tent at the harvest festival smelled of fried dough and cardamom, and Ashley stood at the edge of it holding a photocopied page she had read eleven times since Tuesday. Mr. Lawson had proposed the debate himself: could a rule from an ancient text still bind people who lived three thousand years after it was written, and should anyone care? He had assigned her the verse and told her, with his usual judicious calm, that she had to argue from the text itself, not from what she wished it said. That was the hard part. She had opinions. What she needed was evidence.

She had found the evidence on the photocopy, though it had taken her three readings to see it was evidence at all. The verse, Leviticus 19:9 and 10, told farmers not to reap all the way to the corners of their fields, and to leave the fallen gleanings where they lay, for the poor and the stranger. It was a rule about edges. It never said give charity, exactly. It said leave something unreaped, something inconvenient, on purpose, in the margins.

"So your rule is about farming," Jose said, leaning against the tent pole with a cup of cider. "Look around, Ashley. Bouncy castle. Kettle corn. The closest thing to a field is the parking lot." He was her assigned opponent and her friend in roughly equal measure, which made the whole thing harder. "Nobody here reaps anything. Rule's dead. Text it a eulogy."

"That's the lazy version," Ashley said, and immediately regretted the sharpness, because it sounded less like an argument and more like a peccadillo of her own temper. She softened it. "It says the poor and the stranger. That's who it's for. The field is just where the food was. If the food's somewhere else now, the rule follows the food."

Quinlan appeared with a clipboard, because Quinlan never went anywhere without a clipboard, and announced that the debate would happen at four, in front of the folding chairs, and that Mr. Lawson would judge. Ashley spent the next hour walking the festival grounds, which is what she did instead of rehearsing. She passed the embroidered vestments in the heritage hall, the drum circle that had debilitated into a rhythm nobody could follow once one drummer left, and the food stalls, where a woman was sliding unsold loaves into a crate at the end of the bread table.

"Those going to the dumpster?" Ashley asked.

"Cornerstone Shelter, six o'clock, every night of the festival," the woman said. "We bake too much on purpose. My mother taught it. She called it gleaning, the leftover part."

Ashley stood very still. She had been prepared to argue that the rule could translate, in theory, by analogy, with the appropriate humility about metaphor. She had a whole paragraph about agricultural societies and their equivalents. What she had not been prepared for was the rule standing in front of her in a crate, smelling of rosemary.

At four, the folding chairs filled more than anyone expected, maybe twelve people, maybe fifteen. Jose went first and was good, in his loose, amused way. "An honest farmer followed that rule because his neighbors watched his corners," he said. "There is no field, no corner, no watcher. A modern person following an ancient rule is like wearing someone else's glasses. You can do it, but you're guessing at the prescription."

Ashley had written an opening and abandoned it on the walk over. "The verse doesn't say donate," she said. "It says leave the corners unreaped and the fallen gleanings where they fall, for the poor and the stranger. It's a rule about not taking everything. It assumes you'll be tempted to take everything, and it builds the restraint into the harvest itself. The field changes. The temptation doesn't. The bread table here donates its extra loaves to the shelter every night, and they bake extra on purpose. That's the verse with a price tag instead of a shekel."

She heard Jose exhale beside her. She kept going, though her voice thinned. "What I can't settle is whether the rule binds anyone who doesn't accept the book. I think it binds the farmer who believes it. I think it only invites the rest of us. That's not a clean answer. It's the one the text gives."

Mr. Lawson was quiet for a moment, then said he would call it a draw, and Quinlan recorded it with visible dissatisfaction. Afterward the crowd dispersed toward the kettle corn, and Jose helped Ashley stack the chairs.

"So you win by finding the bread lady," he said. "That was luck, not argument."

"It was the argument," Ashley said. "I just found it before I could make it."

Jose hoisted the last chair onto the rack and grinned. "Then you owe me a rematch. Same rule, my side next time."

"Fine," she said, and handed him the photocopy, corners bent from her pocket. "Keep it. You'll need the edges."

Mr. Eze's office smelled of coffee gone cold and the lemon polish he used on the same desk he'd had, he liked to say, since before Charles was born. Charles sat across from him with the deferral form unsigned in his lap, the paper warm where his hands had been holding it for ten minutes.

"You've read it three times," Mr. Eze said. "It hasn't changed."

"It pays real money. Two years at the firm, they cover the rest of tuition after." Charles turned the form over, though the back was blank. "My dad thinks I'd be insane not to take it. He'd have killed for that offer at eighteen."

"And your mother?"

Charles shrugged. "She said it's my decision, which from her means she hates it."

Mr. Eze leaned back. Outside the window, two juniors were dragging hurdles off the track, one of them Gwenyth, recognizable by the red jacket she wore in every season. Rim was probably at the benches with his headphones, waiting for her, waiting for Charles, waiting for the meeting to end so they could drive to the diner and argue about nothing. Charles had told them he'd have an answer by five.

"Can I tell you something my grandfather told me?" Charles said. "It's the only useful thing anyone's said all week, and it's not even about me."

"I'd like that."

"He went for his checkup last month, and he said the doctor spent half the time asking about habits. Whether he smoked, what he ate, how he slept. He thought it was strange, doctors prying like that, so he asked why, and the doctor told him about a study. The Framingham Heart Study. It started following residents of Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948, and it went on so long, tracking a whole town, that it gave medicine the term 'risk factor.' For habits and conditions that raise your risk of disease later on." Charles looked up. "My grandfather said that before that, doctors mostly waited until you were sick. The whole idea that you could look at what a person does now and see something about their future, that came from a study that ran for decades."

Mr. Eze was quiet for a moment, and Charles had the sense of being watched very carefully, the way his chemistry teacher used to watch a titration for the instant the pink would hold.

"So the deferral feels like a risk factor," Mr. Eze said. "A habit. A decision that predicts something twenty years out."

"I don't know if it does. That's the problem." Charles set the form on the desk, then picked it up again. "Gwenyth says I'm treating a job like it's a tattoo. Rim says everything is existentialism with me, that I think any choice ruins all the others. He said it to insult me, but it's kind of true. My grandfather's doctors aren't certain about any one person either, right? They just know what tends to happen. Tends. That's all anybody gets."

The hurdle crew had moved to the far curve of the track. Gwenyth stacked them in threes now, the same girl who in ninth grade couldn't carry her own backpack and used to make Rim do it. People changed under pressure that nobody could see happening. Charles wondered whether his grandfather, at the first exam in whatever year that was, had known he was becoming evidence.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," Charles said. "There's the way my dad thinks, which is take the sure thing, because the future is a wall and you should get what you can against it. And there's the way the study thinks, which is the future is more like a slope, and you can see where it's heading if you watch long enough. Those aren't the same future. If I sign, I'm betting on the wall. If I tear it up, I'm betting on the slope, on the idea that what I do at nineteen is a habit that compounds." He laughed, short and embarrassed. "Or maybe neither, and I'm just scared of both."

Mr. Eze slid a pen across the desk, not toward the form, just across, and left it in the middle. "I had a student once who deferred. He owns half of a company now. I had another who didn't, and he's the happiest man I know. I realize that's no help."

"It is, actually. It's honest." Charles took the pen. He held it over the signature line without touching down, watching his own hand as if it belonged to one of those other students, one of the futures in the slope that he couldn't see yet and never would, not fully, not until the years had already happened to him.

Gwenyth and Rim were walking toward the parking lot now, Gwenyth looking back at the building once.

Charles put the pen on the desk, folded the form in half, and stood. "Ask me again tomorrow," he said, and went out to meet them.

William had claimed the corner table by the periodicals an hour before closing, and he had spread his materials across it like evidence in a trial no one else knew was happening: the novel, a highlighted photocopy of chapter nine, and a half-finished essay that his teacher, Mr. Chowdhury, had returned with a single question penciled in the margin. "Who is telling you this, and why should you believe him?" The question had followed him out of the classroom and through the weekend, and now, on Sunday afternoon, he intended to answer it or at least to stop feeling ashamed of the B-minus.

The narrator in question was a man named Tulley, who spent the whole book insisting he had done nothing wrong. William had believed him on first read, which was the problem. In his essay he had written that the sister was cruel and the town was small-minded, exactly as Tulley reported them. Mr. Chowdhury's second note, further down the page, read: "Try rewriting one scene from the sister's point of view. Bring both versions on Tuesday."

Leonardo dropped into the chair opposite him with a stack of graphic novels and the particular energy of someone who wanted to be distracted. "You look morose," he said. "Chowdhury again?"

"He wants me to rewrite chapter nine from the sister's side. I don't get what that proves."

"Proves he can make you do work on a Sunday." Leonardo peeled open his first novel. "Francois is coming. He finished the book already, so he says."

Francois arrived ten minutes late, still in his soccer jacket, carrying nothing. He pulled the photocopy toward him without asking and read the margin notes upside down first, then right side up. "Tulley's a liar," he said. "Everyone in my class figured that out by chapter three."

"He's not a liar exactly," William said. "That's what I keep getting wrong. He lies to himself first. He leaves things out. He tells you what he saw and it's true, what he saw, but he only saw half of it." He heard his own voice speed up and slowed it. "That's the thing I can't put in the essay without it sounding like a book report."

Francois shrugged. "So a first-person narrator can only report what that one character sees, knows or chooses to say. A third-person omniscient narrator can reveal anyone's thoughts. Rewrite the scene third person and you'd get the sister's side and Tulley's, both."

William stared at him. "When did you become a pundit?"

"I read the handout. Twice. It's not the same as understanding it, which is why you're the one with the essay." He slid the photocopy back. "Do it. Five minutes. I want to see what happens."

So William wrote. He chose the scene where Tulley stands in the doorway while his sister packs a suitcase, and in the original Tulley notices only her coldness, her refusal to look at him, the loud shutting of drawers. William rewrote it from inside the sister's head, and the moment he did, the room filled with things Tulley had never mentioned: her hands shaking, her counting the money twice, her listening for the sound of the truck she already knew would not come. The coldness, seen from across the room, was fear. The drawers slammed because her fingers would not close softly.

"That's completely different," Leonardo said, reading over his arm. "Same room, same sister, different everything."

"And it's not even that she's more honest than he is," William said, writing fast now in the margin of his own essay. "She could be hiding things too. That's what omniscient buys you, both hides at once. First person, you get one set of eyes and one set of excuses." He looked up. "I don't know yet which version the author wants us to trust, or whether we're supposed to trust either. Maybe that's the actual question."

At the front desk, Mr. Chowdhury was checking in returns; William had not known the librarian worked Sundays until he glanced up and recognized him, and something in him decided not to waste the accident. He carried both versions of the scene to the desk and laid them side by side. "I rewrote it," he said. "First person and third. I'm still not sure what the book wants."

Mr. Chowdhury read neither page. He looked at the gap between them instead. "Bring the uncertainty with you on Tuesday," he said. "It's the most honest thing in your folder."

When William got home he wrote a short note and folded it into the front of his binder, addressed to himself, to be read before class: You believed Tulley the first time because he spoke first and he spoke in his own voice. Remember that the next voice you trust. Then he copied out the sister's paragraph one more time, because her hands were still shaking in it, and he wanted to make sure he had gotten that part exactly right. Outside his window the streetlight came on. He kept writing.

The video arrived at 7:42 in the morning, while Paige was still eating toast over the sink. A warehouse fire, a wall of smoke, a caption in urgent capitals: THIS IS HAPPENING IN OUR CITY RIGHT NOW. Antoine had sent it to the group chat with three exclamation points, and Daria had already forwarded it to her cousin, who worked two streets over from where the smoke was supposedly rising.

By second period, the lab smelled the way it always did, like warm plastic and the lemon wipes the janitor used on the keyboards. Ms. Aydín had posted a new page on the class site, and Paige, who had finished her slideshow early, clicked on it mostly out of boredom. The page was plain, almost ugly: white background, black text, no graphics. It described a method attributed to an educator named Mike Caulfield, four moves you ran through before you shared anything. Paige read it twice.

"SIFT," she said to Daria, who had slid into the seat beside her, phone out, thumb already hovering over the forward arrow. "It's called SIFT. Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their original context."

"You made that up," Daria said.

"It's on the page. Look." Paige turned the monitor, but Daria was already holding out her phone, the fire video playing again, the smoke billowing in its little rectangle. Paige felt the pull of it herself, the way the image insisted on its own importance. A video seemed to reify the caption, to make it solid, as though seeing the smoke proved the smoke was where the caption said it was. But that was a veneer, she thought, a convincing surface over a gap nobody was checking. She had learned that word in English and never had a use for it until now.

"Stop," she said, mostly to herself, and put Daria's phone face down on the desk. Then she typed a frame from the video into the search bar, the image of the smoke plume against a water tower, and waited while the results loaded. The plough of the loading icon, the hum of thirty machines. The results came back in a quiet rush: the same frame, posted two years earlier, on a regional news site, in a city four hundred miles away, in a story about a factory fire that had injured no one. Daria leaned in and read the date aloud, then read it again, as though the numbers might rearrange themselves.

"That's not our water tower," Daria said slowly. "Ours doesn't have the stripe." She was canny that way, quicker than most people gave her credit for; she had simply never aimed that quickness at a video before. She picked her phone up off the desk and, for a moment, held it flat in both hands like something she wasn't sure she trusted herself to carry. Then she opened the group chat and typed, slowly, correcting herself twice, that the fire was old and far away, and that her cousin should stay put.

Paige found better coverage next, out of some stubbornness she couldn't quite explain, scrolling until she confirmed that nothing was burning in their city that morning, that the local paper's live feed was all road closures and a bake sale. It felt good, the checking. It also felt smaller than she had expected. She still didn't know who had taken the old clip and rewritten the caption, or why, or whether the person had meant to frighten anyone at all. That part stayed uncertain, and she let it stay.

Antoine appeared at her shoulder between classes, sheepish, holding his phone like an apology. "So I basically spread a fake fire," he said. "Cool. Great morning for me."

"You did the internet version of yelling fire in a crowded theatre," Daria said, and even he laughed, and for a second the three of them stood in the doorway of the lab, ordinary and relieved, the crisis shrunk to something they could carry.

Then Daria's phone buzzed, and her face changed, went bright and urgent. "Oh my God," she said. "Have you seen this? A shark on the highway. Everyone's saying it's real." Her thumb was already moving toward the forward arrow.

Paige reached over and pressed the phone gently back down toward the table. "Stop," she said.

Ashley had told Albert she'd done this before, which was true in the sense that she had once melted chocolate in a microwave and poured it over strawberries. That was the version of herself she preferred, the girl who knew her way around a kitchen, and she held to it now as she chopped a bar of dark chocolate on the cutting board, the knife ringing against the wood. The kitchen smelled faintly of the onions her mother had sautéed that morning, and the window over the sink was open to a July evening so humid the air felt like a held breath. She was making truffles for Melodie's going-away party, or that was the official reason; the unofficial reason was that she wanted to be the kind of person who made truffles.

"You said you've tempered chocolate," Albert said from the stool by the counter, watching her heap the chopped pieces into a steel bowl.

"I said I'd made chocolate. Tempering is just melting it carefully." She said it with the confidence of someone who had watched one video that afternoon and half of another. The video had been munificent with detail: seed the melted chocolate with a handful of unmelted bits, stir until they dissolved, watch the thermometer slide down to a temperature she could no longer remember. She stirred with a spatula, and the chocolate went glossy and loose, and she felt a warm certainty that she had a talent for this, that talent was simply a matter of deciding you had it.

Albert, who was better at chemistry than at pretending, had brought his notebook. "The cocoa butter forms different crystals," he said. "Only one of them is stable. If you get it right, it sets shiny and it snaps."

"Snap," Ashley repeated, pleased. She pressed a knife tip into a cooled smear on parchment and it broke with a clean, high click, like a small lock opening. She was so delighted that she declared victory early, dropped the truffles onto a plate, and slid the plate into the refrigerator, because in her mind a fridge was where finished things went to become more finished.

They left the kitchen and sat on the porch with Melodie, who was leaving in eleven days for a college none of them had visited, and the talk turned to whether people became themselves or were always themselves, Melodie arguing for the second with the cheerfulness of someone quoting a podcast. Albert called it determinism, everything caused by what came before, and Melodie said that if that were true she'd like to litigate it, and they laughed, and Ashley laughed too, though privately she sided with the idea that you could decide yourself into a new shape and have it hold, the way chocolate supposedly held a shape if you were careful. This was, she would later admit, an analogy she had made up evidence for.

Forty minutes later she carried the plate out of the refrigerator to show them, and the plate was cold, and the porch air was thick, and by the time she reached the steps the truffles had gone strange. Their surfaces were dulled, dusted with a dry, gritty white coating, like frost that had decided to be sand. She touched one and her fingertip came away powdery. "It's ruined," she said, and then, because she was not ready for it to be ruined, "It's still fine underneath. It's just cosmetic."

Albert took the plate and turned it in the light of the porch bulb, frowning at the haze. He looked it up on his phone while Melodie picked up a truffle and rubbed it with her thumb, the bloom smearing like chalk. "Sugar bloom," Albert read. "A dry, gritty white coating. It happens when moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface and the sugar recrystallizes as it dries." He glanced from the cold plate to the wet air and back, and Ashley understood it all at once and without anyone explaining further: the cold chocolate, the humid night, the dew that must have settled on the surface in the minute it took her to cross the yard. She had done this. She had made the frost herself, with the fridge and the evening and her own impatience.

She sat down on the step between them and ate the truffle anyway, and it was bitter and a little gritty on the first bite and then, underneath, perfectly smooth. Melodie asked whether she'd try again tomorrow, temper it properly, and Ashley said maybe, or maybe she'd let the fridge keep its opinions to itself. But later, after they'd gone, she stood in the kitchen with the window closed and the leftover chocolate hardening in its bowl, and she dipped her finger and wrote her name on the parchment, M-E-L, then stopped, and left it there to set.

The radiator in the computer lab clanked like something being executed, and Alicia decided that was a good omen, or at least a dramatic one, which in her experience portended nothing whatsoever except another afternoon in room 214. She had signed up for coding club because Ms. Saleh had said, with a straight face, that building software was "the closest thing to architecture that doesn't require a hard hat," and Alicia had wanted to believe her.

Her project that week was a small Java class called Student, with private fields and getter methods, and a test file that proved it worked. She had written the fields, made them private, and written the getters, and then she had written the test, and then she had stared at the screen with the particular blankness of a person who has done all the assigned steps and understood none of them.

"Your student has a name but no soul," said Melinda, sliding into the next chair with her own laptop balanced on a stack of outdated Java textbooks that the school kept the way museums keep armor, as a reminder that everything becomes obsolescent eventually. "Also your getter for age returns a String. Why."

"Because I panicked," Alicia said. "The number was being weird."

Melinda leaned over and did something fast. "Watch. I'm changing how your class stores the data. Instead of a name field and an age field, I'm going to keep one array of values and get them out by position. Don't argue, just watch."

"That sounds like vandalism."

"It's science."

Melinda rewrote the guts of the class, deleted name and age entirely, and rebuilt the getters to pull from her array instead. Then she ran Alicia's test file. Alicia, who had braced for a wall of red errors the way you brace for a fire alarm, watched every test pass. Nothing broke. Not one line of the test code had changed, and not one test had failed.

Alicia sat back. "Okay, that's creepy. You deleted my fields and my tests don't care?"

"Encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods, so other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data," Melinda said, in the flat reciting voice she used for things she'd read off a poster in the hallway. Then, in her normal voice: "Which is why I can do this to you and you can't stop me."

"You could have led with that."

The sentence unlocked something older. Two years ago, before either of them had written a line of code, Alicia's mother had kept the family budget in a blue notebook, and when Alicia asked how much was left for shoes, her mother never handed over the notebook. She'd just say a number. Once Alicia had tried to read it directly, and her mother had covered the page with her hand and said, "You don't need my columns, you need my answer." Alicia had thought it was about privacy, control, the general parental allergy to being known. Now she understood it had also been a kindness. The answer stayed true even when her mother refinanced something and moved all the numbers to a spreadsheet. The rest of the family had gone on asking the same question and getting the same answer, never once seeing the machinery underneath. She said none of this to Melinda, though she did think, briefly and with pleasure, that her mother had been writing Java since before Java existed.

Ms. Saleh circulated with a mug that said WORLD'S ADEQUATE DEBUGGER, which she claimed she'd bought herself. She looked at Alicia's screen, at the array where fields used to be, and raised one eyebrow in a way that Alicia chose to interpret as approval.

"You let Melinda refactor you," Ms. Saleh said.

"She did it without asking."

"That's how you find out if your walls are real," Ms. Saleh said, and moved on before it could become a lesson, which Alicia appreciated.

That night Alicia opened her messages and found a note from Corey, who had missed club for a dentist appointment and wanted to know what he'd missed. She typed it as a message because Corey insisted that anything important be sent to him in writing, so he could reread it at two in the morning when his brain worked.

COREY: what happened at club, did anything good happen, was there drama

ALICIA: melinda deleted my fields and my tests still passed

COREY: that doesn't sound good

ALICIA: it is actually the whole point. other code talks to the getters, not to the data. so the inside can change and the outside doesn't care. I changed my mind about my mom a little

COREY: your mom was there?

ALICIA: no. long story. I'll explain tomorrow. bring snacks

COREY: always

She closed the laptop and thought about what she still didn't know, which was a lot, and felt, for once, fine about it. The test passing didn't mean her design was good, only that her walls held against one particular act of vandalism. Whether the walls were the right walls was a different question, one she'd have to answer by building more classes and letting more people break them.

The next afternoon Corey arrived with a bag of pretzels and an idea for a class of his own, and Alicia pulled her chair around so they could share one screen, and Melinda cracked her knuckles over the keyboard like a safecracker in a movie.

"Go ahead," Alicia said. "Try to break it."

The map on the wall of Mr. Tse's classroom showed the Atlantic as a lattice of arrows, red ones curling up the western edge and blue ones crawling south along the eastern shore. Grace copied them into her notebook before the bell finished ringing, because Mr. Tse had said on Monday that whoever could explain the arrows by Friday would present at the regional science symposium, and the symposium was in a hotel with a pool, and Grace had never stayed in a hotel with a pool.

She spread her copy out on the cafeteria table at lunch. "I think I have it," she said. "The red ones move fast. Look how long they are, and they're red, like speed, like heat from friction." She tapped the wide scarlet arrow leaving the Gulf. "So warm water races north, and that's why the red one reaches up past us."

Melody leaned over the notebook with her sandwich halfway to her mouth. Gregoire pulled the page closer, frowning. "The blue one off Greenland is long too," he said. "So the cold water races south at the same speed? Then what does the colour do?"

The question sat on the table between them. Grace looked at her own arrows and felt the small vertigo of a floor tilting. "Maybe length is speed," she said slowly, "and colour is something else."

"Colour is something else," Gregoire repeated, testing the sentence the way you test ice before stepping on it. He was the one who had first suggested red meant fast, two days ago, standing at the wall map with his finger on the Labrador coast, and Grace had been grateful for the theory because it catalyzed her whole understanding, had taken the vague dread of Friday and turned it into a plan.

After school she went back to the classroom, where Mr. Tse was stacking chairs. "I won't tell you," he said, which was his way of telling her nothing was broken yet. "But there's a reason the mapmakers gave you two variables instead of one." He left her alone with the wall.

She stood at the map for a long time, tracing arrows with her eyes instead of her finger because the laminated surface had a notice about fingerprints. The red arrows began in the tropics and ended off Norway. The blue arrows began in the Arctic and ended near Africa. She thought of the substrate of the map, the flat blue paper standing in for an ocean that was anything but flat, and thought about what a cartographer wants a sailor or a student to know at a glance. Not how fast. What temperature. She said it aloud to the empty room, quietly. "Warm currents are red arrows, cold currents are blue arrows." The colours were temperature, and she had been reading them as speed, and Gregoire had handed her the mistake in the first place, which meant she could hand it back.

On Thursday she found him at his locker. "I was wrong," she said. "It's not speed at all. Red is warm water, blue is cold. The Gulf Stream is warm, it carries heat north, and that's what keeps northern Europe milder than places at the same latitude. The arrows are temperature." She watched him take it in, watched the flicker of annoyance that precedes a person revising themselves in public. "So my long fast arrow," he said. "Is slow." He laughed, short and rueful. "My whole theory." She nodded, and did not say that his wrong theory had been the substrate her right one grew on, because that would have been generous in a way that cost her something, some share of the discovery she was not ready to surrender.

Melody came with her to watch the Friday presentation, and Mr. Tse signed the symposium form in blue ink that looked, on the page, exactly like cold water. In the hotel that weekend Grace stood at the edge of the pool at nine at night, alone, with the key card in the pocket of her robe. She had explained the map to forty strangers and answered every question, and one question still stuck in her like a splinter she couldn't find: how something as slow and scattered as a current could carry enough heat to change the climate of a whole continent, and whether the maps, with their clean red certainty, were telling her the truth or a convenient version of it. She stepped down into the shallow end, where the water was warm because the hotel kept it that way, and she stayed near the steps.

The video arrived at 9:14 on a Tuesday morning, while Naomi was still at her grandmother's kitchen table finishing toast that had gone cold. Brendan had sent it to the group chat with a single line: this is happening two streets from your grandma's place. The clip showed a flooded intersection, a man clinging to a street sign, brown water pulling a mailbox sideways. Someone behind the camera was shouting in a language Naomi couldn't place. Her grandmother's tap dripped into the sink, and outside the window the street was dry enough to crack.

She watched it three times. The third time she noticed the quality of the light, and after that she couldn't stop noticing it, the way you can't stop feeling a tooth once the dentist names it. It was summer light in the video, hard and high. It was November here. She typed a reply, deleted it, and typed another. Jasmine had already sent three fire emojis and the word SHARE THIS. Naomi put the phone face down on the oilcloth and picked up her grandmother's percolator to refill her cup, and realized she was doing the thing she always did, forwarding first and wondering later, and that she had no idea how to reverse the order.

"I want to check something before I send it," she said. Her grandmother was at the stove, coaxing a second pot of coffee out of grounds that had already given everything they had. "Check it how?" "I don't know yet," Naomi said, and it felt strange and clean to say that out loud.

The following June, she had sat on this same porch with her grandfather while he read the paper, and she remembered him turning a page and pausing over a photograph. "The paper says this was yesterday," he had told her, tapping the caption with one arthritic finger. "But the soldier's coat is wrong for the year they claim." She had been sixteen and had laughed a little, kindly, at how long it took him. Now she wished she had asked what he did next, whether he wrote a letter, whether he simply set the paper down and let the wrongness sit in his lap. He was gone by spring, and the porch chair he used had been left where it was, wicker gone silver.

She took the phone back out. She had heard people talk about reverse image searches, the way you hear about a tool that other, more organized people use. She copied the video's link and pasted it into the search bar, and the engine returned nothing useful, a shrug of blue links about file types and compression. She tried another engine. Nothing. She sat with the sour feeling that the internet had made a promise and quietly withdrawn it, and it would have been easy to give up there, easy to write "not sure, be careful" and let the fire emojis burn on without her.

Then she thought about frames. A video was only pictures in a row, and pictures were what the engines searched. She dragged the little progress bar to the moment the mailbox tipped, paused it, took a screenshot. The frame was blurry with motion, so she moved back a second, paused again, screenshotted again, until she had four stills from the clip saved to her camera roll. She uploaded the clearest one. The results loaded slowly over her grandmother's ancient router, the page rebuilding itself line by line, and then there they were: the same intersection, the same shouting man, dated three summers ago, from a storm in a country an ocean away, embedded in a local news article with a headline in that language she couldn't place.

"Grandma," she said. "Your internet is a crime scene, but it worked." Her grandmother brought two cups over and sat down, and Naomi showed her the video and then the article, side by side. "You can't search a video like this," she said. "You screenshot the frames and search those." Her grandmother squinted at the small screen, held it at arm's length, and nodded the way she nodded at bank statements. "So Brendan is wrong," she said. "Or Brendan was fooled," Naomi said, and felt the difference between those two sentences sit down at the table with them.

She typed to the chat: this is real, but it's from three years ago, not here, link below. Then she added, if you want to check one, this is how I did it, and pasted the screenshots too. There was a long silence, the kind where you can watch the typing dots appear and vanish. She understood, waiting, that she hadn't disabused anyone of anything; she had only caught one clip, one morning, and that the next one would arrive tomorrow, and that she would feel the same visceral pull to share first, the certainty flooding her faster than any argument could follow. Whether she would stop and screenshot again was not a habit yet, only a memory of having done it once. But once was a place to stand. Her grandmother refilled her cup without asking, and Jasmine's reply came through at last: wait, you can do that with any video?

Naomi laughed, and outside the dry street lay quiet under the November sky, and she started typing.

The classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and Dominic had decided, on balance, that he was going to be excellent at this. He had read four articles on interviewing the night before, or possibly three, and he had retained all of the important ones, or the important parts of the important ones, which amounted to the same thing. Ms. Visser had arranged the desks into a interviewing setup at the front, one chair behind the other, a legal pad on the desk to make it official. Molly went first. She sat with her shoulders squared and said she was applying at the garden centre because she genuinely valued horticulture, which was a lie, since Dominic had watched her kill a cactus in biology by forgetting it existed. Her answer was fluent anyway. It occurred to him that fluent lying might be a skill, and that he had it too, though he had never needed to test it.

When her turn ended she came back down the aisle and sat beside him and did not gesticulate the way she usually did when telling a story, hands carving the air, but folded them in her lap as though conserving energy for the next round. "He's going to say tell me about yourself," she said. "He meaning Ms. Visser. She said it to Johan, she said it to me. Have yours ready."

Dominic did have his ready. He had rehearsed it in the shower, and in the mirror, and once quietly during chemistry, which Mr. Whatever-his-name-was had generously overlooked. He was, if anything, overprepared, an autodidact of the job interview, self-taught out of necessity since his father's advice had consisted entirely of "don't be weird."

Johan leaned across the aisle, holding a folded printout like evidence. "My grandfather made me practise handshakes at Easter dinner," he said. "Two hours. My arm still hurts. He's obsessed."

"With handshakes," Molly said.

"With one study. He keeps the printout in his wallet." Johan unfolded the page and flattened it on Dominic's desk. "A 2000 study led by a psychologist named William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions. That's it, that's the whole thing. He's had it in there since before I was born, I think."

"That's the one I read," Dominic said, which was almost true. He had read something about handshakes, and he remembered it involving eye contact and a different decade, but the shape of it was familiar, and the shape of a thing was most of the thing. "Firm handshake, strong eye contact, same principle."

"They're not the same principle," Johan said mildly. "The study's about handshakes."

Dominic waved this off, because the interview was starting, and because he had a system. Ms. Visser called his name.
